II.
Purpose of Testimony
5 
Q.
What is the purpose of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel’s
6 
testimony?
7 
A.
The purpose of the Panel’s testimony is to provide a forecast of the capital
8 
investments of the Company for the twelve-month period ending March 31,
9 
2021 (“Rate Year”), and the three subsequent twelve-month periods ending
10 
March 31, 2022 (“Data Year 1”), March 31, 2023 (“Data Year 2”), and March
11 
31, 2024 (“Data Year 3”) (Data Year 1, Data Year 2, and Data Year 3 are
12 
collectively referred to as the “Data Years”).  The Panel also presents a forecast
13 
for the fifteen-month period (“Gap Period”) between December 31, 2018,
14 
which is the end of the Company’s Historic Test Year, and the beginning of the
15 
Rate Year.
16 
17 
The Panel discusses direct capital expenditures that will (i) increase the safety 
18 
and reliability of the Company’s gas network, (ii) modernize the Company’s 
19 
gas transmission and distribution infrastructure to reduce emissions while 
20 
continuing to meet customer needs, and (iii) enhance resiliency and the 
21 
4236


--- Page 40 ---
Page 7 of 120 
Company’s ability to respond to future weather events.  The Panel will also 
1 
discuss the Company’s practices and policies for maximizing the efficiency of 
2 
its capital delivery program from planning and budgeting through the 
3 
completion of construction.    
4 
5 
The Panel’s testimony provides an overview of the significant projects in the 
6 
Company’s capital plan, including retirement of leak prone pipe (“LPP”) and 
7 
new safety programs to identify and address system risks.  The Panel’s 
8 
testimony also presents an overview of the Company’s pipeline integrity and 
9 
reliability programs that will improve the overall safety and reliability of the 
10 
Company’s gas system, and will also address recently enacted, as well as 
11 
pending, pipeline safety regulations administered by the U.S. Department of 
12 
Transportation 
(“DOT”), 
Pipeline 
and 
Hazardous 
Materials 
Safety 
13 
Administration (“PHMSA”).  The Panel discusses the Company’s plans and 
14 
infrastructure projects necessary to ensure that the Company can reliably serve 
15 
its existing customers as well as forecast demand for new customer connections 
16 
within the Company’s operating territory. 
17 
18 
The Panel also presents the Company’s indirect capital investments, including 
19 
supply chain, inventory management/investment recovery (“IM/IR”), and fleet 
20 
investments.  The Company is also proposing significant investments in 
21 
4237


--- Page 41 ---
Page 8 of 120 
facilities during the Rate Year and Data Years that are necessary to: support the 
1 
Company’s O&M and gas safety programs; make needed upgrades to aging 
2 
facilities; and create more modern and efficient customer support and employee 
3 
work spaces.   
4

5

safety enhancements, and deployment of non-pipeline alternatives.  While

17 
developing its capital and O&M plans, the Company balanced the need for 
18

8 
A.
Several developments have required that KEDNY and other natural gas 
9 
distribution utilities increase their annual capital expenditures.  Notably, 
10 
pipeline safety incidents, such as the tragic events in San Bruno, California, 
11 
Allentown, Pennsylvania, East Harlem, New York, and the more recent incident 
12 
in Merrimack Valley, Massachusetts, have appropriately increased focus on 
13 
pipeline safety and the need to carefully monitor and replace aging pipeline 
14 
infrastructure.  Weather events, such as Superstorm Sandy and the Polar Vortex, 
15 
and the expectation that similar events will continue to occur, require the 
16 
Company to find ways to protect its facilities from severe weather.   
17 
18 
4243


--- Page 47 ---
Page 14 of 120 
In response to these events, the industry has adopted new safety requirements 
1 
and is implementing best practices to modernize and protect gas facilities.  For 
2 
example, since the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, (i) new Commission 
3 
safety regulations and directives now require additional safety inspections of 
4 
inside service lines and plastic fusions; (ii) PHMSA is implementing new safety 
5 
requirements related to transmission system integrity management and 
6

7 
considering a bill that would require licensed professional engineers (“PEs”) to 
8 
review and certify gas facility design plans.  The Commission and utility 
9 
industry review of recent incidents has also resulted in recommendations for 
10 
safety best practices, including overpressure protection improvements and 
11 
enhanced contractor oversight.  These mandated and recommended 
12 
improvements require significant additional investments and compliance 
13 
resources.

16 
Q.
What explains the significant increases reflected in the investment plan?  
17 
A.
The Company’s investment plan reflects increases in both the scope of work 
18 
(units) and the costs elements to perform this work (unit costs).  As discussed 
19 
above, there are several factors that are collectively increasing the size of the 
20 
Company’s investment plan over the next several years, including incremental 
21 
4246


--- Page 50 ---
Page 17 of 120 
work driven by federal and state regulatory mandates and the need to upgrade 
1 
aged infrastructure and replace dated facilities.  At the same time, the Company 
2 
is experiencing increasing unit costs resulting from new work requirements and 
3 
enhanced safety practices, and the rising costs of materials and contractors, in 
4 
part due to increasing demands for these resources across the industry  
5 
6 
Indeed, a primary driver of increases in the capital plan is significantly higher 
7 
unit costs for main installation work across multiple mandated programs, 
8 
including the proactive and reactive main replacement, customer connections, 
9 
corrosion, and city/state construction (“CSC”) programs.  The unit cost 
10 
increases are explained in more detail, below, and unit cost component 
11 
increases for main replacement are shown on Exhibit __ (GIOP-2).   
12 
13 
Another driver of the capital investment plan is a significant increase in the 
14 
volume of work in the Company’s CSC program, which involves the relocation 
15 
and/or protection of gas facilities that conflict with municipal public works 
16 
projects.  As described in detail below, the CSC program scope is continuing to 
17 
grow as New York City is investing billions of dollars to improve its water and 
18 
sewer systems.  As a result of the sharp increase in scope and scale of the City’s 
19 
public works programs, the CSC program now represents more than a third of 
20 
4247


--- Page 51 ---
Page 18 of 120 
the Company’s total capital investment plan, and the work requirements and 
1 
timing of this program are not within the Company’s control. 
2 
3 
Q.
What factors are contributing to the Company’s unit cost increases?   
4 
A.
Exhibit __ (GIOP- 2) shows the components that have contributed to the main 
5 
installation unit cost increase.  The primary source of increased costs is New 
6 
York City’s new restoration and paving requirements that became effective in 
7 
April 2017.  Specifically, changes to Highway Rules §§ 2-01 through 2-09, 2-
8 
11 through 2-14, and 2-20 (“Paving Rules”) now require significantly more 
9 
restoration work, including: 
10 
•
Increasing the size of the area that must be re-paved following an
11 
excavation.  Under the new Paving Rules, the final restoration area is based
12 
on the largest dimension of the excavation.  Under the prior regulations,
13 
KEDNY was authorized to pave the area of individual bell holes.  The
14 
Paving Rules require KEDNY to pave the bell holes in addition to the area
15 
in between those holes.  In some cases, this requirement doubles or triples
16 
the area needing to be repaved.
17 
•
Requiring that base material be replaced in kind or better, which means that
18 
concrete roadways must be replaced with concrete instead of the less
19 
expensive binder material that was previously utilized.  In that regard,
20 
approximately 65 percent of New York City streets are concrete; and
21 
4248


--- Page 52 ---
Page 19 of 120 
•
Requiring more saw cutting of roadway excavations instead of more
1 
efficient and cost-effective jackhammering.
2 
The Historic Test Year was the first full year in which these new paving costs 
3 
were effective, during which the Company performed tens of thousands of 
4 
individual paving jobs in the City at a considerably increased cost.  Indeed, in 
5 
calendar year (“CY”) 2017 to CY 2018, paving restoration costs accounted for 
6 
approximately 46 percent ($526) of the total main replacement unit cost 
7 
($1,147).   
8 
9 
Other factors contributing to an increase in the Company’s main replacement 
10 
unit cost, as shown on Exhibit __ (GIOP-2), include: 
11 
•
Higher base labor (contractor costs): recently renegotiated long-term
12 
contractor agreements resulted in higher base labor contractor costs
13 
•
Mains Size: work scope includes more large-diameter main at higher
14 
replacement costs
15 
•
Increased time and materials (“T&M”): increasingly restrictive
16 
municipal stipulations that limit work time in streets and increasing
17 
costs to comply with arborist regulations (protection of trees on
18 
sidewalks proximate to work sites)

ii.
Gas Safety Integrity Management and Integrity Verification:  IMP
8 
and IVP Programs
9 
Q.
What is the Company’s IMP? 
10 
A.
The Company’s transmission pipeline IMP is a safety program mandated by the 
11 
Pipeline Safety Improvement Act of 2002 and corresponding DOT regulations.  
12 
The IMP identifies and addresses potential issues affecting the physical 
13 
soundness of Company facilities before they become safety or performance 
14 
issues.  The Company conducts baseline and periodic reassessments of 
15 
transmission facilities to identify and evaluate potential threats to “Covered 
16 
Segments” of pipelines, i.e., transmission pipelines that could affect High 
17 
Consequence Areas (areas where a pipeline failure could have significant 
18 
adverse consequences), as well as remediation of significant defects discovered 
19 
during such assessments.  In regions of the United States where older gas 
20 
4264


--- Page 68 ---
Page 35 of 120 
distribution systems are common, IMPs have become a key component of gas 
1 
pipeline safety through improving pipeline integrity.   
2 
3 
Q.
Please describe the IMP capital investments. 
4 
A.
Currently, IMP assessments may be accomplished through either external 
5 
corrosion direct assessment (“ECDA”) or in-line inspection (“ILI”) technology, 
6 
which uses a robotic device known as a “pig” to evaluate the condition of the 
7 
inside of the pipeline.  ILI is considered superior to ECDA because of the ability 
8 
to identify condition problems originating internally.  IMP investments are 
9 
necessary to: (i) support in-line inspections (e.g., installation of pig launchers 
10 
and receivers, and pipe reconfiguration/replacement), and (ii) to resolve issues 
11 
discovered during pipeline inspections conducted through either method.   
12 
13 
The construction activities associated with these expenditures involve the 
14 
installation of “hot tap” fittings, the reconfiguration of such fittings to allow ILI 
15 
passage, the construction of access points to allow tethered in-line inspection 
16 
and, in some cases, the replacement of pipeline segments. 
17 
18 
4265


--- Page 69 ---
Page 36 of 120 
Q.
Please describe the IMP capital investment needs for the Rate Year and
1 
Data Years.
2 
Currently, 21 percent of the Company’s DOT pipeline is ILI enabled, increased
3 
from 17 percent when the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases was filed.
4 
Over the long term, the Company’s plan is to reach 80 percent ILI enablement
5 
of the Company’s DOT piping.  The Company’s IMP capital investments in the
6 
Rate Year and Data Years will drive toward this goal and will significantly
7 
improve the Company’s ability to identify integrity issues.
8

Q.
How are the IMP workplan and associated IMP capital investment forecast 
10 
determined?  
11 
A.
The workplan began in 2002 based on initial assessments using the Company’s 
12 
existing risk model.  Segments were prioritized for ILI enablement over a multi-
13 
year workplan based on a combination of their risk score and other relevant 
14 
factors, such as facility characteristics or geography, to determine what work to 
15 
do when.  Some segments must be re-assessed in certain years according to 
16 
when they were initially assessed.  The workplan is updated annually and as 
17 
required assessments are completed.  Additionally, ILI projects typically 
18 
consist of two years of design and procurement work followed by construction 
19 
in the third year.   
20 
21 
4266

5

11 
A.

12

16

17

18 
segments; (ii) mandating additional pressure testing or replacement for 
19 
pipelines without adequate pressure test records; and (iii) requiring operators 
20 
who lack certain records to establish material properties using approved 
21 
4268

1

2 
operators to perform a detailed threat and risk analysis that includes a records 
3 
review of their systems.   
4 
5 
The Company’s IVP program began in 2011 and includes thorough record 
6 
reviews, pipeline replacement, and retirement of non-essential pipeline 
7

8

CSC
6 
Q.
Please describe what is included in the CSC Program. 
7 
A.
The CSC Program is a mandated program that represents 34 percent of 
8 
KEDNY’s direct capital investment plan in the Rate Year.  This program 
9 
consists of construction work performed to accommodate third-party, 
10 
municipal construction activity that could impact the integrity of the 
11 
Company’s natural gas facilities.  Typical third-party construction activities that 
12 
impact gas facilities include work on water, sewer, and drainage infrastructure, 
13 
street reconstruction, road realignment, and bridge replacement.  State 
14 
regulations and Company procedures require the replacement of eight inch and 
15 
smaller cast iron gas mains if roadway or underground construction is being 
16 
performed in such a way that would impact the integrity of the Company’s 
17 
mains.  Non-cast iron gas mains (i.e., steel and plastic) are not subject to the 
18 
same replacement regulations and are typically supported and protected if not 
19 
in direct conflict with third-party construction.  Direct conflicts are addressed 
20 
through relocation regardless of material type.   
21 
4271


--- Page 75 ---
Page 42 of 120 
1

2

3

4 
increase in the level of municipal construction activity, as Superstorm Sandy 
5 
and recent gas incidents focused attention on the state of municipal 
6 
infrastructure.  Going forward, New York City will invest billions of dollars to 
7 
upgrade its infrastructure, and many of these projects will directly impact 
8 
KEDNY’s gas system.  Thus, the CSC Program is one of the largest programs 
9 
in the mandated category in terms of costs.  The forecast cost for this program 
10

in more detail below.

Q.

9

16

17 
from the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, as well as the Company’s 
18 
proposals toward decarbonizing the gas network (e.g., a new green gas tariff 
19 
offering), as discussed in the Future of Heat Panel’s testimony.

A. Capital Planning, Budgeting, and Sanctioning Process
15 
Q.
Please describe the annual development of the Company’s capital plan. 
16 
Each year, the Company develops a ten-year capital plan to achieve its 
17 
performance objectives of delivering safe and reliable service.  Investment 
18 
Planning compiles proposed spending for programs and individual capital 
19 
projects.  Programs and projects are categorized into one of four spending 
20 
4288


--- Page 92 ---
Page 59 of 120 
rationales (Mandated, Customer Connections, Reliability, and Non-
1 
Infrastructure).   
2 
3 
The Company currently uses a tool, C55 (known internally as “Copperleaf”), 
4 
for the prioritization and optimization of capital investments through a risk 
5 
scoring and prioritization methodology.  This tool uses criteria aligned to a 
6 
common scale to compare dissimilar inputs (e.g., financial and non-financial 
7 
inputs) to determine the set of investments, alternatives, and the timing of 
8 
projects that have the highest potential value.  
9 
10 
After the Companies rank the investments in C55, meetings are scheduled with 
11 
budget sponsors to review value models, project rankings, and various scenarios 
12 
produced through the optimization of investments to meet capital planning 
13 
targets.  Once plan targets have been approved by the Gas Business Unit, they 
14 
are submitted to Finance for review. 
15 
16 
In late fall, the capital plan is reviewed by the New York Jurisdictional 
17 
President (Company Witness John Bruckner) and the Vice President, Finance, 
18 
New York (Company Witness David Doxsee).  The New York Jurisdictional 
19 
President reviews the overall customer, service quality, and financial impacts 
20 
4289


--- Page 93 ---
Page 60 of 120 
of the investment plan and may request changes to the level or mix of 
1 
investments.   
2 
3 
In early winter, the capital plan is presented to the National Grid USA Board of 
4 
Directors and the National Grid plc Executive Committee and, in early spring, 
5 
the capital portfolio is presented to the National Grid plc Board of Directors for 
6 
review and approval.   
7 
8 
Q.
Are there additional approvals needed before a project in the annual 
9 
capital plan may proceed? 
10 
A.
Yes.  Aside from the capital planning and budgeting process, specific delegation 
11 
of authority (“DOA”) approval must be obtained for any project in the ten-year 
12 
capital plan to proceed.  This process includes the sanctioning documentation 
13 
and review for projects over $1 million and other levels of review for smaller 
14 
projects.  Presently, all projects greater than $1 million require some level of 
15 
sanctioning documentation and review.  The U.S. Sanctioning Committee 
16 
(“USSC”) was established by the National Grid USA Board of Directors 
17 
specifically for this purpose.  Projects between $8 million and $25 million are 
18 
reviewed and approved by the USSC.  Projects between $25 million to $203 
19 
million are reviewed by the USSC and then are forwarded to a Senior Executive 
20 
Sanctioning Committee (“SESC”) for review and approval.  For projects 
21 
4290


--- Page 94 ---
Page 61 of 120 
between $1 million and $8 million, the USSC has delegated review to an 
1 
informal committee led by the Investment Planning group and including, but 
2 
not limited to, managers and directors from the Regulatory, Estimating, Asset 
3 
Management, and Procurement groups.  The committee reviews and finalizes 
4 
sanctioning papers for these projects at a weekly meeting, and the committee 
5 
then forwards the final sanction documents to the executive sponsor of the 
6 
project for approval and signature.  Projects less than $1 million do not require 
7 
sanctioning and are approved through a supervisory delegation of authority 
8 
hierarchy based on certain established thresholds.   
9 
10 
Q.
Please explain the difference between the DOA review and approval 
11 
(sanctioning) process and the approved five-year capital plan used to 
12 
forecast the Rate Year and Data Years. 
13 
A.
 The timing of the sanctioning process is not aligned with the capital planning 
14 
process used to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years for purposes of the rate 
15 
filing.  As described above, the Company develops a long-term investment plan 
16 
that is used as the basis for the forecast for the Rate Year and Data Year 
17 
proposals.  Project sanctioning, however, normally occurs immediately prior to 
18 
the FY for which the investment is planned.  For example, the FY 2020 capital 
19 
plan will be formally sanctioned in early 2019.  Thus, the Company’s currently-
20 
4291


--- Page 95 ---
Page 62 of 120 
sanctioned or partially-sanctioned projects do not yet represent the full capital 
1 
forecast proposed in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
2 
3 
Q.
Please describe how the Company’s DIMP impacts its capital investment 
4 
planning. 
5 
A.
The DIMP involves a risk-based assessment of the Company’s distribution 
6 
system to identify threats in seven categories: corrosion, natural forces, 
7 
excavation damage, other outside force damage, material and weld failure, 
8 
equipment failure/malfunction and inappropriate operation.  The DIMP 
9 
requires evaluation and prioritization of the risks that these threats pose, and the 
10 
implementation of measures to address the highest risks with an emphasis on 
11 
leak management, enhanced damage prevention, operator qualification to 
12 
reduce human error and system replacement.  Consistent with the DIMP, the 
13 
Company prioritizes asset replacements in its investment plan based on a risk 
14 
ranking that considers, among other things, leak repair history, types of leak, 
15 
pipe material, surrounding geography, segment length, nearby construction 
16 
activity, field conditions, customer issues, open leaks and engineering 
17 
judgment.  The risk ranking factors are carefully designed to consider known 
18 
differences in the performance of asset subclasses, extensive experience with 
19 
asset failures, current performance data for the asset subclasses for various 
20 
4292


--- Page 96 ---
Page 63 of 120 
threat categories, and subject matter experts’ analysis and opinions on the future 
1 
performance of the assets. 
2

Customer Connection programs are designed to support forecast customer

21 
4293

way.  Customer Connection programs involve the installation of new mains,

Q.
Please describe the Gas System Reinforcement Program in the Customer 
16 
Connections category of spending. 
17 
A.
The Gas System Reinforcements Program contains projects intended to ensure 
18 
that minimum system pressures are maintained throughout the gas network 
19 
during periods of peak demand.  The Company models peak demand based on 
20 
the sendout forecasts developed by Analytics, Modeling and Forecasting 
21 
4295


--- Page 99 ---
Page 66 of 120 
(Company Witness Theodore Poe).  As a result of demand for gas usage in its 
1 
service territory, KEDNY has determined that it is necessary to complete a 
2 
number of projects to ensure its ability to meet peak requirements.  These 
3 
reinforcement projects are essential to ensure the Company can continue to 
4 
serve growing gas usage load.  Without such reinforcements, the Company 
5 
estimates that more than 42,000 existing customers could experience loss of 
6 
service.    
7 
8 
KEDNY experienced new records for sendouts during the last two winter 
9 
heating seasons.  During the winter of 2017/2018, KEDNY recorded four of its 
10 
top ten sendout records, including a firm load record of 1,417,131, dekatherms 
11 
on January 6, 2018, when the average temperature was eight degrees Fahrenheit.  
12 
During the winter of 2018/2019, KEDNY recorded two of its top ten sendout 
13 
records, including a second highest firm load of 1387,550 dekatherms on 
14 
January 21, 2019 when the average temperature was thirteen degrees Fahrenheit.  
15 
16 
As is discussed in Section VII, below, and in the testimony of Company Witness 
17 
Elizabeth A. Arangio, additional capacity expected from Williams’ NESE 
18 
project is critical to meeting this level of increasing demand.  Moreover, the 
19 
recent growth in peak sendout underscores the need to ensure that the 
20 
4296


--- Page 100 ---
Page 67 of 120 
Company’s gas distribution facilities are capable of maintaining minimum 
1 
system design pressures during periods of peak demand.     
2 
3 
Q.
Please provide examples of System Reinforcement projects. 
4 
A.
Examples of System Reinforcement projects include: 
5 
•
Replacing undersized mains with larger diameter mains.  LPP is
6 
targeted whenever practical during this work.
7 
•
Looping or connecting system endpoints by installing new main.
8 
•
System pressure uprates (e.g., 15 pounds per square inch (“psi”) to 60
9 
psi).
10 
•
Installing new district regulators and replacing existing undersized
11 
district regulators.
12 
•
Transferring existing low-pressure customers to an adjacent high-
13 
pressure main (i.e., load shedding).
14 
15 
Q.
What explains the fluctuation in the Gas System Reinforcement forecast 
16 
from year-to-year?

6

15

16 
issues and allow quick pinpointing of the source.  
17 
18

19

20 
to maintain pipeline safety and integrity.”  These rules indicate that Operators 
21 
4312

1

--- Page 117 ---
Page 84 of 120

8

9

10 
to the public and property.

Q.
What are the benefits and costs of this program?      
10 
A.
 The remote shutoff valves add a layer of protection for services that are 
11

12

13 
impacts of recent severe storms (i.e., Superstorm Sandy and Hurricane Irene) 
14

15 
greater protection from future storms.  These valves will operate on a fixed

17 
Automated valves stop the flow of gas as soon as flooding is detected.  This 
18 
will prevent regulator over-pressurization and stop gas from flowing to 
19 
premises with damaged equipment and/or extinguished pilot lights, mitigating 
20 
the risk of a potential incident.  Automated valves also provide a real-time count 
21 
4316


--- Page 120 ---
Page 87 of 120 
of services impacted by flooding to inform the Company’s storm response 
1 
about the resources needed to restore the affected customers expeditiously.  
2 
Lastly, in areas where flooding prevents physical access to valves and 
3 
regulators, remote shut-off valves will allow the Company to interrupt only 
4 
those services impacted by flooding, which could spare entire neighborhoods 
5 
or larger areas from losing gas service because of access issues.  Installation of 
6 
the communication networks through which the valves operate can also be 
7 
leveraged in the future for additional smart devices, such as methane detectors 
8 
that are being developed.

The Company is proposing to ramp-up the program in FY 2020 and the Rate

valves in the Rate Year, with the bulk of the communications network systems 
13 
in the Rate Year as well.  The Company intends to install approximately 8,000 
14 
valves per year in each of the Data Years.  Program costs in the Rate Year are 
15 
approximately $7.4 million in the Rate Year.

Q.
Please describe the Company’s LNG programs. 
5 
A.
KEDNY maintains on-system supply through its LNG facility at the Greenpoint 
6 
LNG Plant.  This plant is a critical component of KEDNY’s gas supply portfolio 
7 
and gas operating network and plays a critical role in meeting peak demand. 
8 
The Greenpoint LNG Plant is capable of supplying 290 million cubic feet of 
9 
gas per day, which is critical for meeting KEDNY’s peak day demand.  
10 
Refilling the tanks is accomplished through liquefaction during the summer 
11 
period when gas supplies are available and less expensive.  The liquefaction 
12 
system can refill at a rate of about 7 to 8.5 million cubic feet of gas per day and 
13 
it takes between 150 and 200 days to refill both tanks.  The Greenpoint LNG 
14 
Plant is a cost-effective means of meeting peak demand, because gas is liquified 
15 
during the summer months when prices are lower and stored for use in the 
16 
winter during peak demand conditions.  KEDNY’s various LNG capital 
17 
programs are necessary to ensure the continued safe, reliable operation of the 
18 
Greenpoint LNG Plant.

Q.
What is included in the Company’s Learning and Development (“L&D”) 
1 
Materials Tools and Equipment Program? 
2 
A.
Historically, L&D has a limited stock of tools for use in training and has relied 
3 
upon tools borrowed from Field Operations to supplement its supply and 
4 
conduct required training of in-house and contractor employees.  With 
5 
workload and training requirements increasing, Field Operations can no longer 
6 
spare tools and equipment sufficient for training purposes, and the limited stock 
7 
of available tools is beginning to deteriorate.  The proposed L&D Materials 
8 
Tools and Equipment Program will purchase new tools and equipment for 
9 
training purposes.  The program will follow an innovative approach whereby 
10 
the new tools will be used for training during the annual training sessions at the 
11 
beginning of each year, and then the new tools will be sent into the field for use 
12 
by the newly-trained employees.  Following annual training, Field Operations 
13 
will send its in-use tools back to L&D for refurbishment and use in 
14 
supplemental training throughout the year.  This tool swap enables better 
15 
training because training will occur on the equipment that will actually be used 
16 
in the field, enhances the quality of tools used in the field, and ensures that L&D 
17 
has a sufficient inventory of tools to conduct supplemental training during the 
18 
year after annual training has concluded.  The program also increases the useful 
19 
life of field tools that are swapped back into L&D for refurbishment that 
20 
otherwise may have failed earlier in the field due to continuous use.

F. Capitalization Policy Change – Main Installation
6 
7 
Q.
Is the Company proposing any changes to its capitalization policies for 
8 
main installation? 
9 
A.
Yes.  Accounting for installation of segments of main under 50 feet in length is 
10 
currently expensed by the Company.  This threshold is arbitrary; moreover, 
11 
there is no similar threshold for main replacement in Niagara Mohawk’s service 
12 
territory.  Applicable accounting principles and regulations permit 
13 
capitalization of new main installations, and there is no minimum threshold.  
14 
The Company is proposing to remove the 50-foot threshold and capitalize all 
15 
main installation activities in accordance with the FERC Chart of Accounts – 
16 
Gas – Operating Expense Instructions, Accounts 367 Mains and 376 Mains.  
17 
This change will standardize the accounting treatment of these work activities 
18 
between National Grid’s New York gas distribution companies.  As discussed 
19 
in the testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel, the Company has 
20 
normalized its Historic Test Year to reflect the change from expense to capital 
21 
4327


--- Page 131 ---
Page 98 of 120 
for distribution and transmission main installation, and the Company’s capital 
1 
investment forecasts also reflect this capitalization change.

2

7 
Q.
Please generally describe the nature of the Company’s gas system O&M 
8 
expenses. 
9 
A.
O&M expenses relate to work performed to provide customer support, respond 
10 
to emergencies, perform safety inspections and other compliance activities, 
11 
restore service, and maintain the life of capital assets.  The Company has a 
12 
significant maintenance program to ensure that system assets are utilized to 
13 
their fullest potential life expectancy.  As gas facilities age, maintenance costs 
14 
increase.  These costs include more frequent inspection and testing required by 
15 
regulatory changes, increased volume of repairs, more significant repair work, 
16 
increased emergency work, and gas pipeline safety enhancements.  These 
17 
expenditures are required to prevent failure and maintain the life of the assets 
18 
until replacement occurs.  The Company’s O&M programs are also designed to 
19 
maintain the service commitments in its gas safety performance metrics, which 
20 
cover various aspects of its performance in the areas of reliability and safety, 
21

Q.
Please describe the Fixed Factor Meter Inspection Program and the 
11 
incremental O&M required for this program. 
12 
A.
Fixed factor meters are used in conjunction with pressure regulated installations 
13 
and that employ a correction method system, based on a billing multiplier, to 
14 
adjust the measured volume of gas delivered to standard pressure conditions.  
15 
KEDNY’s Fixed Factor Meter Inspection Program conducts mandated 
16 
inspections to verify measurement accuracy for billing purposes.  Pursuant to a 
17 
pilot program for extended inspection intervals, KEDNY and KEDLI currently 
18 
conduct fixed factor inspections annually of approximately one-fifth of the total 
19 
fixed factor meter population, such that the entire population is inspected over 
20 
five years.  Niagara Mohawk conducts inspections of its entire population of 
21 
4346


--- Page 150 ---
Page 117 of 120 
fixed factor meters annually.  To better align fixed factor meter processes and 
1 
resources across the three New York gas LDCs, KEDNY and KEDLI propose 
2 
to conduct annual inspections of all fixed factor meters.  KEDNY requires three 
3 
incremental FTEs in the Rate Year and Data Years, specifically union field 
4 
mechanics, to conduct the incremental inspections.

VII. 
Impact of Williams’ NESE Project on KEDNY’s Investment Plan
3 
Q.
Please briefly describe the Transco Northeast Supply Enhancement 
4 
(“NESE”) Project. 
5 
A.
 As discussed in the testimony of Company Witness Elizabeth D. Arangio, 
6 
Williams’ NESE Project will expand the existing Transco interstate pipeline to 
7 
provide an additional 400 million cubic feet of natural gas capacity per day to 
8 
the New York area by the 2020 winter heating season.  National Grid has 
9 
contracted for 100 percent of the gas pipeline capacity that will be created by 
10 
the NESE Project.  This capacity is critical to meeting increasing demand in 
11 
KEDNY and KEDLI’s service areas.  The NESE Project is currently awaiting 
12 
permit approval by the New York Department of Environmental Conservation 
13 
(“NYDEC”).   
14 
15 
4348


--- Page 152 ---
Page 119 of 120 
Q.
What is the impact on the Company’s capital investment plan if NESE is 
1 
not approved?
2 
A.      The Company’s capital investment plan assumes that the NESE Project will be
3 
approved and placed in service.  As stated in the testimony of Ms. Arangio, if 
4 
NESE is not approved, KEDNY will have no choice but to impose a 
5 
moratorium on new and additional gas service in affected areas of the 
6 
Company’s service territories to maintain system reliability.  Moreover, several 
7 
of the Company’s planned Rate Year and Data Years capital programs and 
8 
projects will be drastically reduced, deferred, or removed altogether.  
9 
Specifically, the Company’s customer connections programs would be 
10 
suspended, and planned system reinforcements needed to support increasing 
11 
demand would be reduced by approximately half.  Notably, without additional 
12 
capacity from NESE, the Company will be unable to take its LNG tanks out of 
13 
service for sufficient time to complete needed repairs; thus, the capital project 
14 
described above to make critical repairs to the LNG tanks could not proceed.  
15 
16 
The MRI project will be completed according to the Company’s current plans 
17 
regardless of whether NESE is approved and in service.  While a significant 
18 
benefit of MRI is to enable optimization of the additional capacity NESE will 
19 
provide, the MRI project is nearly complete and includes other important 
20 
reliability benefits independent of NESE, such as increased design day pressure 
21 
4349


--- Page 153 ---
Page 120 of 120 
capability and redundancy to the Brooklyn Backbone.  MRI will be completed 
1 
but will not provide all expected system benefits if NESE is not approved.

15

3 
Q.
Please describe the Company’s overall objective of its infrastructure and 
4

5 
A.
The Company designs its gas infrastructure and operations programs to 
6 
provide safe and reliable gas delivery service to customers at reasonable costs. 
7 
Over the last several years, the Company has significantly increased 
8 
investment to modernize and enhance the resiliency of its gas assets.   
9 
10 
Significant capital investment over the next several years is required to ensure 
11 
that the gas system continues to operate safely while meeting the demands of 
12 
customers and to enable further modernization of the Company’s facilities and 
13 
operations in a manner that achieves meaningful methane emissions 
14 
reductions in furtherance of the Company’s Future of Heat strategy.  The 
15 
proposed plan includes capital and O&M spending to meet both customer 
16 
needs and satisfy state and federal regulatory requirements and goals, 
17 
including retirement of LPP, gas pipeline safety enhancements, and 
18 
deployment of non-pipeline alternatives.  While significant investments are 
19 
required to meet these needs and objectives, in developing its capital and 
20 
O&M plans, the Company balanced the need for spending to achieve safety 
21 
4393

and service objectives with the need to manage costs and minimize impacts on 
1 
customer rates.

9 
Q.
Why is the scale of Company’s capital investment plan increasing? 
10 
A.
Several developments have required that KEDLI and other natural gas 
11 
distribution utilities increase their annual capital expenditures.  Notably, 
12 
pipeline safety incidents, such as the tragic events in San Bruno, California, 
13 
Allentown, Pennsylvania, and East Harlem, New York, and the more recent 
14 
incident in Merrimack Valley, Massachusetts, have appropriately increased 
15 
focus on pipeline safety and the need to carefully monitor and replace aging 
16 
pipeline infrastructure.  Weather events such as Superstorm Sandy and the 
17 
Polar Vortex, and the expectation that similar events will occur in the future, 
18 
require the Company to find ways to protect its facilities from severe weather.  
19 
20 
4394


--- Page 198 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 14 of 110 
In response to these events, the industry has adopted new safety requirements 
1 
and is implementing best practices to modernize and protect gas facilities.  For 
2 
example, since the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, (i) new 
3 
Commission safety regulations and directives now require additional safety 
4 
inspections of inside service lines and plastic fusions; (ii) PHMSA is 
5 
implementing new safety requirements related to transmission system 
6 
integrity management and verification this year; (iii) and the New York State 
7 
Legislature is currently considering a bill that would require licensed 
8 
professional engineers (“PEs”) to review and certify gas facility design plans.  
9 
The Commission and utility industry review of recent incidents has also 
10 
resulted in recommendations for safety best practices, including overpressure 
11 
protection improvements and enhanced contractor oversight.  These mandated 
12 
and recommended improvements require significant additional investments 
13 
and compliance resources. 
14 
15 
Q.
How will the Company support the increased level of capital investment? 
16 
A.
As the Company developed plans to modernize its gas assets, it also began to 
17 
build and enhance its operations, engineering, resource planning, work 
18 
management, and quality control organizations and capabilities to deliver 
19 
increasing levels of capital investment.  The Company will continue to 
20 
develop these capabilities in the Rate Year and Data Years by adding 
21 
4395

Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 15 of 110 
incremental labor resources to execute the capital plan and support the 
1

2 
investment plan includes additional field training resources, facilities, and 
3 
tools to enhance the development of the internal work force.  
4 
5 
Regarding contractor resources, over the past several years, the Company 
6

7

Provide greater work plan visibility to contractors on forecast crew

15 
•

ii.
Gas Safety Integrity Management and Integrity Verification:
8 
IMP and IVP Programs
9 
Q.
What is the Company’s IMP? 
10 
A.
The Company’s transmission pipeline IMP is a safety program mandated by 
11 
the Pipeline Safety Improvement Act of 2002 and corresponding DOT 
12 
regulations.  The IMP identifies and addresses potential issues affecting the 
13 
physical soundness of Company facilities before they become safety or 
14 
performance issues.  The Company conducts baseline and periodic 
15 
reassessments of transmission facilities to identify and evaluate potential 
16 
threats to “Covered Segments” of pipelines, i.e., transmission pipelines that 
17 
could affect High Consequence Areas (areas where a pipeline failure could 
18 
have significant adverse consequences), as well as remediation of significant 
19 
defects discovered during such assessments.  In regions of the United States 
20 
4415


--- Page 219 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 35 of 110 
where older gas distribution systems are common, IMPs have become a key 
1 
component of gas pipeline safety through improving pipeline integrity.   
2 
3 
Q.
Please describe the IMP capital investments. 
4 
A.
Currently, IMP assessments may be accomplished through either external 
5 
corrosion direct assessment (“ECDA”) or in-line inspection (“ILI”) 
6 
technology, which uses a robotic device known as a “pig” to evaluate the 
7 
condition of the inside of the pipeline.  ILI is considered superior to ECDA 
8 
because of the ability to identify condition problems originating internally. 
9 
IMP investments are necessary to: (i) support in-line inspections (e.g., 
10 
installation 
of 
pig 
launchers 
and 
receivers, 
and 
pipe 
11 
reconfiguration/replacement), and (ii) resolve issues discovered during 
12 
pipeline inspections conducted through either method.   
13 
14 
The construction activities associated with these expenditures involve the 
15 
installation of “hot tap” fittings, the reconfiguration of such fittings to allow 
16 
ILI passage, the construction of access points to allow tethered in-line 
17 
inspection and, in some cases, the replacement of pipeline segments. 
18 
19 
Q.
Please describe the IMP capital investment needs for the Rate Year and 
20 
Data Years. 
21 
4416


--- Page 220 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 36 of 110 
Currently, 21 percent of the Company’s DOT pipeline is ILI enabled, 
1 
increased from 17 percent when the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases 
2 
was filed.  Over the long term, the Company’s plan is to reach 80 percent ILI 
3 
enablement of the Company’s DOT piping.  The Company’s IMP capital 
4

A.

12

13

16

17

18 
segments; (ii) mandating additional pressure testing or replacement for 
19 
pipelines without adequate pressure test records; and (iii) requiring operators 
20 
who lack certain records to establish material properties using approved 
21 
4419

methods (e.g., cutting and testing pipe samples).  In advance of a final 
1

2

3

4 
5 
The Company’s IVP program began in 2011 and includes thorough record 
6

7

15

16 
Company’s proposals toward decarbonizing the gas network (e.g., a new 
17 
green gas tariff offering), as discussed in the Future of Heat Panel’s testimony.

A. Capital Planning, Budgeting, and Sanctioning Process
1 
Q.
Please describe the annual development of the Company’s capital plan. 
2 
Each year, the Company develops a ten-year capital plan to achieve its 
3 
performance objectives of delivering safe and reliable service. Investment 
4 
Planning compiles proposed spending for programs and individual capital 
5 
projects. Programs and projects are categorized into one of four spending 
6 
rationales (Mandated, Customer Connections, Reliability and Non-
7 
Infrastructure).   
8 
9 
The Company currently uses a tool, C55 (known internally as “Copperleaf”), 
10 
for the prioritization and optimization of capital investments through a risk 
11 
scoring and prioritization methodology.  This tool uses criteria aligned to a 
12 
common scale to compare dissimilar inputs (e.g., financial and non-financial 
13 
inputs) to determine the set of investments, alternatives, and the timing of 
14 
projects that have the highest potential value.  
15 
16 
After the Companies rank the investments in C55, meetings are scheduled 
17 
with budget sponsors to review value models, project rankings, and various 
18 
scenarios produced through the optimization of investments to meet capital 
19 
planning targets.  Once plan targets have been approved by the Gas Business 
20 
Unit, they are submitted to Finance for review. 
21 
4430


--- Page 234 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 50 of 110 
In late fall, the capital plan is reviewed by the New York Jurisdictional 
1 
President (Company Witness John Bruckner) and the Vice President, Finance, 
2 
New York (Company Witness David Doxsee).  The New York Jurisdictional 
3 
President reviews the overall customer, service quality and financial impacts 
4 
of the investment plan and may request changes to the level or mix of 
5 
investments.   
6 
7 
In early winter, the capital plan is presented to the National Grid USA Board 
8 
of Directors and the National Grid plc Executive Committee and, in early 
9 
spring, the capital portfolio is presented to the National Grid plc Board of 
10 
Directors for review and approval.   
11

capital plan may proceed?

A.
Yes.  Aside from the capital planning and budgeting process, specific 
15 
delegation of authority (“DOA”) approval must be obtained for any project in 
16 
the ten-year capital plan to proceed.  This process includes the sanctioning 
17 
documentation and review for projects over $1 million and other levels of 
18 
review for smaller projects.  Presently, all projects greater than $1 million 
19 
require some level of sanctioning documentation and review.  The U.S. 
20 
Sanctioning Committee (“USSC”) was established by the National Grid USA 
21 
4431


--- Page 235 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 51 of 110 
Board of Directors specifically for this purpose.  Projects between $8 million 
1 
and $25 million are reviewed and approved by the USSC.  Projects between 
2 
$25 million to $203 million are reviewed by the USSC and then are forwarded 
3 
to a Senior Executive Sanctioning Committee (“SESC”) for review and 
4 
approval.  For projects between $1 million and $8 million, the USSC has 
5

6

7

11

12

established thresholds.

Q.
Please describe how the Company’s DIMP impacts its capital investment 
8 
planning. 
9 
A.
The DIMP involves a risk-based assessment of the Company’s distribution 
10 
system to identify threats in seven categories: corrosion, natural forces, 
11 
excavation damage, other outside force damage, material and weld failure, 
12 
equipment failure/malfunction and inappropriate operation.  The DIMP 
13 
requires evaluation and prioritization of the risks that these threats pose, and 
14 
the implementation of measures to address the highest risks with an emphasis 
15 
on leak management, enhanced damage prevention, operator qualification to 
16 
reduce human error and system replacement.  Consistent with the DIMP, the 
17 
Company prioritizes asset replacements in its investment plan based on a risk 
18 
ranking that considers, among other things, leak repair history, types of leak, 
19 
pipe material, surrounding geography, segment length, nearby construction 
20 
activity, field conditions, customer issues, open leaks and engineering 
21 
4433


--- Page 237 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 53 of 110 
judgment.  The risk ranking factors are carefully designed to consider known 
1 
differences in the performance of asset subclasses, extensive experience with 
2 
asset failures, current performance data for the asset subclasses for various 
3 
threat categories, and subject matter experts’ analysis and opinions on the 
4 
future performance of the assets.

stations.  Pressure regulating facilities (or stations) are designed to control 
12 
system pressures and maintain continuity of supply during normal operating 
13 
conditions and during periods of peak gas demand.   
14 
15 
KEDLI has assessed regulating stations on its system, evaluating factors such 
16 
as pressure, location, including whether the station is in a FEMA 100 year or 
17 
500-year flood zone, and the number of dependent customers for each station.
18 
In addition, the assessment considered station condition, including pipe 
19 
corrosion, location and type of overpressure protection, automation, condition 
20 
of vaults, vault covers, wall sleeves, piping vents and ladders.  The results of 
21 
4454

Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel

the assessment were used to create an overall risk rating for each station that 
1 
serves as the basis for prioritizing projects in this program.  The program 
2 
includes full or partial replacement of existing stations, and storm hardening 
3 
upgrades where necessary.

The investments in the Pressure Regulating Facilities Program do not cover

Please describe what is included in the System Automation category. 
21 
4455


--- Page 259 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 75 of 110 
A.
This program will install updated Remote Terminal Units (“RTUs”) at 
1 
multiple city gate and regulator stations.  RTUs provide temperature, pressure 
2 
and flow data back to the Gas Control Room.  RTUs can also monitor gas 
3 
detectors and intrusion alarms and allow Gas Control Operators to adjust flow 
4 
and pressure set points at regulator stations.  The benefits include enhanced 
5 
calibration of network models from automation and telemetry data, improved 
6 
accuracy of network analysis, and enhanced ability to forecast the need for 
7 
capital reinforcements, which will lead to more efficient capital planning.  
8 
Automation allows Gas Control Operators to selectively close valves, raise or 
9 
lower pressures, and shut down take stations.  System alarms also alert Gas 
10 
Control Operators to system issues and allow quick pinpointing of the source.  
11 
12 
PHMSA regulations regarding Control Room Management require Operators 
13 
to ensure that “practices and procedures within their control rooms are 
14 
adequate to maintain pipeline safety and integrity.”  These rules indicate that 
15 
Operators should have telemetry to monitor pipelines, as it would increase 
16 
system awareness and enable a proactive response to abnormal operating 
17 
conditions.  The System Automation program complies with these regulations 
18 
by providing for increased deployment of telemetry on the Company’s system. 
19 
20 
4456


--- Page 260 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 76 of 110 
Currently, KEDLI’s pressure regulation stations are equipped with some form 
1 
of telemetry, but only 96 percent of the system has full remote control of the 
2 
regulators.  Additionally, some of the telemetry equipment was installed years 
3 
ago and the technology has become obsolete.  KEDLI’s System Automation 
4 
program adds automation capabilities to low pressure regulator stations and

Q.
Please describe what is included in the Gas System Reliability – Gas 
10 
Planning/Remote Controlled Valve (“RCV”) Program. 
11 
A.
This program includes capital projects required to maintain system minimum 
12 
pressures on the gas network in the event of an abnormal operating condition 
13 
(failure involving a regulator station, gate station, critical main or other major 
14 
pressure facility on the system).  Gas System Planning ensures that customers 
15 
continue to have reliable service and that no customers experience 
16 
interruptions because of an unplanned outage of a facility under normal winter 
17 
conditions.  The program also involves the installation of additional RCVs on 
18 
transmission pipelines to improve emergency response capability and reduce 
19 
the risk of gas releases.  In the event of a pipeline failure, RCVs allow control 
20 
room operators to stop the flow of gas and to remotely isolate and shut down a 
21 
4457


--- Page 261 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 77 of 110 
portion of the system.  Currently, most transmission pipelines can only be shut 
1 
down using manually-controlled isolation valves, which can take longer to 
2 
close and result in a larger customer impact.  Improving response time 
3 
through the expanded deployment of RCVs reduces the quantity of gas 
4 
released and can limit the harm to the public and property.   
5

11 
system where large numbers of customers would experience a service 
12 
interruption if a single gas facility became inoperable when the average daily 
13 
temperature is five degrees Fahrenheit.

12

13 
A.
In the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, the Company included a 
14

15 
shutoff valves on KEDLI’s approximately 60,000 gas services within the 
16

17 
Because there was no viable shutoff valve mechanism commercially available 
18

19 
The devices became available from the manufacturer during February of 
20

21 
4459


--- Page 263 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 79 of 110 
the significant benefits of these devices, the Company is renewing its proposal 
1 
for this program from FY 2020 through FY 2024. 
2 
3 
Q.
What are the benefits and costs of this program?      
4 
A.
 The remote shutoff valves add a layer of protection for services that are 
5 
especially susceptible to storm surge and flooding that could cause over-
6 
pressurization of the gas facilities connecting customers’ premises.  The 
7 
impacts of recent severe storms (i.e., Superstorm Sandy) demonstrate the need 
8 
for the Company to harden its infrastructure to provide greater protection from 
9 
future storms.  These valves will operate on a fixed communication network 
10 
that will allow for remote operation and monitoring.  Automated valves stop 
11 
the flow of gas as soon as flooding is detected.  This will prevent regulator 
12 
over-pressurization and stop gas from flowing to premises with damaged 
13 
equipment and/or extinguished pilot lights, mitigating the risk of a potential 
14 
incident.  Automated valves also provide a real-time count of services 
15 
impacted by flooding to inform the Company’s storm response about the 
16 
resources needed to restore the affected customers expeditiously.  Lastly, in 
17 
areas where flooding prevents physical access to valves and regulators, remote 
18 
shut-off valves will allow the Company to interrupt only those services 
19 
impacted by flooding, which could spare entire neighborhoods or larger areas 
20 
from losing gas service because of access issues.  Installation of the 
21 
4460


--- Page 264 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 80 of 110 
communication networks through which the valves operate can also be 
1 
leveraged in the future for additional smart devices, such as methane detectors 
2 
that are being developed.    
3 
4 
The Company is proposing to ramp-up the program in FY 2020 and the Rate 
5 
Year, installing approximately 1,000 valves in FY 2020 and approximately 
6 
9,000 valves in the Rate Year, with the bulk of the communications network 
7 
systems in the Rate Year as well.  The Company intends to install 
8 
approximately 16,500 valves per year in each of the Data Years.  Program 
9 
costs in the Rate Year are approximately $15.6 million.

4461


--- Page 265 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel

A.
KEDLI maintains on-system supply through its LNG facility at the Holtsville 
1 
LNG Plant.  This plant is a critical component of KEDLI’s gas supply 
2 
portfolio and gas operating network and plays a critical role in meeting peak 
3 
demand.  The Holtsville LNG Plant has one storage tank and is capable of 
4 
supplying 100 million cubic feet of gas per day.  Refilling the tank is 
5 
accomplished through liquefaction during the summer period when gas 
6 
supplies are available and less expensive.  The liquefaction system can refill at 
7 
a rate of about 6 million cubic feet of gas per day and it can take up to100 
8 
days to refill the tank.  The Holtsville LNG Plant is a cost-effective means of 
9 
meeting peak demand, because gas is liquified during the summer months 
10 
when prices are lower and stored for use in the winter during peak demand 
11 
conditions.  KEDLI’s various LNG capital programs are necessary to ensure 
12 
the continued safe, reliable operation of the Holtsville LNG Plant.

F. Capitalization Policy Change – Main Installation
1 
2 
Q.
Is the Company proposing any changes to its capitalization policies for 
3 
main installation? 
4 
A.
Yes.  Accounting for installation of segments of main under 50 feet in length 
5 
is currently expensed by the Company.  However, this threshold is arbitrary; 
6 
moreover, there is no similar threshold for main replacement in Niagara 
7 
Mohawk’s service territory.  Applicable accounting principles and regulations 
8 
permit capitalization of new main installations, and there is no minimum 
9 
threshold.  The Company is proposing to remove the 50-foot threshold and 
10 
capitalize all main installation activities in accordance with the FERC Chart of 
11 
Accounts – Gas – Operating Expense Instructions, Accounts 367 Mains and 
12 
376 Mains.  This change will standardize the accounting treatment of these 
13 
work activities between National Grid’s New York gas distribution 
14 
companies.  As discussed in the testimony of the Revenue Requirements 
15 
Panel, the Company has normalized its Historic Test Year to reflect the 
16 
change from expense to capital for distribution and transmission main 
17 
installation, and the Company’s capital investment forecasts also reflect this 
18 
capitalization change.

VI. 
Gas O&M Expenses
1 
Q.
Please summarize the Panel’s testimony regarding the costs of operating 
2 
the gas system.  
3 
A.
The Panel addresses major expenses associated with operating the Company’s 
4

5

6 
7 
Q.
Please generally describe the nature of the Company’s gas system O&M 
8 
expenses. 
9 
A.
O&M expenses relate to work performed to provide customer support, 
10 
respond to emergencies, perform safety inspections and other compliance 
11 
activities, restore service and maintain the life of capital assets.  The Company 
12 
has a significant maintenance program to ensure that system assets are utilized 
13 
to their fullest potential life expectancy.  As gas facilities age, maintenance 
14 
costs increase.  These costs include increased volume of repairs, more 
15 
significant repair work, and increased emergency work.  These expenditures 
16 
are required to prevent failure and maintain the life of the assets until 
17 
replacement occurs.  The O&M workload is also increasing to keep pace with 
18 
expanding inspection and testing requirements from new regulatory and 
19 
pipeline safety mandates.  Finally, the Company’s O&M programs are 
20 
designed to maintain the service commitments in its gas safety performance 
21 
4478

VII. 
Impact of Williams’ NESE Project on KEDLI’s Investment Plan
2 
Q.   Please briefly describe the Transco Northeast Supply Enhancement
3 
(“NESE”) Project. 
4 
A.
 As discussed in the testimony of Company Witness Elizabeth D. Arangio, 
5 
Williams’ NESE Project will expand the existing Transco interstate pipeline 
6 
to provide an additional 400 million cubic feet of natural gas capacity per day 
7 
to the New York area by the 2020 winter heating season.  National Grid has 
8 
contracted for 100 percent of the gas pipeline capacity that will be created by 
9 
the NESE Project.  This capacity is critical to meeting increasing demand in 
10 
KEDNY’s and KEDLI’s service areas.  The NESE Project is currently 
11 
4490


--- Page 294 ---
Testimony of the Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 110 of 110 
awaiting permit approval by the New York Department of Environmental 
1 
Conservation (“NYDEC”).   
2 
3 
Q.      What is the impact on the Company’s capital investment plan if NESE is
4 
not approved? 
5 
A.      The Company’s capital investment plan assumes that the NESE Project will be
6 
approved and placed in service.  As stated in the testimony of Ms. Arangio, if 
7 
NESE is not approved, KEDLI will have no choice but to impose a 
8 
moratorium on new and additional gas service in affected areas of the 
9 
Company’s service territories to maintain system reliability.  Moreover, 
10 
several of the Company’s planned Rate Year and Data Years capital programs 
11 
and projects will be drastically reduced, deferred, or removed altogether. 
12 
Specifically, the Company’s customer connections programs would be 
13 
suspended, and planned system reinforcements needed to support increasing 
14 
demand would be reduced by approximately half.  Notably, without additional 
15 
capacity from NESE, the Company will be unable to take its LNG tank out of 
16 
service for sufficient time to complete needed repairs; thus, the capital project 
17 
described above to make critical repairs to the LNG tank could not proceed.

15

16 
2019 rate filing if the Company is unable to obtain incremental natural gas 
17 
supplies from Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line, LLC’s Northeast Supply 
18 
Enhancement (“NESE”) project, which would provide 400,000 
19 
dekatherms/day of incremental gas supply to KEDNY and KEDLI’s gas 
20 
distribution systems to meet forecast demand for natural gas and enhance 
21 
4494


--- Page 298 ---
Page 2 of 8 
reliability for existing customers.  In our direct testimony, the Panel 
1 
identified certain proposals that would be affected if the NESE project were 
2 
not placed in service by the winter of 2020/2021.  As discussed more fully 
3 
by Company Witness Elizabeth D. Arangio, recent decisions by the New 
4 
York State Department of Environmental Conservation (“DEC”) and the 
5 
New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection regarding required 
6 
water permits create uncertainty as to whether and when the NESE project 
7 
may proceed with permitting and construction.  While the Company 
8 
remains cautiously optimistic the NESE project will go forward, and 
9 
therefore is not proposing any changes to its April 2019 filing at this time, 
10 
the Panel addresses the impacts that gas supply constraints would have on 
11 
KEDLI’s forecast capital additions and certain gas operations and safety 
12 
programs should the NESE project not be available during the proposed rate 
13 
plan period.

III. 
Potential Impacts of the NESE Project and Gas Supply Constraints
10 
Q.
Did the Panel’s direct testimony discuss the possibility that the NESE 
11 
project might not be available and that this could affect the Company’s 
12 
filing? 
13 
A.
Yes.  While the Company’s filing was prepared assuming the NESE project 
14 
would be completed by the winter of 2020/2021, the Panel’s direct 
15 
testimony (at 118-120) identified the possibility that the NESE project 
16 
would not be available as planned and explained that KEDLI’s capital 
17 
investment plan would be impacted in that scenario.  Specifically, the Panel 
18 
explained that several planned capital programs and projects could be 
19 
eliminated, modified, or deferred, including the Customer Connections and 
20 
Gas System Reinforcement programs.  Further, without the planned 
21 
4496


--- Page 300 ---
Page 4 of 8 
capacity from the NESE project, the Company would be unable to proceed 
1 
with the planned maintenance and upgrades to the Holtsville LNG facility. 
2 
3 
Q.
Please explain the impact to the Company’s capital investment plan if 
4 
the NESE project is not approved.     
5 
A.
Exhibit ___ (GIOP-1S) is an illustrative capital investment plan reflecting 
6 
the impact in the Rate Year and Data Years should the NESE project not be 
7 
completed on time, including reductions to the Company’s Customer 
8 
Connections, Reinforcements, and LNG programs.  As stated by Company 
9 
Witness Arangio, without the incremental capacity from the NESE project, 
10 
KEDLI will not be able to procure sufficient gas supplies to meet the 
11 
forecast demand from new firm customers, such that connecting additional 
12 
firm load would jeopardize the Company’s ability to provide safe and 
13 
reliable gas service to existing customers.   Therefore, investments in the 
14 
Customer Connections programs associated with serving new firm load 
15 
would not be necessary, including the installation of new main and the 
16 
purchase and installation of new meters and associated AMR devices, as 
17 
well as investments in the low-to-moderate income gas conversion program 
18 
that was proposed by the Company’s Future of Heat Panel.  Similarly, the 
19 
Gas System Reinforcements program would be reduced to remove projects 
20 
4497


--- Page 301 ---
Page 5 of 8 
no longer needed to serve incremental firm load in KEDLI’s service 
1 
territory.   
2 
3 
Finally, without the NESE project, the Company is unable to take the 
4 
Holtsville LNG Tank out of service to perform planned maintenance and 
5 
upgrades.  The Company intends to perform some engineering work for this 
6 
project for the purpose of conducting studies and design work for potential 
7 
limited upgrades to the tank that would not require taking it out of service. 
8

B. Staff’s Blanket Adjustments to Capital Programs

Q.

to the Companies’ capital forecasts.

A.
The SGIOP generally supports the Companies capital plans (SGIOP at 32) but proposes

20

21

22 
adjustments: 
23 
4527


--- Page 331 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 8 of 39 
•
The SGIOP rejects the Companies’ higher inflation rates and other known factors
1 
that are expected to increase Rate Year and Data Year costs for the CSC and
2 
Proactive Main Replacement Programs (e.g. increasing contract costs).  (SGIOP at
3 
46-52).
4 
•
Where the Companies’ forecasts were derived using historic averages of spending
5 
in FY 2017 and FY 2018, the SGIOP believes that forecasts should be based on
6 
“updated” two-year averages or three-year averages to include FY 2019.  (SGIOP
7 
at 38, 58, 74).
8 
•
The SGIOP lacks confidence in the Companies’ Reliability Category forecasts
9 
because there have been historic variances between the Companies’ budgets and
10 
actual spending in this category.  (SGIOP at 61-65).
11 
•
Because of the timing of the Companies’ sanctioning process, which occurs closer
12 
to the Rate Year, sanction papers are generally not yet available for the Companies’
13 
major investments.  The SGIOP claims that without sanction papers, it is unable to
14 
determine whether proposed projects are truly needed, whether forecasts are
15 
reasonable, and whether alternatives were considered.  (SGIOP at 28-29).
16 
17

18

21 
closer to the spending year.  Although it is true that sanctioning documentation is not yet 
22 
available for the Rate Year projects and programs, the Companies’ direct testimony and 
23 
4528

exhibits provided extensive information for each program and project, including data 
1 
sheets (Exhibits __ (GIOP-5) that contain the same information that is typically included

Q.
Does the Panel agree with the SGIOP’s methods and justifications for its proposed 
8 
adjustments? 
9 
A.
No, the SGIOP’s proposed blanket adjustments are not supported by sufficient data and 
10 
analysis.  As discussed below, the SGIOP ignores known, significant cost drivers that will 
11 
increase costs of CSC and Proactive Main Replacement Programs.   Removal of these costs 
12 
from the budgets for these programs will impair the Companies’ ability to deliver high 
13 
priority capital programs that are needed to meet important reliability, safety, and policy 
14 
goals, including work to enable New York City and municipal infrastructure projects and 
15 
to improve safety and reduce methane emissions through replacement of LPP.

17 
Q.
Please describe how the Companies determined their proposed capital forecasts. 
18 
A.
In contrast to the SGIOP’s blanket approach, the Companies determined the appropriate 
19 
basis and methodology for forecasting Rate Year and Data Year investments on a program-
20 
by-program basis.  Following a detailed analysis of each program, including examination 
21 
of historic spending, the Companies determined for each program whether an average of 
22 
historic costs or the HTY represented the best predictor of Rate Year costs.  The Companies 
23 
4529


--- Page 333 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel 
Page 10 of 39 
also determined the projects for which a project estimate, rather than a forecast based solely 
1 
on historic costs, was more appropriate.  In this way, the Companies carefully considered 
2 
any anomalies prior to setting its forecasts for each program.  The Companies’ 
3 
methodologies for deriving program forecasts are provided in the Companies’ testimony 
4 
and exhibits and in response to IR DPS-761. 
5 
6 
Q.
How will the SGIOP’s proposals impact the Companies’ ability to provide safe and 
7 
reliable service? 
8 
A.
In general, the SGIOP’s attempt to more closely align the Rate Year forecasts with the 
9 
Companies’ average historic costs and spending levels shifts funds away from the 
10 
Companies’ highest priority mandated, safety, and reliability programs.  The SGIOP’s 
11 
recommendations will hinder the Companies’ ability to deliver on many of the Companies’ 
12 
and the Commission’s important policy, environmental, and safety objectives.     
13 
14 
More specifically, proposed downward adjustments in the mandated category will 
15 
challenge the Companies’ ability to deliver on aggressive goals for LPP replacement, 
16 
methane reduction, and programs and projects discussed below that are necessary to reduce 
17 
overall system risks.  Proposed adjustments in the Reliability category will compromise 
18 
the Companies’ ability to replace aging facilities and equipment that are critical to system 
19 
operations and to add new equipment that enables the Companies to remotely operate and 
20

23 
4551

to the LNG tanks without being able to access the insides of the tanks to assess the

11 
•
Mini-gate stations:  The Companies’ 10-year station work plan is risk-based and
12 
considers multiple significant factors including the age and current condition of each
13 
station.  As a result of the Storm Hardening Collaborative, the Companies now
14 
specifically consider location in flood zone as a factor in this analysis.  However, as
15 
NYC states, the Clifton Gate and the Citizens Gate stations, and an additional seven

18

23

4

5

6

Meter set elevations:  In accordance with the recommendations of the Storm
10

11 
standardizing guidance for meter set elevations in flood zones and do not
12 
recommend increasing the standard height design.  The Company conducted
13 
outreach among other utilities via a survey regarding the feasibility and practices for
14 
increasing standard height design for meter sets and regulators among its peers.  A
15 
majority of the respondents were not increasing the height of the meter sets or
16 
regulators. The Company also considered the geography of its service territory and
17 
found that the flood baseline varies drastically, which creates a significant challenge
18 
for determining an alternate standard design height. The Company is not
19 
recommending increasing the standard height design for regulators and meters sets
20 
for new installations.  The Company is actively pursuing Remotely Operated
21 
Service Shutoff Valves for the services in the flood plains that will automatically
22 
shut off the gas service in the event of the flooding to mitigate risk for customers
23 
4555

and communities located within flood plains.  This information was provided in the

1 
Substantively, the Companies disagree with a proposal to limit their contractor work force 
2

3 
resources, impairing the Companies’ ability to obtain qualified contractor services at the 
4 
least cost, and risking cost increases that customers would ultimately bear.

6

7

9

11 
performance, safety and cost competitiveness.  Although the majority of the Companies’ 
12 
contract work is performed by union labor – quality, safety and compliance are not 
13 
mutually exclusive to either a union or non-union workforce. 
14 
15 
The Companies’ union and non-union labor force is heavily vetted, as NYSLOF 
16 
acknowledges.  (NYSLOF at 4).  The Companies endeavor to contract only with companies 
17 
that conduct their operations lawfully, safely and ethically and in compliance with all 
18

19 
labor associations.  All contractors that bid on the Companies’ projects must meet ISN 
20

21 
work on gas pipelines must have the associated Operator Qualifications for the tasks they 
22 
are performing.  Operator Qualifications are required per 49 CFR 192 & 195 to work on 
23 
4558

gas pipelines and are not exclusive to union contractors.  In addition to maintaining

15

16

17

Q.
Please explain damage prevention mark outs and how the costs of these 
4 
mark outs are included in the Companies’ rate filings. 
5 
A.
The Companies’ Damage Prevention group performs mark outs of the 
6 
Companies’ underground utilities to allow for safe excavation and prevent 
7 
damage to existing facilities, as required by the Commission’s regulations.  
8 
Damage prevention mark outs are performed when required to support one 
9 
of the Companies’ projects or when customers, third parties, and 
10 
municipalities contact New York State’s Dig Safe One Call Center.  
11 
KEDNY uses internal employees to locate facilities on Company-related 
12 
jobs and a contractor for all third-party Dig Safe mark out requests.  
13 
Conversely, KEDLI sends all Dig Safe mark out requests, whether internal 
14 
or external, to a contractor to mark out facilities.    
15 
16 
The costs associated with damage prevention mark outs are included in 
17 
KEDNY’s O&M expense and KEDLI’s O&M and capital expense.  To 
18 
prepare the rate case forecasts, the Companies increased these expense 
19 
components from the Historic Test Year by standard annual inflation to 
20 
arrive at the Rate Year forecast.

Q.
What are the drivers of the higher contractor bids? 
1 
A.
The increase is attributable to three factors: (i) the prior contractor labor 
2 
rates were based on long-term, dated agreements; (ii) recent unionization of 
3 
the contractor labor force; and (iii) an increased scope of work to 
4 
incorporate locator assurance technology.  The Companies have not bid this 
5 
work in over a decade.  While the prior agreements provided for minimal 
6 
price increases, the rates paid to those contractors were generally lower than 
7 
market prices at the time.  Contractors were no longer willing to accept 
8 
below-market rates during the recent negotiations.  Additionally, the 
9 
contractors providing services under the selected agreements unionized 
10 
during the late Spring and early Summer of 2019.  While the Companies 
11 
were generally aware that these labor forces were unionizing, the increase 
12 
in labor rates experienced was significantly higher than anticipated or 
13 
reflected in the Companies’ initial filing.  In addition, the new agreements 
14 
require that the contractors use updated technology (locator assurance 
15 
technology that enables real-time tracking of technician performance 
16 
against industry standards to improve overall effectiveness of locating field 
17 
work) when marking out facilities.  This requirement expands the scope of 
18 
work required in prior agreements and will require additional training and 
19 
inventory for these contractors. 
20

Q. 
Please describe how the capital budgeting
6 
process should be performed. 
7 
A. 
The capital budgeting process should be both a
8 
top-down and bottom-up process.  The top-down 
9 
perspective should represent the strategic goals 
10 
and objectives for the utility and be 
11 
incorporated into both the capital and O&M 
12 
budgets.  The company should incorporate these 
13 
strategic goals and objectives in the planning 
14 
process.  The bottom-up budgeting consists of 
15 
identifying capital requirements on a project-
16 
by-project basis at the departmental level.  
17 
Ultimately, capital budget development should 
18 
primarily consist of a bottom-up assessment of 
19 
system needs giving due consideration to top-
20 
down financial considerations.

1 
Q. 
Please briefly explain the escalating unit costs
2 
KEDNY is experiencing. 
3 
A. 
KEDNY’s cost to install gas main has been
4

5 
regulations enacted by the New York City 
6 
Department of Transportation (NYCDOT).  As 
7

8

10
