11 
includes larger restoration areas, more 
12 
expensive materials, and different removal 
13 
methods such as saw-cutting roadways instead of 
14 
less expensive methods like jackhammering.  
15 
KEDNY implemented the new requirements on April 
16 
1, 2017. 
17 
Q. 
How have these new requirements impacted KEDNY’s
18 
budgets? 
19 
A. 
As expected, the new requirements have led to
20 
increases in the unit costs to install and 
21 
replace new gas main.  For every linear foot of 
22 
gas main the company installs or replaces, it 
23 
now must perform additional work.  This has led 
24 
4656

1 
Q.

2

3

4

5

7 
Q.

8 
A.
In February 2013, the Commission commenced the Gas Management Audit 
9 
pursuant to PSL Section 66(19).  The Commission selected NorthStar 
10 
Consulting Group (“NorthStar”) to perform the audit.  In August 2014, 
11 
NorthStar released its audit report.  The report, which contained 31 
12 
recommendations, described generally strong performance by National 
13 
Grid’s gas business in a number of key functional areas, including gas 
14 
operations, load forecasting, supply procurement, and customer information 
15 
systems.   
16 
17 
On November 3, 2014, National Grid filed its implementation plan with the 
18 
Commission detailing plans to implement the audit recommendations.  The 
19 
implementation plan was approved by the Commission by Order dated May 
20 
14, 2015.  In the ensuing months, the Company worked collaboratively with 
21 
4812


--- Page 616 ---
Testimony of Philip A. DeCicco 
Page 5 of 6
Staff to implement the recommendations.  By letter dated September 28, 
1 
2018, Staff confirmed that all 31 recommendations had been implemented. 
2 
A copy of the close-out letter is on file with the Commission in Case 13-G-
3 
0009.   
4 
5 
Q.

6

7

8

9

utilities to file implementation plans.

13

14 
2016.  The implementation plan, which addressed 106 recommendations, 
15

0314.

Q.
Please provide an overview of the Companies’ rate filings. 
1 
A.
The current energy landscape is evolving beyond the traditional utility construct of 
2 
years past.  Technology and innovation are driving change in the energy industry, 
3 
and utilities must provide more dynamic, efficient, and interactive services to meet 
4 
heightened customer expectations.  At the same time, the confluence of an industry 
5 
focus on gas safety and the imperative to reduce carbon emissions demands that 
6 
utilities rise to the challenge of delivering a safe and sustainable energy future.  This 
7 
rate filing will enable us to achieve step changes in our performance in these key 
8 
areas and lead the transition to New York’s energy future.  Accordingly, investment 
9 
is required not only to enhance the Companies’ core operations, but also to support 
10 
energy policy objectives.  These rate filings present comprehensive, measured 
11 
proposals designed to align with the Companies’ priorities of (i) maintaining 
12 
affordability and mitigating customer bill impacts; (ii) funding capital programs 
13 
necessary to modernize our gas infrastructure and replace aging and outdated 
14 
information technology systems; (iii) delivering the Future of Heat; (iv) improving 
15 
the customer experience; and (v) preserving credit quality and allowing the 
16 
Companies the opportunity to earn a reasonable rate of return. 
17 
18 
KEDNY and KEDLI seek to increase revenues by $236.8 million and $49.4 
19 
million, respectively, to eliminate revenue deficiencies in the twelve months ending 
20 
March 31, 2021 (“Rate Year”).  For typical residential heating customers, the 
21

Q.
Please describe the Companies’ need to earn a reasonable rate of return. 
7 
A.
Without the rate increase proposed in these filings, current rate levels will not 
8 
permit the Companies to recover their costs of providing safe and reliable service.  
9 
Current rate levels would also not permit the Companies to earn a reasonable rate 
10 
of return on our investments.  The Companies’ proposal brings their respective rates 
11 
of return to reasonable levels, while, as noted above, mitigating the impact on 
12 
customers. 
13 
14 
The Companies’ ability to access capital markets on terms favorable to our 
15 
customers will be directly affected by the rates authorized by the Commission in 
16 
this proceeding.  For decades, the combination of stable earnings, generally 
17 
manageable business risks, and declining or stable market interest rates have 
18 
allowed us to access capital markets on favorable terms and reduce borrowing costs 
19 
for the benefit of customers.  As our portfolio of capital investments grows to meet 
20 
the demands of today’s business, it is increasingly important that we maintain the 
21 
4821

ability to cost-effectively finance our investments.  However, due, in part, to recent 
1

2

3 
reasonable return on equity, funding for incremental capital investments, and 
4 
support for timely recovery of operating expenses such as SIR costs, the Companies 
5 
are at risk of further downgrades, which could impact the Companies’ credit quality 
6 
and raise costs for customers as the cost of borrowing increases.

Q. 
Please describe the differences between the capital investments proposed by 
1 
KEDNY and KEDLI. 
2 
A.
As noted above, there is a significant difference between the revenue deficiencies 
3 
of KEDNY and KEDLI, and that difference is largely attributable to several capital 
4 
cost drivers that arise in KEDNY’s service territory.  New York City is undertaking 
5

6 
of KEDNY’s city/state construction work (“CSC”), which involves the relocation 
7

8

9

10 
KEDNY’s control, and these projects are expensive and prone to a high degree of 
11 
cost variability.  At the same time, KEDNY is experiencing higher unit costs 
12 
resulting from new work requirements, including recent changes to paving and 
13 
restoration requirements in New York City, as well as increased costs for 
14 
contractors due to demand.  These increased costs impact many of the mandated 
15 
programs in KEDNY’s capital investment plan, including CSC and main 
16 
replacement projects.  These factors, which are further compounded by the 
17 
increased volume and scope of construction projects in New York City, have 
18 
contributed to the differences in capital requirements and costs between the 
19 
Companies as these cost drivers are not currently experienced to the same degree 
20 
in KEDLI’s service territory.

3

Information Technology
4 
Q.
What are the Companies’ proposals and strategy for upgrading IT? 
5 
A.
Modern energy networks rely on state-of the-art information systems to monitor, 
6 
manage, and optimize system performance, support state and federal energy goals, 
7 
address emerging utility and market trends, meet evolving customer and business 
8 
demands, and stay ahead of emerging cyber-security threats.  Many of National 
9 
Grid’s legacy systems, however, are at or near the end of their useful lives and 
10 
rely on outdated technology that is insufficient to support evolving business 
11 
requirements.  Aged infrastructure is more prone to outages and extended down 
12 
time, which can negatively impact network reliability and resiliency.  The current 
13 
systems lack the flexibility needed to drive performance improvements and 
14 
efficiencies for the Companies and our customers in the future. 
15 
16 
KEDNY and KEDLI currently utilize outdated and disparate customer systems. 
17 
CSS (supporting KEDLI and Niagara Mohawk) is 20 years old and CRIS 
18 
(supporting KEDNY) is 30 years old.  Neither system can readily support 
19 
escalating customer expectations or increasingly sophisticated billing needs (e.g., 
20 
distributed energy resources).  The CIS Replacement Program will replace these 
21 
4853


--- Page 657 ---
Page 38 of 52 
outdated systems with a modern, flexible, and more capable customer system that 
1 
will meet the requirements of new customer program and rate options, incorporate 
2 
digital and emerging technology solutions, improve customer choice, and reduce 
3 
billing issues and certain costs associated with operating our aged systems. 
4 
5 
The testimony of the IT Panel discusses in more detail the Companies’ investment 
6 
levels, our strategy to deliver on these information systems investments, and how 
7 
we propose to report on these investments to the Commission.

Q.

19

20

21 
4864


--- Page 668 ---
Page 49 of 52 
been impacted by the past release of substances by property owners.  Both 
1

2

3 
to former MGP sites.  The Companies are presently engaged in clean-up activities 
4 
at these sites, which will continue well beyond the Rate Year and Data Years.  
5 
While the Companies actively try to manage and control SIR costs, including taking 
6 
action to reduce MGP site cost responsibility, the scope and timing of activities at 
7 
these sites are ultimately subject to the purview of the EPA and New York State 
8 
Department of Environmental Conversation.  The Companies propose to recover 
9 
future SIR costs in a manner consistent with present recovery methods and maintain 
10 
the existing SIR Recovery Surcharge and annual reconciliation mechanisms to 
11 
defer costs above the allowance for future refund or recovery from customers.  
12 
13 
Company Witness Charles Willard addresses our SIR programs, cost mitigation 
14 
efforts, proposed funding levels, and the status of work at major MGP sites, 
15 
including the Gowanus Canal and Newtown Creek Superfund sites.  The 
16 
remediation of these superfund sites is likely to have a significant impact on 
17 
KEDNY’s cash flows and thus it is particularly important for the Commission to 
18 
approve KEDNY’s SIR cost recovery proposals.

5

7

8

9 
in public utilities.  A return on equity that is below what investors believe they can 
10 
earn on investments in companies with similar risk would impair our ability to 
11 
attract capital, both debt and equity, on reasonable terms.

16 
significant, and thus the rate impacts are significant, as well.  In contrast, KEDLI 
17

III. 
Review of Compensation and Benefits
1 
Q.
Please describe National Grid’s philosophy concerning employee 
2 
wages and benefits.   
3 
A.
National Grid’s overall approach to compensation is to ensure that (i) a 
4 
significant portion of employee compensation is tied to the attainment of 
5 
performance goals that create benefits for customers and are consistent 
6 
with the policy goals established by National Grid’s regulators, (ii) 
7

8 
comparable positions in both the utility industry and general industry and 
9 
is reasonable after considering base and variable pay and benefits in total, 
10

11 
Grid and the performance of each individual in achieving goals that are 
12 
tied to the attainment of customer satisfaction, safety, and reliability 
13 
objectives.  To provide safe, reliable, and efficient utility service to its 
14 
customers, National Grid must attract, retain and engage high performing, 
15 
qualified personnel.  To accomplish this, National Grid provides a total 
16 
compensation package that recognizes and rewards excellence, maintains 
17 
fair and competitive market pay and benefits for employees, and 
18 
encourages employees to improve skills while providing a safe working 
19 
environment.  Doing so under the cost containment pressures faced by all 
20 
companies is a critical challenge.  To meet this challenge, National Grid 
21 
4879

1

4

14

15

16 
A.
The purpose of performing an overall compensation study is to determine 
17

18 
attract a highly qualified workforce.  From this perspective, cash 
19 
compensation – fixed and variable – is best analyzed by comparing the 
20

21 
4884


--- Page 688 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
15 of 64 
compensation provided by other companies with comparable positions.  In 
1 
this case, Willis Towers Watson analyzed the cash compensation provided 
2

3

6

12 
13 
In contrast, acquiring information concerning peer companies’ costs of 
14 
various employee benefits and comparing those costs is very difficult if 
15 
not impossible.  The reason for this is that the cost of various benefits can 
16 
vary dramatically from year to year and from company to company.  For 
17 
example, the cost of pension and other post-employment benefits 
18 
(“OPEBs”) can change because of changes in the funded status of the 
19 
plans established to provide those benefits, the investment performance of 
20 
the plans, and the mortality rate of those participating in the plan. 
21 
4885


--- Page 689 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
16 of 64 
Similarly, the cost of health insurance can vary because of the claims 
1 
experience of individual companies and the age and health of individual 
2 
employees in the workforce and their dependents.  Changes in costs 
3 
associated with these factors do not determine whether the benefits being 
4 
provided by a particular company are competitive.  Instead, it is the 
5 
relative value of the benefits that provides the proper measurement of 
6 
whether a benefits package is sufficient to attract, retain and engage highly 
7 
qualified personnel.  The analyses performed by Willis Towers Watson 
8 
properly consider the relative value of the benefits being provided by 
9 
National Grid and the peer group.

Q.
How did Willis Towers Watson determine the relative value of the
1 
benefits package provided by National Grid and the peer group?
2 
A.
The relative value of the various benefits is established based on a
3 
common set of actuarial assumptions and a single employee population.
4 
This establishes a controlled environment in which differences in value are
5 
exclusively a function of the differences in benefit plan provisions.  The
6 
relative value of various benefits is determined by dividing the value of
7 
the particular benefit for individual companies by the average value of all
8 
the companies in the peer group.  Relative values are developed for each
9 
benefit and for the entire benefit plan.

Q 
Is it correct that the variable pay plan at National Grid is pay-at-risk? 
1 
A.
Yes, that is correct.  National Grid’s variable pay plan is designed to be 
2 
part of a total compensation program; it is a pay-at-risk plan, not extra or 
3 
bonus pay.  This conclusion is borne out by the analysis of total 
4 
compensation prepared by Willis Towers Watson.  The variable pay 
5 
component is labeled “pay-at-risk” because if performance measures are 
6 
not achieved, employees will not receive their variable pay.  This “at-risk” 
7 
compensation allows National Grid to align pay with performance that is 
8 
consistent with the goals of customers and regulators and to allocate 
9 
compensation to those employees who are most deserving.  Thus, variable 
10 
compensation is not “bonus” or “optional” compensation that National 
11 
Grid provides to employees, but a required element in the total 
12 
compensation program and a necessary and prudent cost of doing 
13 
business.

Q.
What do you mean by “target levels?” 
1 
A.
“Target levels” represent a level of performance that is judged to be 50 
2 
percent of stated maximums.  Target performance is best described as an 
3 
above average level of performance that is consistent with overall 
4 
expectations.  Achieving target performance requires employees to 
5 
perform at a high, but nonetheless expected level.  High performers would 
6 
exceed “target levels” while average or below average performers would 
7 
fall below “target levels.”

Q.
Please discuss the Commission policy concerning variable pay. 
10 
A.
KEDNY and KEDLI’s current rates, as adopted by the Commission in the 
11 
2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, reflect an amount of variable 
12 
compensation expense and, most recently, the rates that were adopted by 
13 
the Commission and took effect on April 1, 2018 in the 2017 NMPC Rate 
14 
Case also reflect an amount of variable compensation expense.  
15 
16 
In addition, in a decision involving Orange and Rockland Utilities, Inc. in 
17 
Case 10-E-0362 (“O&R”), the Commission indicated that there were two 
18 
ways a utility could substantiate that variable pay expense should be 
19 
included in the revenue requirement.  First, a utility could attempt to 
20 
justify the inclusion of variable pay expense by demonstrating that: (i) 
21 
4900


--- Page 704 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
31 of 64 
total compensation, including variable compensation for a class or classes 
1 
of employees, is reasonable by reference to a study that compares total 
2 
compensation to that provided by similarly situated companies; and (ii) 
3 
that the variable compensation plan supports the provision of safe and 
4 
adequate service and does not promote employee behavior that would be 
5 
contrary to customer interests or Commission policies.  Second, to the 
6 
extent a utility seeks funding in rates for a variable compensation program 
7 
that would award payments above what would be considered reasonable 
8 
total compensation for a particular class of employees, then the utility 
9 
must demonstrate that such a program will return quantifiable or 
10 
demonstrated benefits to customers in a financial sense or in terms of 
11 
reliability, environmental impact or customer service that justify the 
12 
variable pay expense.

V.
Cost Control Measures 
4 
Q.
What efforts has National Grid undertaken to control costs associated 
5 
with its health and welfare programs? 
6 
A.
National Grid has taken many steps to control the costs associated with 
7 
health and welfare benefit programs.  These steps include: 
8 
(i) The majority of National Grid’s health and welfare benefit plans are
9 
self-insured, which affords National Grid a greater ability to control costs 
10 
than it would have under third-party insurance programs.  Because these 
11 
plans are self-insured, the program costs are directly linked to the 
12 
utilization of benefits.  National Grid’s medical plans also provide 
13 
extensive health and wellness programs designed to reduce health risks 
14 
and thereby help mitigate costs.  These programs, combined with coverage 
15 
for preventive check-ups and screenings, provide a benefit structure that, 
16 
over time, should help to mitigate costs and improve employee wellness.  
17 
(ii) National Grid aggressively negotiates with vendors and periodically
18 
conducts a competitive bidding process to achieve the lowest 
19 
administrative service fees and premiums and to obtain maximum 
20 
discounts when rolling out a new program or upon the expiration of an 
21 
4910


--- Page 714 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
41 of 64 
existing contract.  For example, in late 2017, National Grid negotiated the 
1 
renewal of the contract with its national Pharmacy Benefits Manager 
2 
(“PBM”), CVS Caremark, which resulted in projected savings over the 
3 
term of the contract.  These savings are embedded in the Historic Test 
4 
Year level of expense.
5 
(iii) The prescription drug program is carved out of each medical plan and
6 
is administered in its entirety with a CVS Caremark plan.  Because CVS 
7 
Caremark is National Grid’s PBM for its entire U.S. business, National 
8

(v) Prior authorization for compounded drugs costing more than $300 is

4925


--- Page 729 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
56 of 64 
On an annual basis, National Grid analyzes the funding, recording, and 
1 
administration of OPEBs.  Less frequently, but on a consistent basis, 
2 
National Grid considers more significant changes designed to reduce the 
3 
overall cost of the OPEB plans. 
4 
5 
Q.
What challenges does National Grid face in considering fundamental 
6 
changes to retirement health and life insurance benefits on a frequent 
7 
basis?  
8 
A.
Retiree programs are unique among the collection of employee benefits.  
9 
Unlike health care programs for which employees derive current value, 
10 
retiree programs represent benefits to be provided in the future.  As such, 
11 
their value tends to accrue over a longer period of time.  Because of these 
12 
long accrual periods, significant changes in retiree programs are difficult 
13 
to adjust to when they occur close to or during retirement.  Preparation for 
14 
retirement involves assessing one’s financial preparedness provided 
15 
through benefit plans, Social Security, and individual savings.  Given the 
16 
fixed benefits payable under National Grid’s pension plan, and the 
17 
potential for significant health care expense as participants’ age, retiree 
18 
health insurance benefits are one of the key factors in reaching the 
19 
conclusion that one can retire.  Therefore, and as further outlined below, 
20 
National Grid has reached the conclusion that changes to OPEB benefit 
21 
4926


--- Page 730 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
57 of 64 
levels are only feasible in connection with major benefit alignments either 
1 
following corporate transactions, in connection with labor negotiations, or 
2 
when major legislative changes are made.  Any OPEB benefit change will 
3 
usually be done in connection with other benefit alignments and will 
4 
generally be carefully constructed to affect only those employees who 
5 
have sufficient time to adapt to the changes before reaching retirement 
6 
age.  
7 
8 
Another reason retiree programs are unique is the wide geographic 
9 
dispersion of the participants.  Unlike active employees, who live 
10 
geographically proximate to the Companies’ business operations, retirees 
11 
move to other parts of the United States and other countries.  This makes 
12 
communication with them and implementation of changes to their benefits 
13 
administratively burdensome and costly.  
14

collective bargaining agreement expires, unless they are renegotiated

Management employee benefits can be changed at any time.  However, 
7

8

9

10 
fully evaluating the impact on this connection.  In the case of OPEB 
11 
benefits in particular, a union employee would be unlikely to accept, let 
12 
alone seek, a management job that provides either significantly fewer or 
13 
less valuable benefits than he or she is eligible for under the union 
14

17 
the management team, as they can ably and immediately contribute to 
18 
meeting National Grid’s objective of providing safe and reliable service at 
19 
a reasonable cost.  Requiring union employees to accept benefit reductions 
20 
to move to management would be a significant impediment to any such 
21 
4928


--- Page 732 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
59 of 64 
moves.  National Grid’s desire to facilitate the promotion of union 
1 
employees manifests itself in a three to five-year cycle of OPEB benefit 
2 
level reviews for both union and management employees, absent a major 
3

4 
terms of the collective bargaining agreements.

6 
Q.
Please explain the OPEB analyses performed on an annual basis. 
7 
A.
The annual process to examine OPEBs focuses on the following three 
8 
categories: (i) actuarial assumptions around plan expense and funding; (ii) 
9 
general vendor performance reviews; and (iii) Medicare prescription drug 
10 
program refund administration. 
11 
Actuarial assumptions for expense and funding:  Each year, working with 
12 
its actuary, Aon, National Grid evaluates the proper level of several 
13 
actuarial factors used to determine plan expense and funding, including 
14 
discount rate, medical trend rate, and mortality rate.  Depending on 
15 
economic information and trends at the time, rates are either continued or 
16 
modified as appropriate.  In addition, National Grid evaluates various 
17 
options to ensure optimal funding of these benefits.   
18 
General vendor performance reviews:  All active and retiree benefit plan 
19 
administration is consolidated with a single vendor.  In addition, National 
20 
Grid’s benefits staff periodically meets with the third-party vendors who 
21 
4929


--- Page 733 ---
Testimony of Maureen P. Heaphy 
60 of 64 
are responsible for claims payments to review their performance.  National 
1 
Grid’s arrangements with these vendors are for administrative services 
2 
only, so the focus is on transaction performance and participant 
3 
satisfaction.  National Grid continuously reviews the delivery and 
4 
administration of the benefits under the retiree medical plan with the 
5 
ultimate objective of reducing administration costs and improving the 
6 
delivery of services.   
7 
Medicare prescription drug refund administration:  National Grid obtains 
8 
sizeable subsidies from the government in return for providing retiree drug 
9 
benefits to retirees who are 65 years of age or older (“Post 65 retirees”).  
10 
In 2013, National Grid implemented an Employer Group Waiver Plan for 
11 
Post 65 retiree prescription drug benefits.  This plan was more financially 
12 
advantageous to National Grid primarily because of the large 
13 
pharmaceutical manufacturer discounts on brand drugs as well as federal 
14 
catastrophic reinsurance payments.

III. REGULATORY GUIDELINES AND FINANCIAL
CONSIDERATIONS 
Q.
Please describe the guiding principles to be used in establishing the cost 
5 
of capital for a regulated utility. 
6 
A.
The United States Supreme Court’s precedent-setting Hope and Bluefield 
7 
cases established the standards for determining the reasonableness of a 
8 
utility’s allowed ROE.  Among the standards established by the Court in 
9 
those cases are:  (1) consistency with the returns on equity investments in 
10 
other businesses having similar or comparable risks; (2) adequacy of the 
11 
return to support credit quality and access to capital; and (3) an 
12 
understanding that the means of arriving at a fair return are not controlling, 
13 
only that the end result leads to just and reasonable rates.1 
14 
15 
Based on those standards, the Commission’s order in these cases should 
16 
provide the Companies with the opportunity to earn a ROE that is: (1) 
17 
adequate to attract capital at reasonable terms, thereby enabling them to 
18 
continue to provide safe, reliable service; (2) sufficient to support the 
19 
1  
Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591 (1944) (“Hope”); 
Bluefield Waterworks & Improvement Co., v. Public Service Commission of West 
Virginia, 262 U.S. 679 (1923) (”Bluefield”). 
4957


--- Page 761 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 8 of 103 
financial soundness of the Companies’ operations; and (3) commensurate 
1 
with returns on equity investments in enterprises having comparable risks.  
2 
The authorized ROE should enable the Companies to finance capital 
3 
expenditures at reasonable rates and maintain their financial flexibility over 
4 
the period during which rates are expected to remain in effect.  
5

Q.
Has the Commission conducted a proceeding to review the standard for 
7 
estimating the Cost of Capital for a regulated utility? 
8 
A.
Yes.  On August 21, 1991, the Commission established the GFP to review 
9 
the Commission’s then-current methodology for estimating the cost of 
10 
equity and to examine various alternatives.2 
11 
12 
Q.
Please provide a brief summary of the purpose of the GFP. 
13 
A.
The GFP was initiated because the Commission recognized that the DCF 
14 
method was particularly sensitive to interest rate fluctuations and was 
15 
producing returns far below the returns produced by other methodologies.3  
16 
The Commission’s goal in opening the GFP was to eliminate controversy 
17 
around ROE calculations and attempt to find common ground on 
18 
contentious issues by developing a consensus approach for setting utility 
19 
equity returns.  Among other things, the Commission examined whether 
20 
there should be greater consistency in rate of return determinations from 
21 
2  
Case 91-M-0509, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission to Consider Financial and 
Regulatory Policies for New York State Utilities, Recommended Decision, (issued 
July 19, 1994) (“Generic Finance RD”), at 2.

company to company, such that differences in returns could be directly

2

11

12 
A.
Ultimately, the RD concluded that the Commission should implement a 
13

14

15 
a combination of the DCF and CAPM methodologies.  The RD proposed to

18 
CAPM “should figure prominently in the analysis” because this 
19 
methodology provides fundamental information on interest rates and the 
20 
returns required by stocks as a result of changes in interest rates.  At that 
21 
time, the CAPM was not accorded the same level of prominence as the DCF 
22

3

Q.
Do the principles and intentions of the RD in the GFP require 
8 
adherence to a static formula? 
9 
A.
No.  The GFP and RD did not require rote adherence to a static formula, 
10 
rather, they promoted some basic principles and afforded parties the 
11 
flexibility to investigate approaches to address changing financial market 
12 
conditions.  The RD recognized the benefit of using multiple approaches for 
13 
setting ROE and although it found benefits to a preferred convention for 
14 
setting ROE, it did not bar parties from introducing new cost of capital 
15 
estimation methods or weightings and specifically recognized that there 
16 
may be circumstances where this would be superior.  Capital market 
17 
conditions vary widely over time and each ROE methodology (DCF and 
18 
CAPM) may be impacted differently by identical conditions.  The impact 
19 
of these conditions on ROE must be assessed and interpreted by the 
20 
practitioner to determine if their effects are directionally appropriate and are 
21 
of a reasonable magnitude.  Accordingly, it is incumbent on the practitioner 
22 
to review the results of the analyses and exercise judgment as to how to 
23

--- Page 766 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 13 of 103 
weight those results in the overall ROE determination.  A close read of the 
1 
RD reveals that the Commission expressed some uncertainty around the 
2 
correct level of weighting and certainly indicated a willingness to revisit its 
3 
proposed weightings in the future.  It is particularly fitting that the 
4 
Commission, which is seeking to update the traditional utility regulatory 
5 
model with new, innovative approaches suitable to current industry 
6 
circumstances in the New York Reforming the Energy Vision (“NY REV”) 
7

8 
demonstrate the flexibility to adapt the weightings of each methodology to 
9 
the applicable capital market conditions.      
10 
11 
Q.
Is flexibility of approach and judgment important to ROE 
12 
determination? 
13 
A.
Yes, it is.  When faced with the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts 
14 
are inclined to gather and evaluate as much relevant data (both quantitative 
15 
and qualitative) as can be reasonably analyzed.  Analysts and academics 
16 
understand that ROE models are tools to be used in the ROE estimation 
17 
process, and that strict adherence to any single approach, or the specific 
18 
results of any single approach, can lead to flawed conclusions.  No model 
19 
can exactly pinpoint the correct return on equity; rather, each model brings 
20 
its own perspective and set of inputs that inform the estimate of ROE.  That 
21 
position is consistent with the Hope finding that “[u]nder the statutory 
22 
4963


--- Page 767 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 14 of 103 
standard of ‘just and reasonable,’ it is the result reached, not the method 
1 
employed, which is controlling.”11  
2 
3 
Though each model brings a different perspective and adds depth to the 
4 
analysis, each model also has its own set of inherent weaknesses and should 
5 
not be relied upon individually without corroboration from other 
6 
approaches.  Changes to inputs as a result of changes in economic 
7 
conditions could have widely different effects on the results of the various 
8 
analyses.   
9 
10 
Regardless of which analyses are performed to estimate the investor’s 
11 
required return on equity, the analyst must apply judgment to assess the 
12 
reasonableness of results and to determine the best weighting to apply to 
13 
results under prevailing capital market conditions.  No one model can 
14 
reliably and consistently estimate the cost of capital that meets the fairness 
15 
standard of Hope and Bluefield in all market conditions.  
16 
17 
IV. CAPITAL MARKET CONDITIONS
Q.
Why is it important to analyze capital market conditions? 
18 
A.
The ROE estimation models rely on market data that are either specific to 
19 
the proxy group, in the case of the DCF model, or to the expectations of 
20 
market risk, in the case of the CAPM.  The results of the ROE estimation 
21 
11  Hope, 320 U.S. at 602. 
4964


--- Page 768 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 15 of 103 
models can be affected by prevailing market conditions at the time the 
1 
analysis is performed.  While the ROE that is established in a rate 
2 
proceeding is intended to be forward-looking, the analyst uses current and 
3 
projected market data, specifically stock prices, dividends, growth rates and 
4 
interest rates in the ROE estimation models to estimate the required return 
5 
for the subject company.   
6 
7 
As is discussed in the remainder of this section, analysts and regulatory 
8 
commissions have concluded that current market conditions have affected 
9 
the results of the ROE estimation models.  As a result, it is important to 
10 
consider the effect of these conditions on the ROE estimation models when 
11 
determining the appropriate range and recommended ROE for a future 
12 
period.  If investors do not expect current market conditions to be sustained 
13 
in the future, it is possible that the ROE estimation models will not provide 
14 
an accurate estimate of investors’ required return during that rate period. 
15 
Therefore, it is important to consider projected market data to estimate the 
16 
return for that forward-looking period. 
17 
18 
Q. 
What factors are affecting the cost of equity for regulated utilities in
19 
the current and projected capital markets? 
20 
A.
The cost of equity for regulated utility companies is being affected by 
21 
several factors in the current and prospective capital markets, including: (1) 
22 
the current low interest rate environment and the corresponding effect on 
23 
4965


--- Page 769 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 16 of 103 
valuations and dividend yields of utility stocks relative to historical levels; 
1 
(2) the market’s expectation for interest rates; and (3) recent Federal tax
2 
reform.  In this section, I discuss each of these factors and how it affects the 
3 
models used to estimate the cost of equity for regulated utilities.  
4 
5 
A. THE EFFECT OF MARKET CONDITIONS ON VALUATIONS
6 
Q.
How has the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy affected capital
7 
markets in recent years?
8 
A.
Extraordinary and persistent federal intervention in capital markets
9 
artificially lowered government bond yields after the Great Recession of
10 
2008-2009, as the Federal Open Market Committee (“FOMC”) used
11 
monetary policy (both reductions in short-term interest rates and purchases
12 
of Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities) to stimulate the U.S.
13 
economy.  As a result of very low or zero returns on short-term government
14 
bonds, yield-seeking investors have been forced into longer-term
15 
instruments, bidding up prices and reducing yields on those investments.
16 
As investors have moved along the risk spectrum in search of yields that
17 
meet their return requirements, there has been increased demand for
18 
dividend-paying equities, such as natural gas and electric utility stocks.
19 
20 
Q.
How has the period of abnormally low interest rates affected the 
21 
valuations and dividend yields of utility shares? 
22 
A.
The Federal Reserve’s accommodative monetary policy has caused 
23 
investors to seek alternatives to the historically low interest rates 
24 
4966


--- Page 770 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 17 of 103 
available on Treasury bonds.  A result of this search for higher yield is 
1 
that the share prices for many common stocks, especially dividend-
2 
paying stocks such as utilities, have been driven higher while the 
3 
dividend yields (which are computed by dividing the dividend payment 
4 
by the stock price) have decreased to levels well below the historical 
5 
average.   
6 
Q.
How have higher stock valuations and lower dividend yields for utility 
7 
companies affected the results of the DCF model?  
8 
A.
During periods of general economic and capital market stability, the DCF 
9 
model may adequately reflect market conditions and investor expectations. 
10 
However, in the current market environment, the DCF model results are 
11 
distorted by the historically low level of interest rates and the higher 
12 
valuation of utility stocks. Value Line recently commented on the high 
13 
valuations of electric utilities: 
14 
Even after a pullback in late 2018, most stocks in the 
15 
Electric Utility Industry are still priced expensively, in 
16 
our view. Many of the equities are still trading within 
17 
our 2021-2023 Target Price Range. The industry’s 
18

19 
yields that aren’t significantly higher than the median of 
20 
all stocks under our coverage. For the 3- to 5-year 
21 
period, the group’s average total return potential is just 
22 
5%.12
23 
24 
This is further supported by a recent Edward Jones report on the utility 
25 
sector:

10

11

12

15

16 
given recent market volatility and lagged effect that monetary policy has on 
17 
the economy, it is reasonable to expect the Federal Reserve to be patient 
18 
with future increases.  However, it is important to note, that the Federal 
19 
Reserve is continuing to reduce the size of its balance sheet by no longer 
20 
reinvesting the proceeds of the bonds it holds over the near-term. This 
21 
policy in conjunction with the lagged effect of past increases in the federal 
22 
funds rate suggests that the yields on long-term government bonds should 
23 
continue to increase over the near-term which is consistent with investors’

C. EFFECT OF TAX REFORM ON THE RETURN ON EQUITY AND CAPITAL
1 
STRUCTURE

Q.
Are there other factors that should be considered in determining the 
3 
cost of equity for the Companies?  
4 
A.
Yes.  The effect of the TCJA should also be considered in the determination 
5 
of the cost of equity. The credit rating agencies have commented on the 
6 
effect of the TCJA on regulated utilities.  In summary, the TCJA is expected 
7 
to reduce utility revenues due to the lower federal income taxes and the 
8 
requirement to return excess accumulated deferred income taxes.  This 
9 
change in revenue is expected to reduce Funds From Operations (“FFO”) 
10 
metrics across the sector, and absent regulatory mitigation strategies, is 
11 
expected to lead to weaker credit metrics and negative ratings actions for 
12 
some utilities.27  
13 
14

15 
utilities? 
16 
A.
Yes. Moody’s Investors Services (“Moody’s”) indicated that while the 
17 
TCJA was credit positive for many sectors, it has an overall negative credit 
18 
impact on regulated operating companies of utilities and their holding 
19 
companies due to the reduction in cash flow metrics that results from the 
20 
change in the federal tax rate and the loss of bonus depreciation.  
21 
22

Moody’s noted that the rates that regulators allow utilities to charge 
1

2

4

VI. COST OF EQUITY ESTIMATION
Q.
Please briefly discuss the ROE in the context of the regulated Rate of 
13 
Return. 
14 
A.
The rate of return (“ROR”) for a regulated utility is based on its weighted 
15 
average cost of capital, in which the costs of the individual sources of capital 
16 
are weighted by their respective percentages of total capitalization of the 
17 
4999


--- Page 803 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 50 of 103 
utility.  The ROE included in the ROR is weighted by the percentage of 
1 
common equity in the regulated utility’s ratemaking capital structure. 
2 
3 
Q.
How is the required ROE determined? 
4 
A.
While the cost of debt can be directly observed, the cost of equity and the 
5 
required ROE are market-based and, therefore, must be estimated based on 
6 
observable market information.  The required ROE is determined by using 
7 
one or more analytical techniques that rely on market data to quantify 
8 
investor expectations regarding the range of required equity returns.  
9 
Informed judgment is applied, based on the results of those analyses, to 
10 
determine where within the range of results the cost of equity for a company 
11 
falls.  As a general proposition, the key consideration in determining the 
12 
cost of equity is to ensure that the methodologies employed reasonably 
13 
reflect investors’ views of the financial markets, the proxy group 
14 
companies, and the subject company’s risk profile. 
15 
16 
Q.
What methods did you use to determine the Companies’ cost of equity? 
17 
A.
Consistent with Commission precedent, I used the DCF model and CAPM 
18 
as the primary approaches.  In establishing my recommended ROE, I relied 
19 
on a multi-stage form of the DCF model, and, consistent with the 
20 
Commission’s stated preference, I used both the traditional form of the 
21 
CAPM as well as the Zero-Beta form of that model.  In both forms of the 
22 
5000


--- Page 804 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 51 of 103 
CAPM, I incorporated a forward-looking measure of the Market Risk 
1 
Premium.  
2 
3 
Q.
Why do you believe it is important to use more than one analytical 
4 
approach? 
5 
A.
Because the cost of equity is not directly observable, it must be estimated 
6 
based on both quantitative and qualitative information.  When faced with 
7 
the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts and investors are inclined 
8 
to gather and evaluate as much relevant data as reasonably can be 
9 
analyzed.  As a result, a number of models have been developed to estimate 
10 
the cost of equity.  For that reason, I use multiple approaches to estimate the 
11 
cost of equity.  As a practical matter, however, all of the models available 
12 
for estimating the cost of equity are subject to limiting assumptions or other 
13 
methodological constraints.  Consequently, many finance texts recommend 
14 
using multiple approaches when estimating the cost of equity.  For example, 
15 
Copeland, Koller, and Murrin50 suggest using the CAPM and Arbitrage 
16 
Pricing Theory model, while Brigham and Gapenski51 recommend the 
17 
CAPM, DCF, and “bond yield plus risk premium” approaches.52
18 
50 Tom Copeland, Tim Koller and Jack Murrin, Valuation: Measuring and Managing the 
Value of Companies, 3rd Ed. (New York: McKinsey & Company, Inc., 2000), at 214. 
51 Eugene Brigham, Louis Gapenski, Financial Management: Theory and Practice, 7th 
Ed. (Orlando: Dryden Press, 1994), at 341. 
52 While it has historically been my practice to present the results of a bond yield plus 
risk premium approach in the context of estimating a reasonable ROE, I have not done 
so in this case to limit the number of contested issues.  The result of such an analysis, 
however, would suggest more weight should be placed on the CAPM ROE 
determinations. 
5001

Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 52 of 103 
1 
Q.
How are current market conditions affecting the results of the DCF and 
2 
CAPM models?  
3 
A.
As discussed in Section IV, there is concern that current capital market 
4 
conditions, characterized by historically low Treasury bond yields, are 
5 
causing utility stocks to be overvalued, thereby reducing the dividend yields 
6 
in the DCF model.  Consequently, the results of the DCF model are 
7 
understating the forward-looking cost of equity.  The CAPM method offers 
8 
some balance to the sensitivity of the DCF model to low Treasury bond 
9 
yields.  However, low interest rates also impact the CAPM in two ways: (1) 
10 
if the risk-free rate is based on historical average yields on Treasury bonds, 
11 
it understates the forward-looking risk-free rate, and (2) if the market risk 
12 
premium is based on historical returns on large company stocks minus the 
13 
historical average risk free rate, it understates the forward-looking market 
14 
risk premium.  To adjust for these shortcomings, the risk-free rate in the 
15 
CAPM analysis should also consider projected yields on Treasury bonds, 
16 
and the market risk premium should be based on a forward-looking 
17 
computation of the expected return on the total market less the risk-free rate. 
18 
Market risk premiums based on long-term historical averages are 
19 
unresponsive to movements in interest rates and would likely understate the 
20 
market risk premium and, accordingly, the cost of equity.   
21 
22 
5002


--- Page 806 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 53 of 103 
Q.
What are your conclusions about the results of the DCF and CAPM 
1 
models?  
2 
A.
The results of both models have been affected by market conditions and, 
3 
with traditional data inputs, have a tendency to underestimate the current 
4 
cost of equity.  The DCF model is less reliable in current market conditions 
5 
because dividend yields for utilities are low and not expected to remain at 
6 
current levels.  As discussed in Section IV, reports from Value Line and 
7 
Edward Jones demonstrate the expected change in market conditions 
8 
implies that the ROE calculated using historical market data in the DCF 
9 
model may understate the forward-looking cost of equity. The results from 
10 
the CAPM are also affected by the current artificially low yields on 
11 
Treasury bonds.  The use of projected yields on Treasury bonds in the 
12 
CAPM produces returns that are more reflective of the market conditions 
13 
that investors expect during the period that the Companies’ rates will be in 
14 
effect.  Therefore, properly specified, the CAPM may be a more reliable 
15 
model in current market conditions than the DCF.  Given the sensitivity of 
16 
each model to market conditions and considering the expectation for 
17 
changes in those conditions, it is appropriate to equally weight the results 
18 
of the DCF and CAPM models.

A. DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW MODEL
1 
Q. 
Please describe the DCF approach.
2 
A.
The DCF approach is based on the theory that a stock’s current market price 
3 
represents the present value of all expected future cash flows.  In its most 
4 
general form, the DCF model is expressed as follows: 
5 
ܲ଴=
஽భ
ሺଵା௥ሻభ+
஽మ
ሺଵା௥ሻమ+ ⋯+
஽೙
ሺଵା௥ሻ೙ 
[1]
6 
Where P0 represents the current market stock price, D1 … Dn are all 
7 
expected future dividends, and r is the discount rate, or required ROE.  As 
8 
discussed below, I have not included the constant growth form of the DCF 
9 
model, but instead have focused on a multi-stage form of the DCF model.   
10 
11 
Q.
Please generally describe the DCF model you relied on.  
12 
A.
The multi-stage DCF model is an extension of the constant growth form that 
13 
enables the analyst to specify growth rates over multiple stages.  As with 
14 
the constant growth form of the DCF model, the multi-stage form defines 
15 
the cost of equity as the discount rate that sets the current price equal to the 
16 
discounted value of future cash flows.  A multi-stage DCF model addresses 
17 
the possibility that mean five-year growth rates may not be reasonable in 
18 
perpetuity and that payout ratios could vary over time. 
19 
20 
Q.
Please describe the structure of the multi-stage DCF model.  
21 
A.
The multi-stage DCF model that I have used sets the proxy company’s 
22 
current stock price equal to the present value of future cash flows received 
23 
4901
5004


--- Page 808 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 55 of 103 
over three time periods.  In all three periods, cash flows are equal to the 
1 
annual dividend payments that stockholders receive.  The first period is a 
2 
short-term growth period that consists of the first five years; the second 
3 
period is a transition period from the short-term growth rate to the long-term 
4 
growth rate that occurs over five years (i.e., years 6 through 10); and the 
5 
third period is a long-term growth period that begins in year 11 and 
6 
continues in perpetuity.  The ROE is then calculated as the rate of return 
7 
that results from the initial stock investment and the dividend payments over 
8 
the analytical period. 
9 
10 
Q.
Has the Commission relied on a multi-stage DCF model in prior cases? 
11 
A.
Yes, the Commission has relied on a two-stage form of the DCF model in 
12 
prior cases.53  The two-stage model that the Commission has relied on and 
13 
the multi-stage model that I rely on both define the cost of equity as the 
14 
discount rate that sets the current stock price equal to the discounted value 
15 
of future cash flows that are expressed as projected dividends.  Both models 
16 
project dividends using growth rates over multiple periods.   
17 
53 See Case 10-E-0362, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates,

Service, Order Establishing Rates for Electric Service, (issued June 17, 2011) (“2011 
O&R Rate Order”), at 68-69.   
5005

Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 56 of 103 
1 
Q.
Is the multi-stage form of the DCF model consistent with the intent of 
2 
the two-stage model relied upon by the Commission? 
3 
A.
Yes.  Both the construction of the multi-stage model and the underlying 
4 
assumptions are consistent with the two-stage model relied upon by the 
5 
Commission.  The constant growth DCF model assumes the expected 
6 
growth rate will be constant in perpetuity. The multi-stage forms of the DCF 
7 
model, including both the two-stage model that the Commission has relied 
8 
upon and the multi-stage form of the model that is relied on in my analysis, 
9 
recognize short and long-term growth prospects.

1 
Q.
Why do you believe that earnings growth rates are the appropriate 
2 
growth rates in the DCF model? 
3 
A.
Earnings are the fundamental driver of a company’s ability to pay 
4 
dividends; therefore, earnings growth is the appropriate measure of a 
5 
company’s long-term growth. In contrast, changes in a company’s dividend 
6 
payments are based on management decisions related to cash management 
7 
and other factors.  For example, a company may decide to retain certain 
8 
earnings rather than include those earnings in a dividend issuance.  
9 
Therefore, dividend growth rates are less likely than earnings growth rates 
10 
to reflect investor perceptions of a company’s growth prospects.   
11 
12 
Q.
Is there support for the use of analysts’ earnings growth estimates in 
13 
the DCF model? 
14 
A.
Yes, there is significant academic support for the use of analysts’ earnings 
15 
growth rates.  In addition, the majority of the data that are publicly available 
16 
to investors sets forth analysts’ projections of earnings growth rates.  Value 
17 
Line is the only publication I am aware of that provides projected dividend 
18 
growth rates.

Q.
Why is the long-term GDP growth rate a reasonable estimate of long-
5 
term growth in the multi-stage DCF model? 
6 
A.
Long-term estimates of GDP growth are commonly used in regulatory 
7 
proceedings as a proxy for the long-term growth rate in the multi-stage DCF 
8 
analysis.  That application is based on the common theoretical assumption 
9 
that, over the long-run, all companies in the economy will tend to grow at 
10 
the same constant rate.  That assumption is designed to address the 
11 
uncertainty associated with estimating individual company growth rates 
12 
over very long time horizons and is not meant to suggest that company 
13 
growth rates in the economy will indeed converge in practice over any given 
14 
period.   
15

19

20 
period possible to measure historical real growth in GDP.  This view is 
21 
consistent with Morningstar’s explanation about measuring GDP growth:

Q.

11

12 
years 4-6; and (8) current three-month stock price.  Each of these 
13

14 
using these assumptions, the sustainable growth rate, which is applied over 
15 
the long-term in the Commission’s two-stage model, does not consider any 
16 
actual long-term forecasts for the specific company or the economy.

Q.
Please briefly describe the Capital Asset Pricing Model.
17 
A.
The CAPM is a risk premium approach that estimates the market cost of
18 
equity for a given security as a function of a risk-free return plus a risk
19 
premium (to compensate investors for the non-diversifiable or “systematic”
20 
risk of that security).  As shown in Equation [2], the CAPM is defined by
21 
four components:
22 
ke = rf + β(rm – rf)

4

5

6

7 
concerned only with systematic or non-diversifiable risk because 
8

9 
measured by the Beta coefficient, which is defined as:

14 
that security will respond to a given change in the market return.

In determining the security most relevant to the application of the CAPM, 
2 
it is important to select the term (or maturity) that best matches the life of 
3 
the underlying investment.  As noted by Morningstar: 
4 
The traditional thinking regarding the time horizon of 
5 
the chosen Treasury security is that it should match the 
6 
time horizon of whatever is being valued…  Note that 
7 
the horizon is a function of the investment, not the 
8 
investor.  If an investor plans to hold stock in a company 
9 
for only five years, the yield on a five-year Treasury 
10 
note would not be appropriate since the company will 
11 
continue to exist beyond those five years.80 
12 
Because utility companies represent long-duration investments, it is 
13 
appropriate to use yields on long-term Treasury bonds as the risk-free rate 
14 
component of the CAPM.  In my view, the 30-year Treasury bond is the 
15 
appropriate security for that purpose.  Because the cost of capital is intended 
16 
to be forward-looking, it is appropriate to consider projected measures of 
17 
the market risk premium and interest rates. 
18 
19

20

21 
A.
The estimated market risk premium is based on the expected return on the 
22 
S&P 500 Index, less the 30-year Treasury bond yield.  The expected return 
23 
on the S&P 500 Index is calculated using a DCF model for all companies 
24 
in the index based on market capitalization-weighted growth rates and 
25 
79 Aspen Publishers, Blue Chip Financial Forecasts, Vol. 37, No. 12 December 1, 2018, 
14.. 
80 Morningstar Inc., Ibbotson SBBI 2013 Valuation Yearbook, at 44. 
5022

dividend yields.  The market risk premium implied by each of the three 
1 
Treasury yields discussed above is used in the CAPM analysis.

Q.
Did you consider another form of the CAPM in your analysis? 
10 
A.
Yes.  In prior proceedings, the Commission has relied upon the Zero-Beta 
11 
CAPM (the form of which is sometimes referred to as the “Empirical 
12 
CAPM”84) in estimating the cost of equity.  The Zero-Beta CAPM 
13 
calculates the product of the adjusted Beta coefficient and the market risk 
14 
premium and applies a weight of 75.00 percent to that result.  The model 
15 
then applies a 25.00 percent weight to the market risk premium, without any 
16 
effect from the Beta coefficient.  The results of the two calculations are 
17 
summed, along with the risk-free rate, to produce the Zero-Beta CAPM 
18 
result, as noted in Equation [4] below:   
19 
ke = rf + 0.75β(rm – rf) + 0.25(rm – rf)  
[4] 
20 
where: 
21

2006, at 189.

1 
β = Adjusted Beta coefficient of an individual security 
2 
 
rf = the risk-free rate of return 
3 
 
rm = the required return on the market as a whole 
4 
5 
In essence, the Zero-Beta form of the CAPM addresses the tendency of the 
6 
“traditional” CAPM to underestimate the cost of equity for companies with 
7 
low Beta coefficients such as regulated utilities.  In that regard, the Zero-
8 
Beta CAPM is not redundant to the use of adjusted Betas; rather, it 
9 
recognizes the results of academic research indicating that the risk-return 
10 
relationship is different (in essence, flatter) than estimated by the CAPM, 
11 
and that the CAPM underestimates the “alpha,” or the constant return 
12 
term.85   
13 
14 
As with the CAPM, my application of the Zero-Beta CAPM uses the 
15

16

17

Q.
What was the Commission’s reasoning for developing its weighting of 
1 
the DCF and CAPM methodologies in the RD? 
2 
A.
At the time of the RD, the Commission did not have a significant amount 
3 
of experience with the CAPM.  The RD noted that the Commission had 
4 
historically used the CAPM as a check on its DCF results, and was 
5 
somewhat undecided as to “how far the Commission should go in elevating 
6 
the status of CAPM.”86   The RD opted for a gradual transition towards the 
7 
CAPM, ultimately settling on a 1/3 weighting, indicating that “proposals 
8 
have simply not shown that the CAPM should be raised all at once to parity 
9 
with the DCF analysis in the setting of returns on equity.”87  To the extent 
10 
that this was a consideration in the RD’s weighting determination, the 
11 
Commission’s 25 years of experience with the CAPM since that time 
12 
provides a sound basis for altering the weighting of the two ROE 
13 
methodologies.

16

17

18 
methodologies used to estimate the ROE were left open for additional 
19 
consideration in future rate proceedings.  Since then, the Commission has 
20 
employed the CAPM as one component of the formula used to develop ROE 
21 
estimates.  There does not appear to be any reason to infer that the 
22

Commission has less confidence in the results of the CAPM than those of 
1

2

3

10 
11 
Q.
Are the assumptions used in the CAPM less reliable than the 
12 
assumptions used in the DCF model? 
13 
A.
Not necessarily.  As discussed previously, the CAPM relies on a risk-free 
14 
rate, Beta and the MRP.  The risk-free rate is readily observable and can be 
15 
projected for the forward-looking period.  Beta is estimated using the 
16 
historical relationship between the risk of the stock and the overall market. 
17 
Finally, the market risk premium, while not observable, can be estimated 
18 
for the forward-looking period. My testimony discusses how the dividend 
19 
yield has been affected by market conditions and therefore, while this 
20 
assumption may be easy to calculate using historical data, it is not 
21 
representative of forward-looking market conditions.  Therefore, while the 
22 
CAPM is often criticized as relying on unobservable assumptions, currently 
23 
5029


--- Page 833 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 80 of 103 
the dividend yield in the DCF model is not reflective of projected market 
1 
conditions.

B. REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT
1 
Q.
Please explain how the regulatory framework affects investors’ risk
2 
assessments.
3 
A.
The ratemaking process is premised on the principle that, for investors and
4 
companies to commit the capital needed to provide safe and reliable utility
5 
services, the subject utility must have the opportunity to recover invested
6 
capital and the market-required return on such capital.  Regulatory
7 
commissions recognize that because utility operations are capital intensive,
8 
regulatory decisions should enable the utility to attract capital at reasonable
9 
terms, which balance the long-term interests of investors and customers.  In
10 
that respect, the regulatory framework in which a utility operates is one of
11 
the most important factors considered in both debt and equity investors’ risk
12 
assessments.
13 
14 
Because investors have many investment alternatives, even within a given 
15 
market sector, the Companies’ authorized returns must be adequate on a 
16 
relative basis to ensure their ability to attract capital under a variety of 
17 
economic and financial market conditions.  From the perspective of debt 
18 
investors, the authorized return should enable the Companies to generate 
19 
the cash flow needed to meet their near-term financial obligations, make the 
20 
capital investments needed to maintain and expand their systems, and 
21 
maintain sufficient levels of liquidity to fund unexpected events.  This 
22 
financial liquidity must be derived not only from internally-generated funds, 
23 
but also from efficient access to capital markets.     
24 
5034


--- Page 838 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 85 of 103 
1 
From the perspective of equity investors, the authorized return must be 
2 
adequate to provide a risk-comparable return on the equity portion of the 
3 
Companies’ capital investments.  Because equity investors are the residual 
4 
claimants on the Companies’ cash flows (that is, debt interest must be paid 
5 
prior to any equity dividends), equity investors are particularly concerned 
6 
with the regulatory framework in which a utility operates and its effect on 
7 
future earnings and cash flows. 
8 
9

IX. MULTI-YEAR RATE PLAN
Q.
Would a multi-year rate plan impact your ROE recommendation?   
15 
A.
Yes, it would.  The Commission has in many cases approved three-year rate 
16 
case settlements that often include stay-out premiums.  It is my 
17 
understanding that the Companies will provide four years of forecast data 
18 
in their rate filings.  In keeping with Commission precedent, a stay-out 
19 
premium would reflect the increased risk faced by the Companies under a 
20 
multi-year rate plan. 
21 
22 
5050


--- Page 854 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 101 of 103 
Q.
How has New York typically estimated a stay-out premium?  
1 
A.
The New York approach has typically set the measure of the risk and return 
2 
trade-off using one half of the yield spread between a one-year and three-
3 
year Treasury securities.   
4 
5 
Q.
Does one half of the yield spread between one-year and three-year 
6 
Treasuries sufficiently reflect the risk to equity investors inherent in a 
7 
multi-year stay-out?  
8 
A.
No.  The stay-out premium associated with a multi-year rate plan should not 
9 
only compensate investors for changes in the level of interest rates or 
10 
inflation, but also for the potential risk of under-earning that is introduced 
11 
by “staying out.”  By staying out of rate cases, the utility may not fully 
12 
recover material amounts of capital expenditures and may be required to 
13 
absorb losses due to differences between the cost of service established in 
14 
the rate plan and actual levels of revenue and expense.  The premium should 
15 
compensate the utility and its investors for these additional risks over and 
16 
above interest rate risk.  In the current market environment, there is 
17 
additional risk that the authorized ROE for the latter years of a multi-year 
18 
rate plan will be lower than investors’ future requirements as interest rates 
19 
are expected to increase.  
20 
21 
5051


--- Page 855 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 102 of 103 
Q.
What do you propose as the stay-out premium for a four-year rate 
1 
plan?  
2 
A.
The ROE proposed by the Companies of 9.65 percent will not provide the 
3 
Companies a return commensurate with the return available on investments 
4 
of similar risk over the term of the multi-year rate plan without an adequate 
5 
stay-out premium.  Consistent with prior cases in which a stay-out premium 
6 
was included in multi-year rate plans, I recommend that a stay-out premium 
7 
be included in a multi-year rate plan.  I believe 50 basis points is a 
8 
reasonable, albeit conservative, reflection of the incremental risk to the 
9 
Company under a multi-year stay-out provision.  
10

A. PROXY GROUP COMPOSITION
18 
Q.
What is your position with respect to the proxy group composition?
19 
An appropriately constructed proxy group consists of companies that are
20 
comparable in business and financial risk to the Companies.  The
21 
importance of selecting a proxy group that is similar in overall financial and
22 
business risk to the subject company was endorsed by the United States
23 
Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia (the “DC Circuit”) in the
24 
5067


--- Page 871 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley 
Page 13 of 73 
Petal Gas Storage decision.  The DC Circuit acknowledged that the goal of 
1 
a proxy group is to rely on companies that possess similar risk to the subject 
2 
company for the determination of the cost of equity: 
3 
That proxy group arrangements must be risk-
4 
appropriate is the common theme in each argument. 
5 
The principle is well-established.  See Hope Natural 
6 
Gas Co., 320 U.S. at 603 (“[T]he return to the equity 
7 
owner should be commensurate with returns on 
8 
investments in other enterprises having corresponding 
9 
risks.”); CAPP I, 254 F.3d at 293 (“[A] utility must offer 
10 
a risk-adjusted expected rate of return sufficient to 
11 
attract investors.”).  The principle captures what proxy 
12 
groups do, namely, provide market-determined stock 
13 
and 
dividend 
figures 
from 
public 
companies 
14 
comparable to a target company for which those figures 
15 
are unavailable.  CAPP I, 254 F.3d at 293–94.  Market-
16 
determined stock figures reflect a company’s risk level 
17 
and, when combined with dividend values, permit 
18 
calculation of the “risk-adjusted expected rate of return 
19 
sufficient to attract investors.” 
20 
21 
*** 
22 
What matters is that the overall proxy group 
23 
arrangement makes sense in terms of relative risk and, 
24 
even more importantly, in terms of the statutory 
25 
command to set “just and reasonable” rates, 15 U.S.C. § 
26 
717c, that are “commensurate with returns on 
27 
investments in other enterprises having corresponding 
28 
risks” and “sufficient to assure confidence in the 
29 
financial integrity of the enterprise . . . [and] maintain 
30 
its credit and . . . attract capital,” Hope Natural Gas Co., 
31 
320 U.S. at 603.10
32 
33 
Consistent with the DC Circuit’s decision, I have selected a proxy group of 
34 
companies with comparable investment risk to the Companies.  In contrast,

18

19 
companies as the near-term growth rate, and an estimate of growth in the 
20

21

23 
projections from a single source (i.e., Value Line) for their near-term growth 
24

rate, and a “sustainable growth rate” for their long-term growth rate.   Staff 
1

2

3

4

6

7

8 
discussed in my Direct Testimony, dividend growth is fundamentally driven 
9 
by earnings growth.40  While the model is, indeed, called the “Discounted 
10

11 
expect to receive during the time they own the stock.  Those cash flows are 
12 
quarterly dividend payments plus any capital appreciation that occurs 
13 
between when the stock is purchased and when it is sold.  Dividend 
14 
payments and capital appreciation are both a function of earnings per share 
15 
(“EPS”), which is ultimately what determines the return on equity to the 
16 
investor.  As discussed in my Direct Testimony, dividends are based on 
17 
management decisions related to cash management and other factors, and 
18 
therefore dividend growth rates are less likely to accurately reflect 
19 
investors’ growth expectations than earnings growth rates.41

Q. 
Why is it reasonable to rely on historical averages of real GDP growth 
1 
to approximate future economic activity? 
2 
I disagree with Staff that historical averages “are poor indicators of future 
3 
economic activity.”54  Based on current and recent market conditions, the 
4 
use of historical real GDP growth is more appropriate than using a current 
5 
projection of real GDP growth.  Economists have reviewed historical 
6 
growth patterns related to severe financial crises and have concluded that 
7 
estimates of GDP growth have generally been understated in the decade 
8 
following severe financial crises.  Specifically, the financial crisis and 
9 
recession that began in 2007 were qualitatively different from most other 
10 
U.S. economic downturns, which were followed by a rapid return to pre-
11 
recession overall output growth levels.  In that regard, the current U.S. 
12 
economic growth situation is similar to that following the two most severe 
13 
economic events in U.S. history (i.e., the 1929 stock market crash and the 
14 
1973 oil shock).  Economists who have examined the repercussions of those 
15 
two historical crises (and similar severe financial crises in other countries) 
16 
have found that GDP growth rates tended to be lower during the decade 
17 
following such events.55  Therefore, it would not be appropriate to assume 
18 
that current projections of GDP growth are representative of long-term GDP 
19 
growth starting in 2029 and continuing for the next 200 years. 
20

7

8

9

10

11

12

13 
flows.  Specifically, the XIRR function allows the analysis to reflect the 
14

15

16 
are paid in the second half of the year).  Staff has provided an analysis 
17 
demonstrating that the difference in the underlying assumptions between 
18 
the IRR and XIRR formulas could be as much as 70 basis points.59  In this 
19 
case, the difference in the underlying assumptions between the IRR and 
20 
XIRR formulas has an effect of 11 to 21 basis points on my DCF analysis.

1

2

3

4

5

6

involved in the index.  Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that the average 
8 
growth of the index could be sustainable in the long run.

Q.
Please describe how you derived the delivery forecasts for KEDNY 
1 
and KEDLI. 
2 
A.
On an annual basis, the Companies prepare their gas load forecasts based 
3 
on econometric/statistical forecast models developed for residential, 
4 
commercial/industrial, and multifamily rate groups.  The instant forecasts 
5 
were based on historical billing data from March 2007 through February 
6 
2018.   
7 
8 
Although the Companies maintain their customer data at the internal rate 
9 
code level (67 unique rate codes for KEDNY and 52 unique rate codes for 
10 
KEDLI), the data from these rate codes were aggregated into six rate 
11 
groups: Residential Heating, Residential Non-Heating, Commercial, 
12 
Multi-Family, Temperature-Controlled, and Other.  By aggregating its 
13 
data into these six groups, the Companies developed population sets that 
14 
were large enough for statistical modeling as well as free of variations that 
15 
are not driven by economic factors.  The tables below summarize the 
16 
service classifications that comprised the rate groups: 
17 
18

2 
Two different models were developed for each rate group: (i) a model to 
3 
forecast the number of customers (the number of active, flowing meters), 
4 
and (ii) a model to forecast use-per-customer.  The Companies’ volume 
5 
forecasts are then the product of number of customers multiplied by the 
6 
use-per-customer.  The customer count and use-per-customer models are 
7 
developed using linear regression techniques, and are selected based on 
8 
their adjusted R squared after accounting for the effects of autocorrelation 
9 
and heteroscedasticity.   
10 
11 
In the number of customer (meter count) models, the independent 
12 
variables are a combination of time trends and economic variables, such 
13 
as population, households, employment, and gas and oil prices.  In the

II.
Ratemaking Capital Structure 
1 
Q.
What capital structure does KEDNY propose to use for ratemaking purposes in this 
2 
proceeding? 
3 
A.
For a utility that is part of a holding company structure, New York State Public Service 
4 
Commission (“Commission”) precedent supports setting rates using the utility’s stand-
5 
alone capital structure where the utility can demonstrate that it is financially insulated from 
6 
its parent and its capital structure is reasonable and in line with its own financial and 
7 
business risks.  KEDNY is proposing for ratemaking purposes to use a capital structure 
8 
that contains 48 percent common equity for the Rate Year.  However, as shown in the table 
9 
above, should this proceeding result in a settlement where rates are established for multiple 
10 
years, KEDNY proposes that the capital structure should reflect 49 percent common equity 
11 
in Data Year 1 and 50 percent common equity in Data Years 2 and 3.   
12 
13 
KEDNY believes an increase in common equity in the Data Years is appropriate given the 
14 
interest of maintaining its credit ratings and achieving continued favorable financing for 
15 
the benefit of customers.  KEDNY’s cash flow metrics have been declining over the last 
16 
few years and it is important that the rates established in this proceeding ensure that those 
17 
metrics do not continue to decline further.  As discussed more fully below, the credit rating 
18 
agency Moody’s Investor Services, Inc. (“Moody’s”) has reviewed the Company’s 
19 
business and financial forecasts and does not envision cash flow generation to improve in 
20 
the medium term, citing the impact of the passage of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 
21 
(“Tax Reform Act”) and environmental remediation spending as two main contributing 
22 
factors.  Higher common equity will improve cash generation during a period when 
23 
5207


--- Page 1011 ---
Page 5 of 17 
Moody’s sees limited prospects for improvement, reducing risks of credit rating 
1 
downgrades.   
2 
Moody’s has recognized that changes in utility capital structures to reflect more equity 
3 
could act as an offset to negative cash flow impacts.  It is important that the rates established 
4 
in this proceeding ensure that KEDNY’s cash flow metrics do not decline to a level that 
5 
would not support its current A3 rating. 
6 
7 
Q.
Is KEDNY part of a holding company corporate structure? 
8 
A.
Yes.  KEDNY is indirectly owned by National Grid, which is owned by National Grid plc, 
9 
the ultimate parent of KEDNY. 
10 
11 
Q.
Is KEDNY financially insulated from National Grid plc? 
12 
A.
Yes. KEDNY is financially insulated from National Grid plc, and this insulation is 
13 
recognized by the financial marketplace.  Illustrating this point, in its February 2018 ratings 
14 
report on KEDNY, Moody’s explained that:  
15 
…the strong ring-fencing provisions applicable to New York 
16 
utilities reduces the potential for debt to be pushed down into 
17 
KEDNY. In particular, we view the explicit leverage restriction for 
18 
KEDNY (to maintain a debt to capitalization ratio of less than 56%) 
19 
as providing the greatest credit support at the current rating level.  
20 
This provision compares favorably against other New York utilities 
21 
within the NG group.  Additional ring-fencing provisions imposed 
22 
by the NYSPC for KEDNY that we view as credit supportive 
23 
include: (1) the “special preferred share” provision that reduces the 
24 
probability of bankruptcy in a distressed situation and (2) the 
25 
requirement for KEDNY to hold an investment grade rating. 
26 
Similarly, in its September 2018 report on KEDNY, Standard & Poor’s (“S&P”) stated 
27 
that:   
28 
5208


--- Page 1012 ---
Page 6 of 17 
We assess the group status of BUG [“Brooklyn Union Gas” aka 
1 
“KEDNY”] as core to National Grid PLC. At the same time, we 
2 
assess BUG as insulated, with existing insulation measures 
3 
supporting a one-notch separation between the subsidiary and its 
4 
parent. Key insulating measures include:  
5 
•
Prohibition of dividend distributions if the company does not
6 
maintain investment grade credit ratings with at least two of
7 
the three major ratings agencies.
8 
•
Prohibition of dividend increases and payments if the
9 
company's debt-to-capital ratio exceeds a certain amount.
10 
•
A golden share whose vote is required to file the utility into
11 
a voluntary bankruptcy.
12 
•
Clear economic and strategic incentive from the parent to
13 
maintain BUG's financial strength.
14 
KEDNY issues debt on a stand-alone basis and has a credit rating separate from National 
15 
Grid plc and its affiliates.  Specifically, while KEDNY has senior unsecured ratings of A3, 
16 
A-, and A- from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch Ratings, Inc. (“Fitch”), respectively, Moody’s, 
17 
S&P, and Fitch rate National Grid plc as Baa1, BBB+, and BBB+, respectively.  Moreover, 
18 
KEDNY has distinct business risks from National Grid plc.  KEDNY operates a gas 
19 
distribution business in downstate New York, whereas National Grid plc is an international 
20 
energy company with operations in the United Kingdom and the US, and operates in an 
21 
array of markets and lines of business. 
22 
23 
Q.
On average, did KEDNY’s capital structure include at least 48 percent common 
24 
equity in the Historic Test Year? 
25 
A.
Yes.  KEDNY’s average capital structure during the Historic Test Year consisted of at least 
26 
48 percent common equity.
