ENERGY COST BURDEN ANALYSIS 
17 
Q.
HAS THE PANEL PERFORMED AN ANALYSIS OF THE ENERGY 
18 
COST BURDEN ON UTILITY CUSTOMERS WITHIN NEW YORK 
19 
CITY? 
20 
5344


--- Page 1148 ---
A.
Yes.  We have performed an analysis of the energy cost burden on customers
1 
whose income falls below certain levels.  Our analysis and conclusions are
2 
summarized in Exhibit__(LIP-1).
3 
Q.
PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR ENERGY COST BURDEN ANALYSIS.
4 
A.
We performed a quantitative analysis of the economic burden placed on families
5 
from their electric and gas utility bills, with a particular focus on low income New
6 
York City residents.  We compared data on actual energy cost burdens to the
7 
policy the Commission set on page 3 of its May 20, 2016 Order Adopting Low
8 
Income Program Modifications and Directing Utility Filings in Case 14-M-0565,
9 
or Low Income Order, that “an energy burden at or below six percent of household
10 
income shall be the target level for all 2.3 million low income households in New
11 
York.”  That is, New Yorkers should pay no more than six percent of their
12 
household income for utility expenses.  Additionally, based on the Commission’s
13 
guidance that gas bills should account for no more than half of utility burden, we
14 
compared gas costs against a three percent affordability threshold to understand
15 
how gas bills impact energy cost burden.1  We are using the results from that
16 
analysis to support our proposal to provide more assistance to those families in
17 
New York City whose energy burdens exceed – in some cases significantly – the
18 
Commission’s affordability targets.
19 
Q.
WHO PERFORMED THE ANALYSIS?
20 
1 See Low Income Order at 23 (“Gas service (whether designated as heating or non-heating) is discounted 
to one-half of a customer’s total home energy burden.”). 
5345


--- Page 1149 ---
A.
Mr. Patané and Ms. D’Onofrio performed the analysis with assistance from others
1 
within the New York City Mayor’s Office of Sustainability and the Mayor’s
2 
Office of Economic Opportunity.
3 
Q.
ON WHAT DATA IS THE ANALYSIS BASED?
4 
A.
The analysis started with the publicly available 2017 Public Use Micro Sample,
5 
which is part of the American Community Survey, or ACS.  The survey is
6 
conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau on an ongoing basis and asks a
7 
representative sample of Americans questions related to income, housing, and
8 
other topics.  The ACS is designed to provide measures of socioeconomic
9 
conditions on an annual basis for states and larger localities.  It offers a statistically
10 
representative sample for New York City.  As discussed in its general handbook,
11 
the ACS uses a weighting method to ensure that its estimates are consistent with
12 
official Census Bureau population estimates by age, sex, race, and Hispanic origin,
13 
as well as estimates of total housing units.
14 
The ACS is a standard tool for measuring need.  According to the Census 
15 
Bureau, information from the ACS generates data that helps determine how more 
16 
than $675 billion in federal and state funds are distributed each year.  In questions 
17 
related to housing, the ACS asks respondents to report the cost incurred for 
18 
electricity and gas in the previous month and the cost incurred for fuel oil or 
19 
kerosene in the past 12 months.  Because costs are reported as incurred, they are 
20 
presumed to be net of any direct utility discounts.  Also reported in the ACS is 
21 
5346


--- Page 1150 ---
income from wages, transfer payments, self-employment, retirement income, and 
1 
investment. 
2 
Q.
HOW DID YOU DEFINE THE TERM “ENERGY COST BURDEN” FOR 
3 
PURPOSES OF YOUR ANALYSIS?   
4 
A.
For our analysis, we defined energy cost burden as the sum of (1) reported out-of-
5 
pocket monthly natural gas expenses multiplied by 12 plus (2) reported out-of-
6 
pocket monthly electricity expenses multiplied by 12 plus (3) reported annual 
7 
other energy expenses, such as fuel oil or kerosene purchases, minus an estimated 
8 
HEAP benefit, divided by annual pre-tax income.  Tax credits and non-cash 
9 
subsidies are not included in the income calculation.  A family is determined to be 
10 
energy cost burdened if its energy cost burden is greater than six percent.  Six 
11 
percent is both the State target and a target level used by energy affordability 
12 
experts, including, for example, Fisher, Sheehan & Colton Public Finance and 
13 
General Economics, who report a Home Energy Affordability Gap and whose 
14 
work was relied upon by Department Staff and the Commission in establishing the 
15 
State’s target. 
16 
Q.
HOW DID YOU DEFINE THE TERM “GAS COST BURDEN” FOR 
17 
PURPOSES OF YOUR ANALYSIS?   
18 
We defined gas cost burden as reported out-of-pocket monthly gas expenses 
19 
multiplied by 12 minus a HEAP estimate divided by the same pre-tax income used 
20 
for energy cost burden.  A family is considered gas cost burdened if their gas cost 
21 
burden exceeds three percent (half of the total electric plus gas affordability 
22 
5347


--- Page 1151 ---
target).  This is in line with the guidance established by the Commission for 
1 
implementing the low income utility discounts.  
2 
Q.
PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR METHODOLOGY FOR CALCULATING A 
3 
HEAP ESTIMATE. 
4 
A.
To calculate a HEAP estimate, we took the average New York City non-
5 
emergency HEAP benefit paid for the 2017 federal fiscal year, as reported in the 
6 
New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance’s Temporary and 
7 
Disability Assistance Statistics released in September 2017.  This yields an 
8 
average HEAP benefit of $46.50.  This comparatively low amount reflects the fact 
9 
that most NYC residents do not receive a full HEAP benefit because many are 
10 
renters and do not directly pay for their heating bills. We deducted this HEAP 
11 
estimate from both gas heat and gas non-heat customers; however, we believe this 
12 
to be a conservative approach that underestimates energy cost burden and gas cost 
13 
burden for gas heat customers.  Since gas non-heat customers typically receive 
14 
their HEAP benefit directly, we adjust reported gas expenses to reflect this 
15 
unreported HEAP benefit. However, gas heat customers who are eligible for 
16 
HEAP typically have their HEAP benefit paid directly to the utility who applies 
17 
the discount to their bills. Therefore, the gas heat bills reported to the ACS would 
18 
likely already reflect the HEAP deduction.   
19 
By deducting an additional $46.50 from gas heat customers’ annual bills, 
20 
we are likely inflating the amount of HEAP benefits they receive since their 
21 
reported annual bills should already be net of the full HEAP benefit they receive 
22 
5348


--- Page 1152 ---
which is typically over $300. However, we applied the average HEAP benefit to 
1 
all customers as a conservative estimate. 
2 
Q.
HOW DO YOU DETERMINE WHETHER A CUSTOMER IS GAS HEAT 
3 
OR GAS NON-HEAT? 
4 
A.
The ACS data collects information on household gas expenses, but does not 
5 
distinguish the use of that gas.  Therefore, to approximate whether a customer is a 
6 
gas heat or a gas non-heat customer, we applied a monthly bill threshold, above 
7 
which a customer is likely a gas heat customer and below which a customer is 
8 
likely a gas non-heat customer.  To do this, we created a histogram of reported 
9 
utility bills and identified that a cutoff of $40 most accurately reflects the number 
10 
of heat versus non-heat customers reported in KEDNY Exhibit__(RDP-2CU) (this 
11 
exhibit does not distinguish between low-income and other customers).  We 
12 
believe this is a reasonable cutoff.  For a KEDNY residential heating customer to 
13 
pay a total bill of $40 per month, under National Grid’s proposed rates, the 
14 
customer would have to use only 10 therms per month.  This usage level is eight 
15 
times below average, suggesting that not many residential heating customers are 
16 
paying bills this low.  Similarly, the average KEDNY residential non-heat 
17 
customer uses 10 therms per month for a projected total bill of $41.69 under 
18 
proposed rates, which adds additional credence to our cutoff.2 
19 
2 See KEDNY Exhibit___(RDP-4CU), Schedule 4, pp. 1, 2. 
5349


--- Page 1153 ---
Q.
WHAT THRESHOLDS DID YOU USE IN THE ANALYSIS TO
1 
CONSIDER A FAMILY AS “LOW INCOME?”
2 
A.
We use a threshold of 60 percent of State median income, or 60 SMI, to determine
3 
whether a family is low income.  60 SMI is the maximum income eligibility for
4 
HEAP, which is the assistance program with the highest income cutoff that enables
5 
participation in National Grid’s low income programs, and is also the income
6 
threshold utilized in the Low Income Order.  Low income thresholds, but not
7 
National Grid’s low income programs, are adjusted for family size.
8 
The thresholds used for SMI are included in Exhibit__(LIP-2).  The 
9 
Federal thresholds identified in the Exhibit are as reported by the Federal 
10 
Department of Health and Human Services.  State thresholds are those used for 
11 
the 2016-2017 HEAP season.  All thresholds used are those from the same year in 
12 
which the ACS data was reported, thus corresponding to economic conditions and 
13 
costs in the year the survey was conducted.  
14 
The analysis is conducted at the family level.  A family is defined as a 
15 
resource sharing unit composed of related individuals and domestic partners.  This 
16 
is different from a household, since multiple families, subfamilies, or unrelated 
17 
individuals may reside in the same apartment, home, or other housing unit.  
18 
Families within a housing unit are defined using the methodology the Mayor’s 
19 
Office of Economic Opportunity developed for the New York City poverty 
20 
measure using guidelines the National Academy of Sciences suggests, and 
21 
5350


--- Page 1154 ---
comparable to the method the U.S. Census Bureau uses in estimating their 
1 
Supplemental Poverty Measure.  
2 
Q.
WHY WAS THE ANALYSIS PERFORMED AT THE FAMILY LEVEL? 
3 
A.
Poverty levels are defined based on family size and income, not household 
4 
income. Therefore, to properly evaluate energy costs against the low income 
5 
thresholds noted in Exhibit__(LIP-2), the family units created for the New York 
6 
City poverty measure are used.  We note that this differs from the Commission’s 
7 
usage of households to determine energy cost burden.  In our analysis, more than 
8 
one family unit in a household would mean that we identify in the census data 
9 
more than one “resource sharing unit” in that household.  For example, a group of 
10 
family members plus an unrelated couple who are identified as boarders would be 
11 
considered two families under our analysis, and utility costs would apportioned 
12 
out to each family according to size.  In other words, when there are multiple 
13 
families in a household, our analysis would show that each is paying less in costs 
14 
than the combined household and those costs are held relative to each family’s 
15 
income to determine their cost burden.  Our understanding is that the vast majority 
16 
of households in the New York City are single-family households, and so we 
17 
expect the implication of performing our analysis at the family level (as opposed 
18 
to the household level) to be minor.  
19 
Q.
PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW YOU DEFINE THE NATIONAL GRID 
20 
SERVICE TERRITORY? 
21 
5351


--- Page 1155 ---
A.
Our analysis focuses only on New York City customers. For our analysis, we only
1 
use responses from respondents living in Staten Island, Brooklyn, and all Queens
2 
Community Districts, except Districts 1, 2, 7, 8, and 11, which are assumed to be
3 
Con Edison gas customers.  Community districts are the most granular geographic
4 
division we can make that balances available information with the need for
5 
sufficient responses for statistical significance.
6 
We understand that, by only using this subset of data, we essentially are 
7 
limiting our analysis to the KEDNY service territory, plus the Rockaways portion 
8 
of the KEDLI service territory.

PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW YOU DEFINE A NATIONAL GRID 
10 
CUSTOMER? 
11 
A.
For our analysis, respondents who live in the areas that we defined above and who 
12 
report directly paying some amount greater than zero for gas are considered 
13 
National Grid customers. 
14 
Q.
WHAT DOES THE PANEL MEAN BY DIRECTLY PAYING FOR 
15 
UTILITY SERVICE? 
16 
A.
Within New York City, many families with income levels below 60 SMI live in 
17 
apartment houses or other dwellings in which heat or heat and electricity are 
18 
provided by the landlord.  This includes master-metered buildings.  The utility 
19 
costs for these families may be included in their rent payments or in bills issued 
20 
by their landlords rather than by Con Edison or National Grid.  The numbers 
21 
presented in our analysis are for families who pay some amount greater than $0 
22 
5352


--- Page 1156 ---
for utility bills.  We were not able to differentiate whether those bills are paid 
1 
directly to Con Edison and National Grid or to some other party, such as energy 
2 
service companies.  Similarly, directly paying for gas implies that the family is 
3 
paying some amount greater than $0 for gas bills. 
4 
Q.
PLEASE EXPLAIN THE PROCESS FOR CALCULATING ENERGY 
5 
COST BURDEN AND GAS COST BURDEN. 
6 
A.
Our analysis was conducted in R.  R is a programming language for statistical 
7 
computing and data visualization supported by the R Foundation for Statistical 
8 
Computing.  First, we cleaned the data to eliminate group quarters and responses 
9 
from outside New York City from the base population, and superimposed family 
10 
units on the census households.  Group quarters include facilities like prisons, 
11 
college dorms, nursing homes, and homeless shelters where costs are typically 
12 
shared over the institution and are not billed directly to tenants or residents.   
13 
Next, we created variables to represent annual utility expenses.  For fuel 
14 
oil, the number reported in the ACS is already annualized.  For electric and gas, 
15 
we multiplied the recorded response by 12.   
16 
We then sorted families into income bands, by comparing family income 
17 
against different income ranges.  We then created a variable for all utilities, which 
18 
is the sum of these values, minus a HEAP estimate. The HEAP estimate we used 
19 
is the average non-emergency benefit paid to New York City residents in the 2017 
20 
HEAP season, or $46.50.  Then, we created a variable called “utility burden” 
21 
which divides the sum of all utilities minus the HEAP estimate, by pre-tax income 
22 
5353


--- Page 1157 ---
for each family.  If that ratio is greater than six percent, the family is considered 
1 
energy cost burdened.  Similarly, we created a variable called “gas burden” which 
2 
is the annualized gas costs minus the estimated HEAP benefit, divided by pre-tax 
3 
income.  If that ratio is greater than three percent, the family is considered gas cost 
4 
burdened. 
5 
Next we applied filters that restrict the data set to National Grid customers. 
6 
First, we identified respondents whose reported natural gas bill greater than $0. 
7 
Then we identified respondents who live in the National Grid service territory, as 
8 
described above. 
9 
Following this step, we applied a set of gas discounts and cost increases 
10 
that reflect hypothetical discount scenarios, and estimated bill increases from the 
11 
pending rate case.  We did this by adding the annualized gas increase or decrease 
12 
to the annualized gas bill and recalculating whether the gas cost burden is over 
13 
three percent.   
14 
Finally, we generated tables for gas heat and gas non-heat customers that 
15 
show the different impacts of the hypothetical cost increases or decreases and how 
16 
these scenarios change the number of families that are gas cost burdened using the 
17 
60 SMI threshold. 
18 
Q.
WHAT ARE YOUR FINDINGS? 
19 
A.
Schedule 1 of Exhibit__(LIP-3) shows the existing energy and gas cost burden 
20 
and how the 2017 low income energy cost burden landscape would change under 
21 
various adjustments to low income customers’ utility bills. There are six tables in 
22 
5354


--- Page 1158 ---
Schedule 1.  Each table has a similar structure but represents a different look at 
1 
the data. Table 1 looks at energy burden for all customers. Table 2 looks at gas 
2 
burden for all customers.  Table 3 looks at energy cost burden for non-heat gas 
3 
customers. Table 4 looks at gas cost burden for non-heat gas customers. Table 5 
4 
looks at energy cost burden for heating gas customers. Table 6 looks at gas cost 
5 
burden for heating gas customers. 
6 
As shown in Table 1 of Schedule 1 of Exhibit__(LIP-3), in the National 
7 
Grid service territory, there are 220,470 families living under 60 SMI who pay 
8 
more than six percent of their income toward their energy bills.  This number 
9 
represents 18 percent of all customers in the National Grid service territory and 55 
10 
percent of all National Grid customers under 60 SMI.  Additionally, in the 
11 
National Grid service territory, there are 148,168 families living under 60 SMI 
12 
who pay more than three percent of their income toward their gas bills (Table 2).  
13 
This number represents 12 percent of all customers in the National Grid service 
14 
territory and 37 percent of all customers in the National Grid service territory 
15 
under 60 SMI.  These results demonstrate that National Grid’s existing low income 
16 
discounts are not sufficient to satisfy the Commission’s goal that no low income 
17 
customer pays more than six percent of income to energy costs, or more than three 
18 
percent of income to gas costs. 
19 
We also found that gas cost burden disproportionately impacts low income 
20 
families.  Only 33 percent of all customers in the National Grid service territory 
21 
have income levels under 60 SMI, but low income customers represent 68 percent 
22 
5355


--- Page 1159 ---
of gas cost burdened families.  Put another way, 37 percent of all low income 
1 
families are gas cost burdened; in contrast, only 9 percent of non-low-income 
2 
families are gas cost burdened. 
3 
We also see that both energy and gas cost burden are more acute for gas 
4 
heat customers. As seen in Table 4 of Schedule 1, 15 percent of low income non-
5 
heat gas customers are gas cost burdened, whereas over 60 percent of gas heat low 
6 
income customers are gas cost burdened, as shown in Table 6 of Schedule 1.  Said 
7 
differently, of the 141,168 National Grid low income customers who are gas cost 
8 
burdened, 22 percent are non-heat gas customers and 78 percent are gas heat 
9 
customers. Looking to Tables 3 and 5, whereas 42 percent of low income gas non-
10 
heat customers are energy cost burdened, nearly 70 percent of low income gas heat 
11 
customers are energy cost burdened. These findings highlight the need for greater 
12 
focus on gas heat customers. 
13 
In the columns to the right in each table, we see the impacts of various 
14 
hypothetical incremental discounts, that is, what happens if instead of rates 
15 
increasing as proposed, monthly bills were discounted by some amount 
16 
incremental to existing discounts. Looking at Table 6, we see that meeting the

18

11

New York’s low income households have an energy burden at or below six percent 
19 
of household income.  Moreover, because our proposed discount levels are based 
20 
on actual income and energy burden data rather than on an assumption that low 
21 
income customers earn the maximum threshold of 60 SMI, they would bring more 
22 
5367


--- Page 1171 ---
low income customers up to the Commission’s targeted energy burden level of no 
1 
more than six percent of income.  In other words, our proposed increases to current 
2 
discount levels arguably would make National Grid’s EAP more inclusive for the 
3 
thousands of low income households for whom existing discount levels are 
4 
inadequate. 
5 
Q.
DO YOU CONSIDER YOUR PROPOSED DISCOUNT CALCULATION 
6 
METHODOLOGY TO BE A “TOP DOWN” APPROACH? 
7 
A.
No.  To the contrary, we consider our methodology to be a “bottom up” approach.  
8 
That is, we first analyzed actual income data to develop the appropriate low income 
9 
household energy burdens, and then calculated the amount of bill discounts needed 
10 
to achieve an energy burden of no more than six percent of household income.  We 
11 
then extrapolated those increased bill discounts to determine what budgets are 
12 
necessary for the Companies’ respective EAPs, while still remaining within the 
13 
Commission’s established policy that the total budget for a utility’s low income 
14 
program may not exceed two percent of total operating revenues.  Importantly, we 
15 
did not first set each utility’s program budget to the maximum two percent cap as a 
16 
starting point, and then allocate dollars among the different tiers of bill discounts. 
17 
RECONNECTION FEES 
18 
Q.
WHAT ARE RECONNECTION FEES? 
19 
A.
Reconnection fees are charges that a customer must pay to a utility to reconnect 
20 
gas service that has been discontinued for non-payment.   
21 
Q.
WHAT 
ARE 
THE 
COMPANIES’ 
POLICIES 
REGARDING 
22 
5368


--- Page 1172 ---
RECONNECTION FEES FOR LOW INCOME CUSTOMERS? 
1 
A.
KEDNY currently charges customers a reconnection fee of $66.13 (plus 
2 
reimbursement of the Company’s City Marshall fees and court filing fees) if 
3 
service is to be reconnected at the meter or an existing curb valve, and a 
4 
reconnection fee of $300 if service is to be reconnected at the utility’s main by 
5 
excavation of the street.  However, KEDNY also offers a one-time credit of the 
6 
reconnection fee to low income customers participating in its EAP whose service 
7 
was disconnected for non-payment.   
8 
KEDLI currently charges its customers a $78 reconnection fee, but waives 
9 
this fee for low income customers.   
10 
Q.
DO YOU RECOMMEND ANY CHANGES TO THE COMPANIES’ 
11 
RECONNECTION FEE PROGRAMS?  
12 
A.
Yes.  While we appreciate that KEDNY provides low income customers a one-
13 
time waiver of the reconnection fee, we propose that KEDNY eliminate their 
14 
reconnection fees altogether for all low income customers.   
15 
Q.
WHY SHOULD KEDNY ELIMINATE ITS RECONNECTION FEES FOR 
16 
LOW INCOME CUSTOMERS?  
17 
A.
Eliminating reconnection fees for low income customers is appropriate because it 
18 
will provide them with a better opportunity to remain utility customers and pay 
19 
their utility bills.  In particular, low income customers who are facing termination 
20 
of service already have demonstrated an inability to pay utility bills.  Requiring 
21 
these customers to pay a fee to reconnect their gas service detracts from the amount 
22 
5369


--- Page 1173 ---
they can put toward paying their past due bills, and creates an additional financial 
1 
barrier for them to overcome.  Customers and the utilities would be much better 
2 
served if this money was instead put towards direct payment of the customers’ 
3 
utility bills.  
4 
Moreover, the amount collected for reconnections is very small when 
5 
considered in context.  According to National Grid’s response to City IR-106, on 
6 
average over the last five years, KEDNY collected approximately $1.3 million in 
7 
reconnection fees annually from all customers.  According to National Grid’s 
8 
response to DPS IR-260, approximately $174,000 of that amount was collected 
9 
annually from low income customers over the same time period.  These amounts, 
10 
and in particular the amount collected from low income customers, are insignificant 
11 
when considered in context of the revenue requirement increase that KEDNY is 
12 
seeking in this rate case, approximately $196 million in the Rate Year.  We also 
13 
understand that each Company’s actual annual gas revenue requirements are in the 
14 
billions of dollars.   
15 
Conversely, KEDNY’s reconnection fees are substantial, particularly from 
16 
the perspective of a low income customer.  As previously noted, KEDNY charges 
17 
a reconnection fee of $66.13 (plus fees) for reconnecting service at the meter, which 
18 
represents nearly 58 percent of an average KEDNY low income heating customer’s 
19 
monthly gas bill.  Thus, in context, the loss of these reconnection revenues would 
20 
be inconsequential for the Companies, but the savings could be material for a 
21 
customer who already cannot afford his or her utility bill. 
22 
5370


--- Page 1174 ---
Finally, elimination of KEDNY’s reconnection fees for low income 
1 
customers is appropriate to harmonize the utility’s practices with those already 
2 
adopted by KEDLI.  This eliminates the possibility of low income customers 
3 
residing in different portions of New York City (for example, on the Rockaways 
4 
versus in Brooklyn) being subject to different rules on reconnection fees.

HRA FILE MATCHING PROCESS

9

Q.

15

The current matching process was developed to provide notification to HRA’s 
16

17

18 
HRA providing their names and limited information necessary for their

20 
programs.  HRA does not disclose to National Grid which type of benefit(s) any of 
21 
HRA’s clients receive – only that they qualify to be enrolled.  Every time a match 
22 
5371


--- Page 1175 ---
is performed, there are some HRA clients who choose to opt-out; HRA does not 
1 
disclose any information regarding these clients to National Grid.

HAS HRA HISTORICALLY RECEIVED FUNDING FROM NATIONAL

4

6

Q.
WHAT DO THE COMPANIES PROPOSE IN THIS RATE CASE?

The Companies do not propose any changes to both the existing file matching 
10

Q.
WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION REGARDING THE HRA FILE 
12 
MATCHING PROCESS? 
13 
A.
The file matching process and reimbursement mechanism have worked well over 
14

15

Q.
WHAT CAPACITY DOES HRA HAVE TO INCREASE THE NUMBER OF 
21 
MATCHES PERFORMED EACH YEAR? 
22 
5372


--- Page 1176 ---
A.
HRA could increase the match frequency from twice a year to four times a year,
1 
or quarterly.
2 
Q.
WHAT BENEFITS DO THE PANEL ANTICIPATE AS A RESULT OF
3 
MORE FREQUENT MATCHES?
4 
A.
We believe that performing the match twice as often will improve the accuracy of
5 
customer enrollment in the Companies’ low income programs.  Performing the
6

7

While we considered other possible frequencies of the matching process,

income programs, with the administrative costs and resources that would be

required of HRA to perform the matches more than four times a year.

Q.
DOES THE PANEL BELIEVE THAT MORE FREQUENT MATCHES

WILL INCREASE THE NUMBER OF CUSTOMERS ENROLLED IN THE 
16

A.
Possibly.  As stated above, more frequent matches will provide greater 
18 
opportunities for eligible persons to participate in the Companies’ low income 
19 
programs.  However, more frequent matches may not necessarily equate to a 
20 
sizable increase in participation levels.  This is due to perpetual movement of 
21 
individuals and families coming on and off assistance benefits based on eligibility.  
22 
5373


--- Page 1177 ---
We will not know the exact impact more frequent matches would have on program

enrollment until HRA does a full year of quarterly matches.

WHAT IS YOUR PROPOSAL FOR REIMBURSEMENT LEVELS FOR 
3

As HRA will be performing the match twice as often as it does currently, we 
5

6

7

9

HRA’s administrative costs include the cost of the opt-out process, including the 
11

12 
perform the matches.  As in any organization, there is a cost associated with each 
13

14 
Q.
WHAT COSTS ARE NOT INCLUDED IN HRA’S REQUEST FOR 
15 
REIMBURSEMENT? 
16 
A.
HRA dedicates many hours of its employees’ time to this effort.  Its employees 
17 
must refine the programming language, run the match, perform quality control, 
18

21 
5374


--- Page 1178 ---
This time is taken away from these employees’ primary job duties and 
1

2 
HRA continues to be willing to contribute its employees’ time for more 
3

4

5 
by HRA to perform quarterly matches, it is likely well in excess of the amount for 
6 
which reimbursement is sought. 
7 
Q.
CAN HRA ALLOCATE CITY FUNDS TO THIS EFFORT? 
8 
A.
No.  HRA’s role is to administer its own low income programs, not utility low 
9 
income programs.  HRA’s funding, whether from federal or state sources, or 
10 
through the City’s budget process, is intended and budgeted to support its own 
11

12 
allocated.  For example, funds for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program 
13 
could not be used to provide energy-related benefits.  For these reasons, HRA does 
14 
not have any funding available to support National Grid’s low income programs.   
15 
Q.

20

21

22 
5375


--- Page 1179 ---
of eligibility for the low income program.  HRA therefore could not share the

4

LOCAL LAW 152 
3 
Q.
PLEASE PROVIDE A BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE DEVELOPMENT OF 
4 
LOCAL LAW 152. 
5 
A.
The New York City Council introduced Local Law 152 as Int. No. 1088-2016 on 
6 
February 24, 2016.  The Committee on Housing and Buildings amended the 
7 
legislation as Int. No. 1088-A on November 15, 2016 and the City Council 
8 
approved it as amended on November 16, 2016.  Mayor Bill de Blasio signed 
9 
Local Law 152 into law on December 6, 2016; it is codified as Article 318 of 
10 
Chapter 3 of Title 28 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York.  
11 
Exhibit__(AF-2) contains copies of Int. No. 1088-2016, Int. No. 1088-A, and 
12 
Local Law 152. 
13 
The City Council introduced Local Law 152 as part of a package of 
14 
legislation with the goal of improving gas safety, responding to three major gas-
15 
related explosions that occurred in New York City during the preceding two 
16 
years.  Each of the three gas-related explosions that precipitated the legislation 
17 
package tragically resulted in fatalities and injuries, as well as displacement of 
18 
residents.  As noted in the Committee on Housing and Buildings’ April 12, 2016 
19 
Committee Report, which is attached hereto as Exhibit__(AF-1), the three 
20 
explosions were the East Harlem Explosion, wherein two buildings at 1644 and 
21 
1646 Park Avenue collapsed on March 12, 2014; the East Village Explosion, 
22 
5380


--- Page 1184 ---
wherein one building was damaged and three buildings were destroyed as a result 
1 
of an explosion at 121 Second Avenue on March 26, 2015; and, the Brooklyn 
2 
Explosion, in which an explosion occurred at 4206 13th Avenue on October 3, 
3 
2015. 
4 
Effectively, the objective of Local Law 152 is to improve gas safety and 
5 
avoid further tragedies by requiring building owners to inspect their buildings’ 
6 
gas piping systems. 
7 
Q.
PLEASE DESCRIBE DOB’S RULE TO IMPLEMENT LOCAL LAW 152. 
8 
A.
DOB regularly promulgates rules pursuant to local laws that authorize such 
9 
rulemaking in accordance with the City Administrative Procedure Act, codified as 
10 
Section 1041 et seq. of Chapter 45 of the New York City Charter.  In doing so, the 
11 
substance of DOB rules must comport with the legislative intent and text of the 
12 
enabling local law and cannot exceed the limits the City Council imposed.  On 
13 
November 26, 2018, DOB published notice in the City Record of its proposal to 
14 
add Section 103-10 to Title 1 of the Rules of the City of New York, or “RCNY,” 
15 
pursuant to Local Law 152.  DOB held a public hearing and received comments 
16 
on proposed 1 RCNY §103-10 on January 2, 2019.  I note that the rulemaking is 
17 
ongoing and no final rule has yet been adopted. 
18 
Pursuant to Local Law 152, the proposed 1 RCNY §103-10 is intended to 
19 
promote public safety by requiring periodic inspections of gas piping systems in 
20 
buildings and the correction of conditions identified by such inspections.  
21 
Moreover, the proposed rule is intended to effectuate Article 318 of Chapter 3 of 
22 
5381


--- Page 1185 ---
Title 28 of the Administrative Code, which was added pursuant to Local Law 152, 
1 
by clarifying procedural and substantive requirements associated with the law.  In 
2 
particular, proposed 1 RCNY §103-10 includes provisions that pertain to: 
3 
•
the periodic inspection cycle schedule and inspection requirements;
4 
•
inspector qualifications for performing periodic inspections of gas piping
5 
systems;
6 
•
the required scope of inspection;
7 
•
reporting and certification requirements;
8 
•
requirements for reporting unsafe or hazardous conditions; and
9 
•
civil penalties for failure to file required certifications.
10 
Q.
PLEASE EXPLAIN THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE CITY’S 
11 
REQUIREMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SERVICE LINE INSPECTIONS 
12 
AND 
THE 
COMPANIES’ 
REQUIREMENTS 
AS 
GAS 
UTILITY 
13 
COMPANIES. 
14 
A.
On April 20, 2015, in Case 15-G-0244, entitled Order Establishing Statewide 
15 
Inspection Schedules and Procedural Requirements, the Public Service 
16 
Commission (“Commission”) adopted a new definition of gas service line, 
17 
thereby expanding the Commission’s jurisdiction and adding two additional 
18 
inspection requirements to the Operation and Maintenance programs of gas utility 
19 
companies regulated by the Commission.  On pages 1-2 of the Order, the 
20 
Commission directed that following this change in definition, gas utility 
21 
companies must complete “leakage surveys and atmospheric corrosion 
22 
5382


--- Page 1186 ---
inspections starting from a building’s outside wall up to the outlet of the gas 
1 
meter.”   
2 
As provided in 16 NYCRR § 255.3(43), attached as Exhibit__(AF-3), the 
3 
new definition of gas “service line” reads as follows: 
4 
[T]he piping, including associated metering and pressure reducing
5 
appurtenances, that transports gas below grade from a main or
6 
transmission line to the outlet of the customer meter or at the
7 
connection to a customer’s piping, whichever is further
8 
downstream where a meter is located within the building; if a
9 
meter is located outside the building, the service line will be
10 
deemed to terminate at the outset of the building foundation wall.
11 
12 
In contrast, Local Law 152 delineates the scope of gas piping systems 
13 
inspections as follows: “At each inspection, […] all exposed gas lines from point 
14 
of entry of gas piping into a building, including building service meters, up to 
15 
individual tenant spaces shall be inspected […].”  The legislative history of Local 
16 
Law 152 shows that this language originated in Int. No. 1088 and remained 
17 
unchanged in Int. No. 1088-A, and Mayor de Blasio signed it into law as Local 
18 
Law 152.  DOB’s proposed 1 RCNY §103-10 incorporates this scope via 
19 
reference to §28-318.3.2 of the Administrative Code. 
20 
Whereas Local Law 152 requires gas piping inspections of exposed gas 
21 
lines from the point of entry into a building to individual tenant spaces, the 
22 
Commission’s inspection requirements set forth in 16 NYCRR § 255.3(43) cover 
23 
piping “from a main or transmission line to the outlet of the customer meter or at 
24 
5383


--- Page 1187 ---
the connection to a customer’s piping, whichever is further downstream where a 
1 
meter is located within the building.”  Taken together, these two jurisdictional 
2 
schemes result in three conceivable scenarios. 
3 
First, where a meter is located outside a building, National Grid must 
4 
conduct its inspection through the meter and up to the meter’s outlet; the building 
5 
owner’s licensed master plumber would be responsible for all piping from the 
6 
point of entry from the meter and up to the tenant spaces. 
7 
Second, where a meter is located inside a building (for instance, the 
8 
building’s basement), National Grid would be responsible for inspecting all 
9 
piping from the main/transmission line into the building, through the meter to the 
10 
meter outlet; the building owner’s licensed master plumber would be responsible 
11 
for inspecting all piping from the point of entry into the building, through the 
12 
meter and up to the tenant spaces. 
13 
Third, where a building contains meters only in individual tenant spaces, 
14 
National Grid would be required to inspect all piping from the main/transmission 
15 
line into the building, piping throughout the building, piping into and within 
16 
individual tenant spaces up through the meter and up to the meter outlet; the 
17 
building owner’s licensed master plumber would be responsible for inspecting all 
18 
piping from the point of entry into the building, and piping throughout the 
19 
building up to the tenant spaces. 
20 
These three scenarios illustrate, except for buildings with exterior meter 
21 
locations, that every building will have some length of piping subject to both 
22 
5384


--- Page 1188 ---
Local Law 152 and Commission-required inspections.  It should be noted, 
1 
however, that it is conceivable that there will be some buildings not subject to 
2 
DOB’s jurisdiction, such as Federal buildings, and, therefore may only be subject 
3 
to Commission-required inspections.  Although most buildings could be inspected 
4 
twice, the inspections will not be “duplicative,” as Staff suggests on page 77 of its 
5 
Pipeline Safety Panel’s direct testimony, as the Commission-required inspections 
6 
do not cover customer piping downstream of the meter outlets.  Two separate 
7 
inspections may bolster safety in that one inspection may reveal conditions that 
8 
were either missed by the other or arose between inspections. 
9 
Q.
WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO THE STAFF PIPELINE SAFETY 
10 
PANEL’S CRITICISM THAT DOB’S RULE DOES NOT ALIGN WITH 
11 
FEDERAL AND STATE OPERATOR QUALIFIED TRAINING AND 
12 
QUALIFICATION STANDARDS? 
13 
A.
Such criticism is misplaced.  It appears that the criticism is motivated by an 
14 
incorrect concern that if Local Law 152 inspections are not performed by operator 
15 
qualified individuals, such inspections – and, presumably, such inspection data – 
16 
will not be able to satisfy National Grid’s obligations with respect to 
17 
Commission-required inspections of service lines.  Implicit in such criticism is the 
18 
erroneous presumption that Local Law 152 inspections – paid for by building 
19 
owners – ought to satisfy the Commission-mandated service line inspections, the 
20 
responsibility for which the Commission determined properly belongs to National 
21 
Grid.  
22 
5385


--- Page 1189 ---
The criticism regarding the lack of a requirement in proposed 1 RCNY 
1 
§103-10 that inspection entities be operator qualified misses obvious foundational
2 
characteristics of Local Law 152 – the City is not trying to duplicate the 
3 
Commission’s requirement or relieve gas utility companies from their 
4 
Commission mandates.  Rather, the City is only requiring inspections of gas 
5 
piping within DOB’s jurisdiction and imposing qualification requirements 
6 
consistent with the City’s scope of inspections.  The Staff Pipeline Safety Panel 
7 
fails to appreciate the distinction between the Commission’s and the City’s 
8 
jurisdiction.   
9 
In sum, it is inappropriate to suggest that the City and DOB ought to 
10 
incorporate State and Federal operator qualification requirements.  The operator is 
11 
National Grid—not DOB, not the building owner, and not the master plumber 
12 
retained by the building owner; and the Commission, not the City, is responsible 
13 
for ensuring that National Grid uses personnel with the requisite operator 
14 
qualifications. 
15 
Q.
WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO THE STAFF PIPELINE SAFETY 
16 
PANEL’S CRITICISM THAT DOB’S PROPOSED RULE DOES NOT 
17 
EXPLICITLY REQUIRE INSIDE INSPECTIONS FOR NATURAL GAS 
18 
PIPING IN TENANT SPACES? 
19 
A.
That criticism is misplaced insofar as it presupposes that DOB has the rulemaking 
20 
authority to mandate inspections within tenant spaces.  DOB’s rulemaking 
21 
authority is limited by the applicable statute or local law.  In the context of Local 
22 
5386


--- Page 1190 ---
Law 152, the City Council did not provide authority to DOB to conduct 
1 
inspections within tenant-owned spaces, and I offer no position on whether the 
2 
City Council could do so legally.   
3 
The Staff Panel’s suggestion that DOB’s rule should include gas piping 
4 
within individual tenant spaces suggests that the Panel did not understand Local 
5 
Law 152, as the suggestion is inconsistent with the City Council’s unambiguous 
6 
intent in specifying—in both Int. No. 1088 and Int. No. 1088-A—that “all 
7 
exposed gas lines from point of entry of gas piping into a building, including 
8 
building service meters, up to individual tenant spaces shall be inspected ….”   
9 
The Staff Pipeline Safety Panel further comments on page 78 of its pre-
10 
filed direct testimony that “[i]f the proposed rules do not require inspections 
11 
within tenant spaces, the inside piping associated with meters inside apartments 
12 
would not be inspected by the plumber and would require a separate inspection by 
13 
the Companies.”  The concern raised here is similarly misplaced – Local Law 152 
14 
and proposed 1 RCNY §103-10 are not intended to supplant or facilitate the 
15 
obligations the Commission imposed on National Grid.  Moreover, as noted 
16 
above, this statement also demonstrates the Panel’s lack of understanding of the 
17 
scope of Local Law 152.  In addition, it should also be noted that the attempt to 
18 
use the Local Law 152 inspection as a means of satisfying National Grid’s 
19 
inspection obligations with respect to the Commission, Staff is, in effect, 
20 
attempting to disburden National Grid while placing the expense of Commission-
21 
imposed inspection duties on the building owner. Such an attempt is especially 
22 
5387


--- Page 1191 ---
misplaced in view of the Commission’s recommendations, discussed below, on 
1 
how National Grid can address its concerns about performing inspections within 
2 
tenant spaces. 
3 
Q.
HAS THE COMMISSION ADDRESSED THE INSPECTIONS WITHIN 
4 
TENANT SPACES? 
5 
A.
Yes.  The Commission addressed the concern about access to tenant spaces at 
6 
length in its Order Establishing Statewide Inspection Schedules and Procedural 
7 
Requirements issued on April 20, 2017 in Case 15-G-0244.  While the 
8 
Commission acknowledged that gaining access to inside gas services is a 
9 
challenge for National Grid in performing the required state inspections, it 
10 
provided concrete guidance to National Grid on how to surmount this challenge. 
11 
Specifically, on page 33 of the Order the Commission noted that, “[t]he easiest 
12 
and most obvious first step for all LDCs is for each to develop safety-related 
13 
inspection notices to leave at customers’ premises, to include as bill inserts, or 
14 
place on company websites.” 
15 
Moreover, the Commission highlighted the fact that Public Service Law 
16 
§65(9) provides National Grid the requisite legal authority to enter, at reasonable
17 
times, any building, room, or place supplied with gas for purposes of inspecting 
18 
meters, pipes, and fittings used for supplying or regulating the supply of gas.  
19 
Additionally, Public Service Law §65(9) allows National Grid to charge 
20 
customers one hundred dollars if a customer prevents or hinders the gas utility 
21 
company’s officer/agent from entering the premises to make an inspection.  
22 
5388


--- Page 1192 ---
Lastly, the Commission ruled in the April 20 Order that under certain 
1 
circumstances National Grid may disconnect service when a customer has paid 
2 
the one hundred dollar fine but still refuses to provide access.   
3 
In sum, the concern the Staff Pipeline Safety Panel raised about Local 
4 
Law 152 inspections stopping at individual tenant spaces appears out-of-place 
5 
when viewed in light of the scope of Section 65 of the Public Service Law and the 
6 
Commission’s directives and recommendations to National Grid for gaining 
7 
access to such spaces.  The Commission – not Local Law 152 or DOB’s proposed 
8 
1 RCNY §103-10 – requires National Grid to inspect individual tenant spaces 
9 
where such spaces contain meters, and the Commission gave National Grid the 
10 
means to do so.

Q.
WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO THE STAFF PIPELINE SAFETY 
12 
PANEL’S CRITICISM THAT THE PROPOSED TIMEFRAMES FOR 
13 
INSPECTION CYCLES IN DOB’S PROPOSED RULE DOES NOT ALIGN 
14 
WITH NECESSARY FEDERAL AND STATE TIMELINES? 
15 
A.
As the Panel acknowledged, Local Law 152 specifically provides DOB’s 
16 
commissioner with the discretion to modify the inspection frequency to be 
17 
consistent with the cycle adopted by the Commission.  However, that the 
18 
proposed rule does not reflect the same cycle now is reasonable given that DOB is 
19 
establishing the necessary operational processes to receive and track the required 
20 
certifications of inspections that building owners must file with DOB.  While the 
21 
inspection frequency could be changed in the future, a longer frequency during 
22 
5389


--- Page 1193 ---
the initial rollout cycle allows DOB additional time to establish these operational 
1 
processes.  
2 
Furthermore, from the perspective of building owners, a frequency of one 
3 
year and three years for business districts and residential districts, respectively, 
4 
would likely pose significant financial burdens on buildings owners. Tailoring 
5 
inspection frequencies to align with National Grid’s inspection frequency as 
6 
mandated by the Commission may be more convenient for National Grid, but it 
7 
could unfairly shift the expense of inspections from National Grid to building 
8 
owners.  Additionally, shorter frequencies of inspections could strain the stock of 
9 
qualified plumbers available to perform the inspections required by Local Law 
10 
152 and the Commission.  In view of these considerations, DOB has opted to 
11 
refrain from exercising its discretion to align the Local Law 152 inspection 
12 
frequency with the Commission’s inspection frequency at this time.  Upon 
13 
completion of at least one full cycle of periodic inspections, DOB may revisit the 
14 
inspection cycle.

ACCOUNTING AND RATEMAKING TREATMENT OF LPP PLANT 
19 
ASSETS RECLASSIFIED TO REGULATORY ASSETS 
20 
Q 
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TYPICAL ACCOUNTING TO RECLASSIFY THE 
21 
NET BOOK VALUE OF THE LPP PLANT ASSETS TO REGULATORY ASSETS. 
22 
5399


--- Page 1203 ---
A.
The typical accounting consists of a credit to plant in service and an equivalent debit to
1 
accumulated depreciation to remove the LPP amounts from the plant and accumulated
2 
depreciation accounts.  To the extent that the Companies’ plant accounts are not fully
3 
depreciated, the typical accounting would leave the net book value as a debit balance in the
4 
accumulated depreciation accounts.  The Companies then would credit the accumulated
5 
depreciation and debit regulatory assets for amounts equivalent to the net book value.
6 
Q.
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TYPICAL ACCOUNTING FOR COSTS OF
7 
REMOVAL AFTER PLANT COSTS HAVE BEEN RECLASSIFIED TO
8 
REGULATORY ASSETS.
9 
A.
In such cases, the costs of removal typically are added to the regulatory assets.  This is
10 
different than if the costs still were recorded in the plant accounts.  In that latter
11 
circumstance, actual costs of removal are debited to accumulated depreciation and the
12 
estimated net negative salvage costs included in the depreciation expense are credited to
13 
accumulated depreciation.
14 
Q.
PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TYPICAL CALCULATION OF AMORTIZATION
15 
EXPENSE.
16 
A.
Amortization expense typically is calculated as the amount of the regulatory asset divided
17 
by the remaining amortization period (months or years).  Alternatively, it could be a dollar
18 
amount of amortization expense allowed by the Commission.
19 
Q.
DOES IT APPEAR THAT THE COMPANIES PLAN TO FOLLOW THE
20 
TYPICAL ACCOUNTING TO RECLASSIFY THE NET BOOK VALUE OF THE
21 
LPP PLANT ASSET TO REGULATORY ASSETS AND TO CALCULATE
22 
5400


--- Page 1204 ---
AMORTIZATION EXPENSE ON A STRAIGHT-LINE BASIS OVER THE 
1 
REMAINING AMORTIZATION PERIOD? 
2 
A.
No.  It appears that the Companies’ plan to maintain the gross plant amounts as the 
3 
regulatory assets and maintain the accumulated depreciation as accumulated amortization. 
4 
I conclude this because the Companies calculated their proposed depreciation rates on 
5 
gross plant, not net plant.10  I also conclude that the Companies’ plan is to continue debiting 
6 
the actual costs of removal to accumulated amortization and crediting the amortization 
7 
expense, which includes the estimated costs of removal, to the accumulated amortization.  
8 
I conclude this because the Companies calculated their proposed depreciation rates on 
9 
gross plant, not net plant, and embedded the costs of removal into the proposed 
10 
depreciation rates.11

amortization will commence the month after the costs of removal are deferred.

Commission retains the authority to revisit the depreciation (amortization) rates in 
8 
subsequent rate proceedings if necessary and appropriate, but will have the advantage of 
9 
actual costs that are known and measurable.

AMORTIZATION PERIOD SHOULD NOT BE ACCELERATED 
11 
Q.
DESCRIBE 
THE 
COMPANIES’ 
PROPOSAL 
TO 
ACCELERATE 
THE 
12 
AMORTIZATION AND RECOVERY OF THE NET BOOK VALUE AND 
13 
ESTIMATED COSTS OF REMOVAL OVER TWENTY YEARS.   
14 
A.
Mr. Norman proposes a twenty-year amortization period.  He claims that this “is necessary 
15 
to fully recover all appropriate costs for these facilities within the retirement period 
16 
proposed.”12 
17 
Q.
IS IT NECESSARY OR APPROPRIATE TO RECOVER THESE COSTS “WITHIN 
18 
THE RETIREMENT PERIOD PROPOSED”? 
19 
A.
No.  The “retirement period” is not a valid basis for setting the amortization period.  After 
20 
the LPP assets are retired, there no longer is any nexus to the prior service lives.  The 
21 
12 Direct Testimony of Mr. Paul Normand at 7. 
5402


--- Page 1206 ---
reclassification of the plant costs to regulatory assets severs any relationship with or 
1 
conceptual underpinning to the prior service lives of the assets.  The Companies implicitly 
2 
acknowledge this fact in their own proposal to use a twenty-year amortization period in the 
3 
calculation of the depreciation rates.  Mr. Norman recommends a twenty-year average 
4 
service life in the proposed depreciation rates.  However, the weighted average remaining 
5 
service lives for the LPP plant assets is only ten years, assuming that they are retired and 
6 
replaced uniformly over the next twenty years.  The Companies’ proposal implicitly 
7 
recognizes that the amortization of the regulatory assets is no longer tethered to the service 
8 
lives of the assets, but rather is simply an amortization period that will be determined by 
9 
the Commission and reflected in the depreciation (amortization) rates.

A.
The average remaining service lives for each plant account are shown in the depreciation 
13 
studies attached to Mr. Norman’s testimonies.  For KEDNY, they range from 9.5 years to 
14 
30.0 years,13 with  an average of 25.8 years. .For KEDLI, they range from 6.4 years to 38.2

16 
Q.
WHY SHOULD THE COMMISSION MAINTAIN THE SERVICE LIVES 
17 
REFLECTED IN THE PRESENT DEPRECIATION RATES AND REJECT THE 
18 
COMPANIES’ PROPOSAL TO ACCELERATE THE AMORTIZATION USING A 
19 
TWENTY-YEAR AMORTIZATION PERIOD? 
20 
13 Exhibit___(LK-4) page 1 column (14). 
14 Exhibit___(LK-5) page 1 column (14). 
5403


--- Page 1207 ---
A.
This approach will mitigate the impact on customers of the Companies’ proposal to
1 
accelerate the LPP plant assets’ retirement and replacement.  The Company’s proposal
2 
unnecessarily drives up the revenue requirement and compounds the impact of increased
3 
gas rates on customers. The retirement and replacement of the LPP plant assets results in
4 
two sets of costs that are included in the revenue requirement in these rate proceedings and
5 
in future rate proceedings.
6 
The first set of costs is related to the return on and amortization of the net book 
7 
value of the retired plant costs plus estimated costs of removal.  The second set is related 
8 
to the return on the net book value and depreciation of the plant in service costs of the 
9 
replacement plant costs plus estimated costs of removal.   
10 
The two sets of costs overlap and both will be included in the revenue requirement 
11 
until the first set is fully amortized and recovered.  Under the Companies’ proposal, the 
12 
recovery of the first set of costs will be accelerated even as the second set of costs is 
13 
incurred and added to the revenue requirement.   In this manner, the Companies’ proposal 
14 
compounds the impact on customers over the shortened recovery period.    
15 
Q.
WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION? 
16 
A.
I recommend that the Commission maintain the present depreciation rates and the service 
17 
lives reflected in those depreciation rates for the amortization period rather than accelerate 
18 
the recovery by shortening the amortization period to twenty years.

ESTIMATED COST OF REMOVAL SHOULD NOT BE INCREASED 
20 
Q.
PLEASE DESCRIBE MR. NORMAND’S STATISTICAL CALCULATION OF 
21 
THE ESTIMATED COSTS OF REMOVAL. 
22 
5404


--- Page 1208 ---
A.
Mr. Normand calculated historical annual percentage costs of removal for each of the plant
1 
accounts.  He first calculated the costs of removal per mile by dividing the cost of removal
2 
by the miles of mains retired for each of the mains plant accounts and the cost of removal
3 
per service by dividing the cost of removal by the number of services retired for the services
4 
plant accounts.  He then calculated the average annual cost of removal per mile and the
5 
average cost per service using different numbers of years, i.e., three years, four years, and
6 
seven years.  He then settled on three-year annual averages for each account that had data.
7 
Finally, he calculated the annual cost of removal as a percentage of the gross plant.  In
8 
some cases, he used the results from a similar account for another account that had no
9 
data.15
10 
Q.
ARE THE RESULTS OF THESE CALCULATIONS RELIABLE AND
11 
REASONABLE TO USE AS THE ESTIMATED COSTS OF REMOVAL?
12 
A.
No.  The results are unreliable and are not reasonable to use as the estimated costs of
13 
removal.  Mr. Norman’s statistical approach may be appropriate for long-lived assets in the
14 
context of a normal depreciation study with limited retirements and costs of removal;
15 
however, the Companies’ plan to retire all their remaining LPP plant assets, is well outside
16 
the context of a normal depreciation study.
17 
In this case and considering the magnitude of the retirements and the related costs 
18 
of removal, the superior approach is not to rely on estimates at all, but instead to defer the 
19 
actual cost of removal to the regulatory assets.  This approach replaces the uncertainty of 
20

Q.
WHAT ABOUT THE NATURE OF THE ALLEGED VIOLATIONS 
20 
RAISES CONCERNS ABOUT PRUDENT SYSTEM MANAGEMENT? 
21 
5421


--- Page 1225 ---
A.
These alleged violations, if proven true, are fundamentally safety violations
1 
resulting from a material oversight failure by National Grid.  Pages 13-14 of the
2 
Order to Show Cause concisely summarize the nature of the alleged violations.
3 
The New York State Department of Public Service Staff found: (i) that the Queens
4 
Pipeline had been installed improperly, “either in very close proximity to, or
5 
directly in contact with, various other underground utilities;” (ii) installation of
6 
mains and main replacements were done by unqualified contractors; and (iii)
7 
joining work was completed by unqualified workers.  That these alleged violations
8 
arose from unqualified contractors and not National Grid employees does not
9 
exculpate the Companies.  The consequences of a gas pipeline rupture are the same
10 
regardless of whether a contractor or employee violated safety regulations.
11 
Moreover, National Grid is responsible for managing its contractors as well as its
12 
systems.  If National Grid wants to increase the scale and scope of its capital
13 
programs at ratepayer expense, it must first demonstrate that it can do so safely
14 
and prudently, including identifying gaps in its current project management and
15 
oversight approach, and developing strategies to remediate those gaps to ensure

that safety concerns are avoided or mitigated.

Q.
WHAT ARE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS?
18 
A.
In our view, the Main Replacement and Service Replacement Programs should be
19 
planned to more thoroughly take advantage of bundling projects, minimizing
20 
disruptions to the communities, and ensuring construction is as efficient as
21 
possible, thereby reducing the overall program costs.  We recommend that the
22 
5422


--- Page 1226 ---
Companies’ risk model for main replacement be reviewed annually to ensure 
1 
maximum optimization of main work and that the Companies continue to identify

opportunities to coordinate with City projects involving street works.   
3 
 Additionally, the Companies must be able to exhibit that the safety and 
4 
reliability of their systems is improved at a rate commensurate with the proposed 
5 
spending, and that the capital programs are prudently managed at a level 
6 
commensurate with the spending.  If that cannot be shown, then the main 
7 
replacement programs should be decelerated to an appropriate rate.  Finally, given 
8 
the magnitude of the capital budgets the Companies are requesting, we 
9 
recommend that the Commission require a reconciliation mechanism so that any 
10 
amounts unspent are returned to customers.  
11 
Q.
ARE THE COMPANIES PROPOSING ANY CHANGES TO EXISTING 
12 
RECONCILIATION MECHANISMS? 
13 
A.
Yes, they are.  The Companies propose to continue the downward-only net plant 
14 
capital tracker that was approved in the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases. 
15 
We support this proposal.  However, the Companies also have an existing CSC 
16 
tracker mechanism that currently requires a 90 percent deferral of the difference 
17 
between forecast and actual CSC spending.  The Companies propose to modify 
18 
this tracking mechanism to a full reconciliation of the difference between forecast 
19 
and actual spending.  KEDNY also proposes to add an O&M tracker “that would 
20 
fully reconcile the difference between forecast and actual spending in the non-
21 
5423


--- Page 1227 ---
reimbursable “Support and Protect” O&M expense category” which are certain 
1 
non-reimbursable CSC O&M expenditures.    
2 
Q.
DO YOU AGREE WITH THE PROPOSED CHANGES TO THE CSC-
3 
RELATED RECONCILIATION MECHANISMS? 
4 
A.
No.  The Companies state that the proposed CSC tracker changes and the new 
5 
Support and Protect O&M expense tracker is based on the “increasing volatility 
6 
and scope of unplanned CSC projects…”  However, the City’s Policy Panel 
7 
testimony, which is being filed concurrently with this testimony in these cases, is 
8 
recommending that National Grid designate a high-ranking official to serve as a 
9 
designated liaison with the City specifically with respect to CSC projects, and that 
10 
National Grid submit regular reports to the Commission regarding the status of 
11 
pending CSC projects so that performance can be objectively tracked over time.  
12 
These recommendations, if adopted, should help address the Companies’ stated 
13 
concerns over increased volatility and scope surrounding CSC. Therefore, the 
14 
proposed changes to the CSC tracker are not necessary.  
15 
In addition, given the size and scope of the CSC program, a full 
16 
reconciliation mechanism introduces additional, unknown ratepayer exposure.  
17 
For example, KEDNY has a CSC budget of almost $300 million per year, so even 
18 
a 10 percent variation between forecasted and actual costs could have significant 
19 
ratepayer impacts.  The Companies should not be insulated from these variations, 
20 
and doing so would reduce the Companies’ incentives for accurate forecasts and 
21 
effective cost management.  Indeed, the Companies themselves recognize the 
22 
5424


--- Page 1228 ---
importance that accurate forecasting plays within the ratesetting process, 
1 
particularly as it relates CSC costs.  In response to DPS-352, KEDNY argues for 
2 
setting rates using its forecast of actual CSC costs, noting that the “CSC tracker 
3 
is…not a substitute for setting rates.”  The Companies’ proposal for a full CSC 
4 
reconciliation mechanism would, however, create just such the substitute that the 
5 
Companies claim they want to avoid.  
6 
For these reasons, the Commission should reject the proposed changes to 
7 
the Companies’ CSC tracker and reject the similar, but related, O&M tracking 
8 
mechanism.

4 
Q.
WHY IS THE COMPANIES’ REPLACEMENT OF LEAK-PRONE
5 
MAINS AND SERVICES IN FLOOD PRONE AREAS IMPORTANT?
6 
A.
During a flood, the pressure of the flood waters outside of the gas main can be
7 
greater than the pressure in the gas main, especially as it pertains to low pressure
8 
mains and services.  This causes water to enter through any of the leaks (e.g.,
9 
cracks, holes) present in the pipe.  Once there is water intrusion in the mains, it
10 
can be a lengthy process to dewater the main, which can require shutting off gas
11 
to the affected main and relighting the system.
12

C.
ENHANCED RESIDENTIAL METHANE DETECTORS
7 
Q.
WHAT IS NATIONAL GRID’S PLAN REGARDING THE ENHANCED 
8 
RESIDENTIAL METHANE DETECTION PROGRAM? 
9 
A.
This Program would seek to install commercially available plug-in methane 
10 
detectors in residential customer homes.  It is an expansion of the Residential 
11 
Methane Detection Pilot Program initiated in the 2016 Rate Cases and, beginning 
12 
in the Rate Year and continuing for the next three years thereafter, would result in 
13 
54,000 detectors installed in KEDNY’s service territory each year and 36,000 in 
14 
KEDLI’s each year, for a total planned deployment of 360,000 detectors.  National 
15 
Grid, on page 44 of its Gas Safety Panel testimony, proposes to specifically target 
16 
“room set meter customers, low income customers, multi-use residences, and 
17 
customers served by smaller diameter (two and four inch) cast iron piping.”  The 
18 
detectors will be accompanied by an educational brochure and distributed in 
19 
customer-facing interactions, such as service inspections. 
20 
Q.
HOW DOES NATIONAL GRID PROPOSE TO IMPLEMENT THIS 
21 
PROGRAM? 
22 
5443


--- Page 1247 ---
A.
According to the information provided in the Gas Safety Panel’s direct testimony
1 
and National Grid’s response to CNY-128, the success of the Program is heavily
2 
dependent on customers installing and operating the devices, as well as
3 
understanding how the devices themselves work and the safety features provided.
4 
National Grid will distribute the detectors to customers along with a brochure and
5 
the manufacturer’s instructions so that the customer may install it.  National Grid
6 
proposes to send a follow-up letter and brochure, and each device will contain a
7 
unique bar code, which National Grid will scan into its system at the time of
8 
distribution, so that National Grid can track methane calls from households that
9 
have methane detectors.  Otherwise, National Grid has proposed no other quality
10 
control or customer guidance linked to this program.  Under this proposal, National
11 
Grid’s job effectively ends once the detector is in the customer’s hands and does
12 
not provide a centralized tracking mechanism for potential leaks.
13 
Q.
WHAT IS THE CITY’S ASSESSMENT OF NATIONAL GRID’S
14 
PROPOSAL?
15 
A.
Conceptually, we support this Program.  Methane leaks are dangerous, and
16 
improving detection can protect customers, especially the most vulnerable that are
17 
being specifically targeted by this Program.  Nevertheless, the Program’s design
18 
and implementation, as proposed by the Companies, raises concerns.
19 
Q.
WHAT CONCERNS DOES THE CITY HAVE?
20 
A.
Essentially, there is no quality control, limited customer guidance, and no
21 
centralized tracking system.  These issues could render an otherwise conceptually
22 
5444


--- Page 1248 ---
helpful program ineffective because it is entirely dependent on the customer to 
1 
properly install, maintain, and use the device, with little meaningful support from 
2 
National Grid. 
3 
Q.
 WHAT QUALITY CONTROL ISSUES HAVE YOU IDENTIFIED? 
4 
A.
National Grid does not know whether a detector works before delivering it to a 
5 
customer.  Considering that National Grid seeks to install 360,000 detectors, even 
6 
a one percent error rate – not complete failure, but less-than-ideal performance – 
7 
can place an unacceptable number of customers in jeopardy and reduce the ability 
8 
of this Program to detect leaks.  In addition, because the manufacturer’s instructions 
9 
direct residents to call 911 in the event that the alarm sounds, false positives due to 
10 
device error or improper installation could place added unnecessary burdens onto 
11 
the City’s emergency response resources.  Moreover, per the response to CNY-128, 
12 
the detectors have a seven-year useful life, but the Companies have no plan to 
13 
replace the detectors, meaning that the Program will end once the detectors no 
14 
longer function.   
15 
Q.
WHAT QUALITY CONTROL MEASURES WOULD HELP ADDRESS 
16 
THESE CONCERNS? 
17 
A.
A simple and effective measure would be to test a representative sample of 
18 
detectors to ensure they work as intended, including the device’s detection range 
19 
and sensitivity to methane leaks not located on the customer’s premises or methane 
20 
from organic or biogenic sources.  This also would include testing the end-of-life 
21 
warning that the manufacturer’s instructions indicate will sound after seven years, 
22 
5445


--- Page 1249 ---
per Attachment 3 to CNY-128.  Seven years is a long time for a customer to 
1 
remember that they must eventually replace their detector, and this delay can place 
2 
customers in jeopardy if they assume that their detector works because no end-of-
3 
life alarm sounded. 
4 
Q.
IS RELYING ON CUSTOMERS TO TEST THEIR OWN DETECTORS 
5 
SUFFICIENT? 
6 
A.
No.  The brochure and manufacturer’s instructions ask that the customer test their 
7 
own detector weekly to make sure the alarm is sounding properly.  However, it is 
8 
too easy for a customer to forget to test their alarm every week, no matter how 
9 
colorful the brochure, and it is reasonable to assume many recipients of these 
10 
detectors will not test on a weekly basis.  Considering that this is a ratepayer-funded 
11 
program, ratepayers should have assurances that National Grid will make an 
12 
attempt to ensure that the detectors at the heart of their Program work, even if 
13 
customers forget to test them.  Our recommendations in this regard are set forth 
14 
below. 
15 
Q.
COULD YOU ELABORATE ON THE LACK OF CUSTOMER 
16 
GUIDANCE? 
17 
A.
Yes.  Per CNY-128, National Grid gives customers: (i) a brochure that summarizes 
18 
what the detectors do and how to install them; (ii) the manufacturer’s instructions 
19 
for installation and all associated warnings; and (iii) the detector itself. 
20 
Additionally, National Grid will follow up with a letter and a second brochure.  
21 
Aside from this, there is apparently no other customer guidance. 
22 
5446


--- Page 1250 ---
The lack of customer guidance threatens to derail this Program.  First, there 
1 
is no assurance that the customer has actually installed a detector – the Company 
2 
representative that provides the detector does not perform the installation, nor does 
3 
that representative observe its installation.  Second, no guidance is provided 
4 
regarding correct installation and maintenance outside of the brochure and 
5 
manufacturer’s instructions.  The 12-page set of instructions, provided as 
6 
Attachment 3 to CNY-128, is itself a barrier.  A customer is not likely to read such 
7 
a document to ensure proper installation.  Accordingly, the customer may miss 
8 
important instructions such as: the manufacturer recommends that several detectors 
9 
be installed; the detector cannot receive noisy power, such as if another device with 
10 
a large load is on the same circuit; or that “turbulent air,” such as from fans on a 
11 
hot day, impede the functioning of the device. Customer testing of the device will 
12 
not indicate to them whether it has been properly installed per this guidance. 
13 
Moreover, customers have to fill out and place the labels that remind them what to 
14 
do if the detector sounds.  All of these instructions are buried in pages 3 through 5 
15 
of the manufacturer’s instructions, and missing any one of these important points 
16 
could render the detector ineffective. 
17 
Q.
WHAT DO YOU RECOMMEND TO REMEDY THIS ISSUE? 
18 
A.
We recommend two improvements.  First, a Company representative should install 
19 
the detector and provide concise verbal instructions regarding its use.  Having 
20 
already been tested, this would ensure that a functioning device is placed in the 
21 
appropriate location.  Additionally, it provides another means of informing the 
22 
5447


--- Page 1251 ---
customer of important information without requiring them to read a lengthy 
1 
document. 
2 
Second, twice each year during the four-year deployment schedule, the 
3 
Companies should test a sample of in-service detectors to ensure proper 
4 
functioning.  This will give the Companies an opportunity to identify and resolve 
5 
any problems with the detectors, before wide-scale deployment is completed. 
6 
Q.
WOULD THESE IMPROVEMENTS IMPOSE ADDITIONAL COSTS? 
7 
A.
We do not believe so.  Company installations and sample testing should be able to 
8 
be accommodated within the budget requested. 
9 
Q.
DO YOU HAVE ANY ADDITIONAL SUGGESTIONS RELATED TO THE 
10 
RESIDENTIAL METHANE DETECTORS? 
11 
A.
Yes.  We understand that Con Edison is pursuing a similar, but different, program 
12 
for residential methane detection, whereby the detectors will have the ability to 
13 
communicate directly with Con Edison via the AMI meters and infrastructure that 
14 
Con Edison is currently deploying.  We understand that National Grid does not 
15 
currently have any plans for deploying AMI meters.  However, in the long term, 
16 
there will be a need to monitor gas usage much more closely both from a safety and 
17 
supply perspective.  The Companies should therefore re-examine the potential 
18 
deployment of AMI and, in doing so, examine whether they can utilize residential 
19 
methane detectors that have the capability to sync up with AMI, to ensure 
20 
consistency with Con Edison (and across the City).

D.
REMOTE SERVICE SHUTOFF VALVES
22 
5448


--- Page 1252 ---
Q.
WHAT ARE THE COMPANIES’ PROPOSALS REGARDING REMOTE
1 
SERVICE SHUTOFF VALVES?
2 
A.
On pages 85-87 of KEDNY’s GIOP testimony and pages 78-80 of KEDLI’s, the
3 
Companies propose to install remote service shutoff valves at customers located in
4 
the FEMA 100-year and 500-year floodplains.  Per the response to DPS-561, the
5 
valves will be in both the 100-Year and 500-Year floodplain.  These valves,
6 
National Grid avers, would use a communications network that would allow the
7 
valves, once they detect flooding, to selectively stop the flow of gas to areas
8 
affected by flooding without impacting other areas.  In doing so, the Companies
9 
can prevent the negative effects of water infiltrating gas mains, which is discussed
10 
elsewhere in this testimony.  This program was originally planned to begin in 2017,
11 
but lack of a commercially available shutoff valve delayed the program.  KEDNY
12 
proposes to install 29,000 valves (an expansion from the original program proposal
13 
of 25,000 valves), and KEDLI 60,000.
14 
Q.
WHAT IS THE CITY’S ASSESSMENT OF THIS PROPOSAL?
15 
A.
Our response is twofold.  First, we have concerns about how this program will be
16 
managed.  Second, the data this program would generate presents an excellent
17 
opportunity for collaboration with the City.  Despite the concerns about program
18 
management, given the potential benefits to facilitate faster service restoration and
19 
minimizing equipment damage, we recommend approving this proposal, while
20 
simultaneously granting the City the ability to leverage the data for its own flood-
21 
5449


--- Page 1253 ---
monitoring programs.  Moreover, we support the placement of valves in both the 
1 
100-Year and 500-Year floodplain.
2 
Q.
WHAT ARE THE CITY’S CONCERNS REGARDING PROGRAM 
3 
MANAGEMENT? 
4 
A.
Fundamentally, this is a nascent, untested technology, and the Program itself has 
5 
already seen significant delays.  Originally, as KEDNY and KEDLI discuss in their 
6 
GIOP testimonies, they proposed to launch this Program in calendar year 2017.  
7 
There was no commercially available shutoff mechanism at the time; the valves 
8 
have only become available as of February 2019.  The valves are truly brand new, 
9 
too.  Per CNY-78, the valves have only been tested at the manufacturer’s facilities 
10 
and not in a live situation.  Indeed, the Companies have not yet completed their lab 
11 
testing of the valves.  Moreover, per CNY-78(d), no other gas utility is using these 
12 
valves.  Thus, this is a pilot not only for National Grid, but for the gas industry as 
13 
a whole.   
14 
Considering past delays and the untested nature of the valves, it is 
15 
reasonable to anticipate issues arising that could impact the effectiveness of this 
16 
program.  These include, but are not limited to, equipment failure in real world 
17 
conditions and improper installations.  These concerns are not theoretical.  Several 
18 
years ago, Con Edison installed a new technology, called a Vent Line Protector 
19 
(“VLP”) Device, which was designed to perform a similar function to the remote 
20 
service shutoff valves; namely, protect gas customers during a flooding event.  Over 
21 
80 percent (1,837 out of 2,204) of these VLP Devices were initially improperly 
22 
5450


--- Page 1254 ---
installed, and some of the devices were defective, thus requiring remedial action by 
1 
Con Edison.6  National Grid should take care to avoid a similar outcome with the 
2 
remote sensor shutoff valves. 
3 
Q.
SHOULD THIS PROPOSAL BE IMPLEMENTED DESPITE THESE 
4 
ISSUES? 
5 
A.
Yes.  Despite our concerns, we agree that this program nevertheless has the 
6 
potential to offer significant benefits, particularly during flooding events.    Because 
7 
of the storm hardening benefits and the opportunity for collaboration, which is 
8 
described below, the City supports this proposal with certain enhancements.  First, 
9 
the Companies should implement a plan to methodically and robustly test these 
10 
devices to ensure they operate as designed, and to gradually deploy such devices in 
11 
phases.  The Companies also need to perform outreach to educate customers on 
12 
how these remote operated shut off valves will work, and what they are intended to 
13 
prevent.  The Companies should further confirm there will be no “accidental” 
14 
automatic shutoffs of gas as a result of the operation of these sensors, and that they 
15 
only will trigger if there is sufficient flooding to cause water intrusion and possible 
16 
damage to customer equipment.   
17 
Q.
HOW DOES THIS PROPOSAL PRESENT AN OPPORTUNITY TO 
18 
SUPPORT THE CITY’S OWN FLOOD MONITORING EFFORTS?

4
