5 
specific areas affected, indicating that this data is quite granular, perhaps even to
6 
an individual sensor.  This data can do more than just protect customers in the event
7 
of flooding – it can be used to track the extent, duration, and frequency of floods.
8 
This type of tracking is one of the primary objectives of the “Jamaica Bay
9 
Community Flood Watch Project” (the “Flood Watch Project”).
10 
Q.
COULD YOU ELABORATE ON THE FLOOD WATCH PROJECT?
11 
A.
Yes.  Due to climate change, the City is experiencing more regular and more
12 
extreme tidal flooding, called “sunny day flooding.”  As sea levels rise, this will
13 
only get worse, shifting the flood maps in unexpected ways.  The Flood Watch
14 
Project seeks to document this sunny day flooding in the Jamaica Bay watershed
15 
through citizen science reports so that the City and its citizens can create maps and
16 
make predictions about the extent of flooding and its effects.  The data the Remote
17 
Service Shutoff Valve Program will generate would be a valuable resource to help
18 
improve the Flood Watch Project’s efforts to help improve forecasts of flooding
19 
and coastal hazards.
20 
Q.
WHAT 
DATA 
WOULD 
BE 
REQUIRED 
TO 
MAXIMIZE 
THE
21 
EFFECTIVENESS OF THE REMOTE SHUTOFF VALVE PROPOSAL?
22 
5452


--- Page 1256 ---
A.
The City would need access to the following data points for each valve in the City 
1 
and the Rockaways:
2 
•
The latitude and longitude of each valve;
3 
•
The elevation of each valve; and
4 
•
The date, time, and duration of the flood event.
5 
The City does not request this data in real time; rather, the City requests that 
6 
National Grid share this data with the City in monthly reports, in a readily-
7 
accessible format like Microsoft Excel. 
8 
Q.
WHY DO YOU SUPPORT VALVE PLACEMENT IN BOTH THE 100-
9 
YEAR AND 500-YEAR FLOODPLAINS? 
10 
A.
Flooding is not just a problem in the 100-Year floodplain; flooding in the 500-Year 
11 
floodplain has the same similar consequences despite being less frequent, and those 
12 
customers therefore require the same protection.  Importantly, as sea levels rise, 
13 
there will be increasing likelihood of flooding in both the current 100-year and 500-
14 
year floodplains.  Data from the valves will help the City better understand what 
15 
areas are regularly experiencing more flooding due to climate change.  Monitoring 
16 
the growth of the floodplain is vital and can only be done if the valves are there to 
17 
collect the data.

CONCERNS ON IMPACTS TO NYC GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE ASSETS 
10 
Q.
WHAT ARE NYC GREEN INFRASTRUCTURE ASSETS? 
11 
A.
In New York City, Green Infrastructure, or GI, refers to an array of practices that 
12 
use or mimic natural systems to manage stormwater runoff.  Stormwater is either 
13 
directed to engineered systems for infiltration or detained at a slower rate before it 
14 
enters the combined sewer system.  Types of Green Infrastructure include: 
15 
•
Rain Gardens – vegetated or landscaped depressions in the sidewalk
16 
designed with an engineered soil that promote infiltration of stormwater
17 
runoff into the underlying soil.
18 
•
Stormwater Greenstreets – similar to Rain Gardens, but constructed in the
19 
roadway and usually larger than a Rain Garden.
20 
•
Green Roofs – roofs made up of a top vegetative layer that grows in an
21 
engineered soil, which sits on top of a drainage layer.
22 
5454


--- Page 1258 ---
•
Permeable Paving – using a range of materials and techniques, permeable
1 
pavers or porous concrete allows water to seep in between paving materials
2 
and be absorbed into the ground.
3 
Through Green Infrastructure implementation, DEP is working toward a
4 
reduction of 1.67 billion gallons a year in Combined Sewer Overflows (“CSOs”) 
5 
by 2030.  CSOs can negatively affect water quality and recreational uses in local 
6 
waterways.  Through the end of 2018, 4,585 Green Infrastructure Assets had been 
7 
either constructed or were in construction.  Approximately 5,500 Assets are 
8 
planned to enter construction in 2019. A significant portion of these Assets are 
9 
located in National Grid’s service territory in Brooklyn and Queens. 
10 
Q.
WHAT 
ARE 
YOUR 
CONCERNS 
RELATED 
TO 
GREEN 
11 
INFRASTRUCTURE ASSETS AS THEY PERTAIN TO NATIONAL 
12 
GRID? 
13 
A.
Our primary concern is that NYC Green Infrastructure Program Assets are being 
14 
damaged by National Grid street work.  For example, in north Brooklyn, DEP has 
15 
recorded damage to 47 Assets from National Grid work crews, totaling 
16 
approximately $160,000 in damages.  The damage is primarily from sediment and 
17 
cement intrusion into the right-of-way Green Infrastructure Program Assets, 
18 
which damages the engineered soils and plants located within the Assets.  Other 
19 
impacts include structural damage from National Grid pipe installations either 
20 
through or adjacent to Green Infrastructure Program Assets.  National Grid and its 
21 
contractors should be following the green infrastructure protection stipulations 
22 
5455


--- Page 1259 ---
required by the DOT Street Opening Permit.  It is clear to DEP that National Grid 
1 
and its contractors are either unaware of these protection stipulations or have not 
2 
fully adhered to them.  
3 
An additional concern about DEP Green Infrastructure Assets is 
4 
limitations to siting and construction due to interferences with existing National 
5 
Grid infrastructure.  DEP will continue to review these locations with National 
6 
Grid, but when there is no alternate location for the Asset, DEP retains the right 
7 
to request National Grid to relocate their infrastructure.  National Grid should 
8 
respond within 10 business days to DEP’s request for relocation.  In the event that 
9 
National Grid cannot move its infrastructure, National Grid must provide a 
10 
specific in-depth justification.  In instances where the infrastructure can be moved, 
11 
it should be relocated in a mutually agreed upon timeframe.  
12 
For new National Grid infrastructure or relocation of existing 
13 
infrastructure, National Grid should consider Green Infrastructure Program 
14 
implementation, and the infrastructure should be installed with consideration to 
15 
the future implementation of Green Infrastructure Assets.  These considerations 
16 
include placing natural gas lines six feet instead of three feet from the curb line 
17 
when feasible, which will allow for DEP to install right-of-way Green 
18 
Infrastructure Assets. 
19

8

9

nearby (see below):

CONCERNS WITH PROPOSED GAS SAFETY METRICS 
18 
AND PERFORMANCE MEASURES 
19 
Q.
ARE 
THE 
COMPANIES 
SEEKING 
ANY 
PERFORMANCE 
20 
INCENTIVES?  
21 
5458


--- Page 1262 ---
A.
Yes.  The Companies are proposing to modify the following performance
1 
measures: Leak Prone Pipe Replacement, Emergency Response, Leak
2 
Management, Damage Prevention, and Gas Regulations Performance.
3 
Q.
ARE THE PERFORMANCE INCENTIVES THAT THE COMPANIES
4 
SEEK JUSTIFIED?
5 
A.
No.  Fundamentally, we disagree with the Companies’ proposals, which
6 
essentially seek to reward them for doing basic prudent utility work.  Several of
7 
the proposed performance metrics are coupled to shareholder incentives for certain
8 
natural gas distribution operations activities that should not be incentivized –
9 
emergency response and damage prevention – because these activities are within
10 
industry norms of utility operations as required by federal regulations.
11 
The CFR provides minimum pipeline safety regulations governing, in part, 
12 
the operations of a utility’s natural gas distribution system (See 49 CFR Part 192).  
13 
The CFR requires prompt and effective response to and reports of gas odor in or 
14 
near a building, and to every type of emergency that involves or could involve 
15 
natural gas or a natural gas pipeline facility.  The effectiveness of an operator’s 
16 
emergency response program is a factor considered for risk reduction within the 
17 
Distribution Integrity Management Program (“DIMP”) regulations in 49 CFR Part 
18 
192 Subpart P.  The DIMP regulations also require an operator to identify and 
19 
implement measures to address risks to its system and ultimately to people and 
20 
property.  This includes performance of an effective leak management program, 
21 
which provides that an operator act appropriately to mitigate the hazards 
22 
5459


--- Page 1263 ---
associated with each leak.  For non-hazardous leaks, appropriate action may 
1 
include scheduling the line for repair and continued reduction in leak count.   
2 
Other proposed performance metrics are tied to rewarding the Companies 
3 
for accelerating the implementation of certain capital investment programs or 
4 
modifying the damage prevention metrics to eliminate components that measure 
5 
damages that are wholly within each Companies’ control.  Below is a description 
6 
of our analysis of each proposed incentive, and an explanation of why such 
7 
incentive should be rejected by the Commission.  
8 
For ease of reference, Exhibit__(NYCGISP-3) includes an overview of our 
9 
recommendations for the Companies’ various gas safety-related incentive 
10 
mechanisms and safety metrics. 
11

20

22 
5460

target.  The LPP mileage targets for the NRA are set well below the levels that

14

The Companies are proposing a series of positive incentives for their 30 minute 
17

18

19

20 
Q.
DO YOU OPPOSE THE  PROPOSALS?  
21 
5462


--- Page 1266 ---
A.
Yes, they are not acceptable.  The Companies should not be rewarded for simply
1 
maintaining a safe gas system, which is their fundamental role.  Additionally,
2 
neither Company has received an NRA under this performance metric.
3 
Reallocating BPs to this measure is thus just as inappropriate here as it is for the
4 
LPP retirement metric – considering the Companies’ past emergency response
5 
performance, the Companies’ proposal then simply becomes a reduced penalty for
6 
violating the Commission’s gas safety regulations.
7 
Q.
PLEASE PROVIDE THE BASIS FOR YOUR OPPOSITION TO THE
8 
COMPANIES’ PROPOSED EMERGENCY RESPONSE INCENTIVE
9 
PROPOSALS.
10 
A.
 As a threshold matter, it is the utility’s responsibility to provide safe and reliable
11 
gas service, including responding to gas leaks in an appropriate time frame to
12 
minimize the harmful consequences of gas emergencies to its customers, its
13 
employees, the general public, property, and the environment.  The Companies are
14 
proposing to revise the Emergency Response Safety Performance Measure so that
15 
the Company receives an incremental positive incentive for having met a 30
16 
minute response rate to emergency calls.
17 
The expectation to meet a response time target at or below 30 minutes is a 
18 
current industrywide norm.  Prudent operators will continue to strive to improve 
19 
upon (lower) this norm.  Federal regulations (49 CFR Part 192) require an operator 
20 
to implement an emergency response program that will minimize the hazard 
21 
5463


--- Page 1267 ---
resulting from a gas pipeline (distribution system or transmission system) 
1 
emergency by providing a prompt and effective response to gas emergencies.   
2 
Moreover, CFR §§ 192.605(a), 192.605(b), 192.605(c), and 192.615(a) 
3 
require an operator to follow procedures for conducting operations, maintenance, 
4 
and emergency response activities, including procedures for responding promptly 
5 
to a report of gas odor inside or near a building.  The emergency response 
6 
procedures an operator is required to establish in writing and to follow include 
7 
emergency plans requiring performance of prompt and effective response to a 
8 
notice of every type of emergency that involves or could involve gas or a gas 
9 
pipeline facility (see CFR §§ 192.605(c), 192.615(a)(3)).    
10 
The presumed expectation for the operator to minimize the risk from the 
11 
activities of natural gas delivery is also set by the DIMP regulations (49 CFR § 
12 
192.1007).  The specific contribution of prompt and effective emergency response 
13 
to risk minimization is the reduction of the consequences of failures that result in 
14 
gas release or to situations that could imminently result in gas release.   
15 
The regulatory requirements to provide a prompt and effective response to 
16 
gas emergencies, and the inequity of rewarding shareholders for performance that 
17 
the Companies are required by regulation to do, are the bases for our opposition 
18 
to the Companies’ proposed emergency response incentive proposal. 
19

Q.
WHAT HAS BEEN NYCEM’S EXPERIENCE WITH LEAKING GAS
1 
MAINS?
2 
A.
We are aware of at least one gas explosion in New York City – at Lexington Avenue
3 
and East 54th Street – that has been attributed to the accumulation of gas in a
4 
subterranean structure from a gas main with a small leak.  An investigation into that

Q, 
WHAT HAPPENED IN THAT INCIDENT?
8 
A.
One City employee was seriously injured and two other City employees also were
9 
injured.

5469


--- Page 1273 ---
Q.
WHAT ARE NYCEM’S CONCERNS WITH GAS ACCUMULATIONS IN
1 
SUBSURFACE STRUCTURES?
2 
A.
If there is a leak in a gas main, the emitted gas will travel to and collect in any voids.
3 
Many subsurface structures, such as manholes and service boxes, are not sealed.
4 
Gas can travel along pipes, mains, conduits, and ducts into these structures and
5 
accumulate.  Over time, the potential exists for the gas to reach a concentration
6 
level at which it can become explosive in the presence of a flame or heat source.
7 
In the incident we discussed, a City crew was repairing potholes using a torch to
8 
soften the asphalt.
9 
There are a number of electrical and plumbing activities in which a heat 
10 
source is in or near one of these subsurface structures or sparks are produced from 
11 
cutting metal.  Based on these concerns, the City would like the Commission to 
12 
take action to reduce, to the maximum extent possible, the potential for natural gas 
13 
to accumulate in these structures and potentially cause explosions. 
14 
Q.
DO YOU HAVE ANY PERSPECTIVE ON HOW OFTEN THESE 
15 
CONCERNS ARISE WITHIN NEW YORK CITY OVER THE COURSE OF 
16 
A YEAR? 
17 
A.
When NYCEM investigated the Lexington Avenue incident, we learned that there 
18 
were approximately 4,000 active gas leaks of all types and 423 leaks in 
19 
subterranean structures as of January 2016.  Both Con Edison and National Grid 
20 
have taken action to reduce the number of gas leaks since 2016.  Nevertheless, there 
21 
is still significant room for improvement. 
22

3 
opposed to workable (type 1, 2, or 2A) leaks.  This is illustrated in the charts below:

2 
Q.
PLEASE DISCUSS THE BENEFITS TO THE PUBLIC OF ELIMINATING 
3 
GAS LEAKS. 
4 
A.
There are two primary benefits to doing so.  The first is public safety.  If gas leaks 
5 
are fixed as they are identified, there would be far less opportunity for gas to migrate 
6 
to subsurface structures and accumulate to explosive concentrations.  Although gas 
7 
explosions are rare in New York City, every recent gas explosion has resulted in 
8 
injuries or death for one or more people.  These injuries and deaths are avoidable, 
9 
and reasonable efforts should be taken to avoid them.  The death of a single New 
10 
York City resident was sufficient cause for the Commission to institute rigorous 
11 
stray voltage inspection and repair requirements.  The Commission should take a 
12 
similarly aggressive approach with respect to eliminating gas leaks.  
13 
Q.
WHAT IS THE SECOND PRIMARY BENEFIT? 
14 
A.
Methane is a very potent greenhouse gas, many times more potent than carbon 
15 
dioxide.  Eliminating gas leaks will reduce fugitive emissions of natural gas into 
16 
the atmosphere and help to combat global warming.  It is our understanding that 
17 
the State, and the Commission in particular, are taking multiple actions to reduce 
18 
greenhouse gas emissions, including increasing reliance on renewable and carbon-
19 
free resources and seeking substantial expansion of energy efficiency measures.  As 
20 
part of its portfolio of actions, the Commission can, and should, direct National 
21 
5475


--- Page 1279 ---
Grid and the other gas utilities to take steps to reduce and eliminate natural gas 
1 
emissions from pipe leaks to the maximum extent practicable. 
2 
Q.
ARE YOU AWARE OF THE PRACTICES OF OTHER UTILITIES 
3 
REGARDING THEIR GAS LEAK BACKLOG? 
4 
A.
We are not aware of the details of all utilities, but within New York State we are 
5

6

7

9

10 
have corporate requirements to repair all gas leaks of all types each year and strive 
11 
to satisfy these requirements.  According to those Panels’ exhibits, their leak 
12 
backlogs are minuscule: across all types of leaks (1, 2A, 2, and 3), NYSEG and 
13 
RG&E have a three-year average of 10 leaks and 12 leaks, respectively.  We 
14 
understand that the NYSEG and RG&E leak backlog figures may be influenced

16

17

13 
reported, so this proposal does not represent an improvement on the performance
14 
measures already in place.

10  See Case 16-G-0058 et al., Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates, Charges, Rules

A.

entire NRA of 100 BPs.  Under the Companies’ proposal, going forward the

4

7

13 
In light of the allegations in the Order to Show Cause – again, which may grow as

11

13

NEED FOR FAIRNESS AND BALANCED CONSIDERATION 
3 
OF CUSTOMER AND SHAREHOLDER INTERESTS

Q.
IN REVIEWING THE COMPANIES’ RATE FILING, HOW SHOULD THE 
5

6 
SHAREHOLDERS?  
7 
A.
The Companies initially were seeking annual revenue requirement increases of 
8 
$236.9 million and $49.4 million, respectively.    Based on the Corrections and 
9 
Update Filing (“C&U Filing”), the requested annual revenue requirements are 
10 
$195.6 million and $61.0 million for KEDNY and KEDLI, respectively. 
11 
There is a need to balance the Companies’ proposals for their gas systems 
12 
with the impacts of those proposals on customers.  Rates should not be considered 
13 
an unlimited source of funding for the utilities.  The Commission must carefully 
14 
review and evaluate the Companies’ proposals, and it must make adjustments to the 
15 
requests to ensure that the rates charged to customers are fair and reasonable. 
16 
The Companies are planning unprecedented capital spending.  We trust that 
17 
most of the projects included in the Companies’ capital plans are, on their face, 
18 
legitimate utility projects.  However, we question whether the Companies have the 
19 
ability and internal resources to properly manage such a large spending plan and 
20 
ensure that all expenditures are prudent, and proper practices are in place to prevent 
21 
waste.   
22 
5501


--- Page 1305 ---
In this regard, the recent Order Instituting Proceeding and to Show Cause, 
1 
issued by the Commission on July 12, 2019 in Case 17-G-0317 (“Show Cause 
2 
Proceeding”), is particularly troubling. In that Order, the Commission sets forth 
3 
detailed allegations by DPS Staff of more than 1,600 violations of Commission 
4 
regulations by the Companies. These violations indicate a lack of proper safety 
5 
practices and failed supervision, and resulted in a yet-to-be determined sum of 
6 
unnecessary spending.  Although the extent of the damages resulting from the 
7 
Companies’ operations will be determined in Case 17-G-0317, the detailed 
8 
allegations suggest that a particularly rigorous review of the Companies’ projected 
9 
costs is required here.

1

PLEASE 
EXPAND 
ON 
THAT
17 
STATEMENT.
18 
A.
The City recognizes that sometimes rewards may be needed to induce certain
19 
behavior.  In the case of utilities, shareholder incentives – both positive and
20 
negative – have been used to discourage poor performance and encourage the
21 
utilities to do tasks they otherwise may not want to do.  At the same time, the
22 
5503


--- Page 1307 ---
Commission has very broad power to order the utilities to take certain actions or 
1 
refrain from taking other actions.  Violations of Commission Orders can result in 
2 
monetary penalties of hundreds of thousands of dollars or more.  In fact, in response 
3 
to CNY-1, the Companies identify $13.9 million (KEDLI) and $21.2 million 
4 
(KEDNY) of penalties that are owed to customers and should be returned. 
5 
Accordingly, there is no reason to provide shareholder incentives to the 
6 
Companies related to any action that the Commission requires them to take or not 
7 
to take, and for which the Companies would be liable for penalties for failure to 
8 
comply.  An example of this is providing safe and adequate service by expeditiously 
9 
responding to gas leak and odor calls – there is no reason to reward the Company 
10 
for the timeliness of such actions, which are required pursuant to good utility 
11 
practice. 
12 
On the other hand, for discretionary actions taken by the Companies, the 
13 
use of shareholder incentives may be appropriate.  In such cases, though, the 
14 
incentives should reward only superior performance, not business-as-usual 
15 
conduct.  The City Energy Efficiency and Gas Infrastructure and Safety Panels 
16 
address the Companies’ proposed incentives in detail. 
17 
Q.
HOW 
SHOULD 
THE 
COMPANY’S 
ENERGY 
EFFICIENCY 
18 
PERFORMANCE BE MEASURED? 
19 
A.
The City’s Energy Efficiency Panel addresses this topic in detail.  We note that the 
20 
Companies have been administering energy efficiency programs for many years, 
21 
and arguably have been doing so more aggressively in recent years.  There is now 
22 
5504


--- Page 1308 ---
sufficient information available to determine baseline performance levels.  Any 
1 
shareholder incentives should start at levels above baseline performance, and any 
2 
increases in the incentives should be commensurate with achievements well above 
3 
the initial levels. 
4 
Q.
HOW IS THIS PROPOSAL CONSISTENT WITH THE BALANCE YOU 
5 
HAVE BEEN EMPHASIZING? 
6 
A.
Reducing gas usage and gas peak demand benefits all customers because it reduces 
7 
the need for additional infrastructure. That reduced need, coupled with lower 
8 
demand and usage, should result in lower commodity and delivery prices for 
9 
customers. For these reasons, coupling shareholder incentives with achieving high 
10 
levels of energy savings creates a win-win outcome for shareholders and customers.  
11 
The recent gas moratorium declared by the Companies only highlights the urgent 
12 
need to accelerate energy efficiency and demand response measures to better 
13 
manage their gas systems. 
14 
Q.
WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF THE REQUESTED RATE INCREASES ON 
15 
LOW INCOME CUSTOMERS? 
16 
A.
The City’s Low Income Panel presents a recently completed analysis of energy cost 
17 
burdens on New York City residents.  The results of this analysis are striking and 
18 
should be considered in evaluating the Companies’ revenue requirements and 
19 
shareholder incentive requests. 
20 
Q.
WHAT DID THE ANALYSIS REVEAL? 
21 
5505


--- Page 1309 ---
A.
In 2016, the Commission established that New Yorkers should not pay more than
1 
six percent of their income on utility expenses.  It then adopted parameters for
2 
utility low income programs that it believed would achieve this target.  At that time,
3 
the City raised numerous concerns about the methodology used and the results
4 
obtained.  Based upon the results of the City’s most recent analysis, as discussed in
5 
more detail in the City’s Low Income Panel testimony, we continue to believe that
6 
the methodology is flawed.
7 
The City’s analysis reveals that the discounts established by the 
8 
Commission are not sufficient to reduce the energy cost burden for low income 
9 
families to six percent or below.  In fact, with the current KEDNY and KEDLI 
10 
discounts, there are more than 220,470 low income families (under 60 percent of 
11 
the State Median Income) in the KEDNY service territory and the Rockaways 
12 
portion of the KEDLI service territory whose energy cost burdens exceed six 
13 
percent of their pre-tax income.  The Companies’ proposed rate increases, if 
14 
adopted without any corresponding changes to existing low income discounts, 
15 
likely will exacerbate these figures.  The City’s Low Income Panel has several 
16 
specific recommendations designed to provide additional protections for low 
17 
income customers. 
18 
Q.
HOW DOES THE IMPACT ON LOW INCOME CUSTOMERS RELATE 
19 
TO THE BALANCING OF CUSTOMER AND SHAREHOLDER 
20 
INTERESTS? 
21 
5506


--- Page 1310 ---
A.
KEDNY and KEDLI are proposing budgets of $25.5 million and $5.5 million,
1 
respectively, for gas low income programs in the Rate Year.  At the same time, they
2 
are seeking more than $45 million and $29 million in shareholder incentives, as
3 
well as an increase in its allowed return on equity that has a value, based on the
4 
Companies’ response to CNY-64, of $35.3 million.  In other words, the Companies
5 
are seeking benefits for their shareholders that are more than three and a half times
6 
larger than the assistance they propose to provide to their customers with the lowest
7 
income levels.  In our view, the benefits sought for shareholders are not in balance
8 
with the benefits that may be received by customers.
9 
Q.
WHAT ELSE SHOULD THE COMPANIES DO TO HELP THEIR LOW
10 
INCOME CUSTOMERS?
11 
A.
As discussed by the City’s Low Income Panel, KEDNY and KEDLI should
12 
provide deeper discounts to these customers to reduce their energy cost burdens.
13 
In addition, reconnection fees are particularly burdensome for low income
14 
customers, and should be eliminated altogether. Finally, the Companies should
15 
adopt certain improvements to their existing file-matching process with the New
16 
York City Human Resources Administration, or HRA, to better identify and enroll
17 
eligible low income customers into the utilities’ low income programs.
18

The Commission has the authority to provide a more equitable and appropriate
21

22 
5507


--- Page 1311 ---
recommends the immediate return of certain customer credits being held by the 
1 
Companies.  As discussed by the City’s Energy Efficiency and Infrastructure and 
2 
Safety Panels, the size of the shareholder incentives should be materially reduced, 
3 
and City Witness Lane Kollen is recommending a significant downward adjustment 
4 
to the Companies’ rate requests based on his analysis and rejection of a change to 
5

Q.
PLEASE COMMENT ON THE COMPANIES’ RESPONSE TO THE 
3 
STALLED NESE PROJECT. 
4 
A.
On May 15, 2019, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation 
5 
(“DEC”) refused to grant a water certificate needed for the NESE project to 
6 
proceed.  On May 16, 2019, in response to the DEC rejection, the Companies 
7

8 
service, effectively imposing a gas moratorium.  On June 5, 2019, the New Jersey 
9 
Department of Environmental Protection followed suit and denied permits required 
10 
by the NESE project.   
11 
On June 11, 2019, the Companies filed supplemental testimony to address 
12 
the consequences of the unavailability of the NESE pipeline.  The supplemental 
13 
testimony states that the loss of the NESE project would result in additional 
14 
increases to the requested KEDNY and KEDLI revenue requirements of $5.7 
15 
million and $15.2 million, respectively.  Other than quantifying the impact on 
16 
revenue requirements, the supplemental testimony did not offer any alternative 
17 
plans that the Companies would pursue if the NESE pipeline is not built.  The 
18 
Companies maintained a similar approach in its C&U Filing filed on July 3, 2019.   
19 
Q.
DO YOU HAVE CONCERNS WITH HOW THE COMPANIES HAVE 
20 
ADDRESSED THE NESE PIPELINE? 
21 
5509


--- Page 1313 ---

Yes, very much so.  The New York and New Jersey approvals sought by the NESE

2

3

Q.
WHAT SHOULD THE COMMISSION DO?
15 
A.
The Commission should require the Companies to develop and file testimony
16 
addressing how they will operate their systems, without a moratorium, if the NESE
17

18

21 
5510

Commission needs to require them to find ways to operate their systems so that

4 
response programs, which could provide load relief for the Companies’ system. In 
5

16 
territory.

In addition, the Commission should ensure that parties are given a proper

17

18 
will receive gas service for their homes and buildings.  It would be unjust and unfair

21

Q.
WHAT ACTIONS SHOULD THE COMPANIES UNDERTAKE WITH 
20 
RESPECT TO STRANDED COSTS? 
21 
5513


--- Page 1317 ---
A.
Given the goals of deep decarbonization and the clean energy transition, the
1 
composition of utility infrastructure will change over time.  In particular, the need
2 
for the Companies’ extensive gas infrastructure may diminish.  At present, KEDNY
3 
and KEDLI are planning to spend approximately $2.3 billion over the next four
4 
years to replace leak-prone pipe. As the demand for gas diminishes, the propriety
5 
of these investments will need to be re-examined.  As for the investments already
6 
made and/or being made over the prospective term of this rate case, there is a
7 
potential for some to become stranded.  We recommend that the Companies, in
8 
coordination with interested parties, begin to examine the risk of stranded assets
9 
and conduct research and analysis into opportunities to mitigate those risks.
10 
Q.
DOES THE CITY HAVE ANY ADDITIONAL COMMENTS ON THE
11 
POTENTIAL STRANDED ASSET RISK?
12 
A.
There could be a unique opportunity to address a subset of potential stranded asset
13 
concerns regarding ongoing leak-prone pipe replacement while advancing the
14 
City’s and State’s beneficial electrification goals.  We recommend that the
15 
Companies conduct a feasibility study that includes the following elements:
16 
•
Identification of neighborhoods with high-concentrations of leak-prone
17 
pipe that need to be replaced;
18 
•
An assessment of whether it is technically feasible to not replace the leak-
19 
prone pipe in certain neighborhoods without affecting other customers, such
20 
as at the end of pipeline segments or at the edges of the Company’s gas
21 
service territory;
22 
5514


--- Page 1318 ---
•
An assessment of the technical feasibility of deploying district energy
1 
systems, such as a shared geothermal ground source heat pump system, that
2 
could be used to provide heating and cooling needs and domestic hot water
3 
for those buildings within identified neighborhoods; this assessment should
4 
consider the feasibility of different types of geothermal (e.g., standing
5 
column well systems, closed and open loop systems) and other types of
6 
district systems to determine best fit (e.g., low carbon high / low-
7 
temperature hot water and /or steam loops).  The City proposes that such an
8 
assessment be conducted in phases, as follows:
9 
a.
Phase One – Retain a consultant to complete a high-level Desktop
10 
Study on the feasibility of deploying district energy systems in the
11 
Companies’ service territories, leveraging existing studies and data.
12 
The Desktop Study should align district energy deployment with
13 
leak-prone pipe removal to increase financial feasibility and avoid
14 
stranded assets;
15 
b.
Phase Two – Based upon the initial Desktop Study, identify ten to
16 
twenty sites that indicate high potential and/or represent unique use
17 
cases and complete a detailed assessment of those sites to
18 
supplement the Phase One Desktop Study, including an assessment
19 
of local site characteristics, customer interest, detailed load data,
20 
financial feasibility, and more detailed design (with the goal of
21 
ranking the sites based on benefits, costs, and feasibility);
22 
5515


--- Page 1319 ---
c.
Phase Three – Conduct a Pilot at several high potential sites, which
1 
would be selected to maximize the potential for success and
2 
replicability.  To the extent possible, the different Pilot sites should
3 
test different use cases, and should include the deployment and
4 
operation of the geothermal district or another type of district system
5 
based upon the assessments in Phases I and II, as well as the
6 
establishment of a viable regulatory, ownership, and governance
7 
structure; and
8 
d.
Phase Four – Assess the scalability of the Pilot to additional
9 
locations.  As part of this Phase, the consultant should identify what
10 
interventions and/or regulatory changes are needed to lead to greater
11 
adoption of district systems, as well as the projected benefits and
12 
costs of expanding the Pilot.
13 
•
Consideration of a regulatory model in which the avoided costs of the leak-
14 
prone pipe replacements in the selected neighborhoods can be used to offset
15 
the capital costs of a district energy system.
16 
We also recommend that the performance of the feasibility study be preceded by a 
17 
scoping discussion with interested parties to develop specific details for both the 
18 
study contents and the manner in which the study is performed.

13

14

15

16

18

19

20

21

22 
5517


--- Page 1321 ---
National Grid’s own experience with implementing a shared geothermal pilot in

8

10

11

investments contemplated by the Companies.

6 
to allow for the expedited review.

Q.
PLEASE DISCUSS THE PROBLEMS THAT HAVE ARISEN ON CITY 
15 
INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS BECAUSE OF DELAYS BY THE 
16 
COMPANIES. 
17 
A.
As brief background, DDC is the primary construction project manager for the 
18 
City’s in-street infrastructure projects.  DDC manages the capital projects 
19 
undertaken by DEP related to the water and sewer systems, and by DOT related to 
20

21 
5527


--- Page 1331 ---
substantially involved in coordinating City infrastructure projects with the City’s 
1 
utilities. 
2 
At the outset of a City infrastructure project, DDC sends a 10-day 
3 
notification letter to the Companies requesting that they provide the expected 
4 
amount of time it will take to protect or relocate their facilities so that they are not 
5 
damaged during construction. DDC consistently has challenges getting timely 
6 
responses on whether National Grid has facilities that conflict with City-planned 
7 
projects, how National Grid plans to accommodate our projects, and the timeline 
8 
for supporting and protecting National Grid facilities. Further, National Grid has 
9 
challenges completing their relocation and protection work within committed 
10 
timelines due to a limited contractor pool that is certified to do this work. 
11

DDC completes over 90 infrastructure projects each year.  The number of work 
14

15 
or two requests or 10 or more requests.

22 
5528

and construction responses.  On occasion, problems have arisen because of delays

16

18 
the Companies’ work can take longer than projected. Recently, DDC has shared 
19

20

21

22 
5529

4 
percent design.  DDC also reserves the right to request schedule updates if there are 
5

6 
The schedule submission should include major milestones and phasing 
7

8 
area and by street segment. Further, traffic stipulations for relocation work should

22 
5530


--- Page 1334 ---
are not shown on any drawings or maps.  When such facilities are encountered, the 
1

2

3 
Q.
WHAT IS THE EFFECT OF THESE DELAYS ON THE OVERALL 
4 
PROJECTS? 
5 
A.
Delays mean additional time and additional costs.  Projects take longer than 
6 
anticipated, which inconveniences the public.  Longer timeframes also can translate 
7 
to higher costs.  In this case, higher costs are likely for both Companies’ protection 
8 
and relocation work and for the overall City project – in our view, with better 
9 
information and better communications and coordination, these delays and 
10 
incremental costs can be avoided.

COST AND REVENUE ALLOCATION 
18 
Q.
HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE ECOSS STUDY PRESENTED BY THE 
19 
COMPANIES? 
20 
5540


--- Page 1344 ---
A.
Yes.  The Companies’ ECOSS and proposed revenue allocation was presented by the Rate
1 
Design Panel.  The Company’s ECOSS is a traditional study wherein revenue requirements
2 
are allocated among customer classes on the basis of cost causation.
3 
Q.
WHY IS AN ECOSS IMPORTANT?
4 
A.
An ECOSS illustrates the costs a utility incurs to serve each customer class.  It is widely
5 
accepted that costs should be allocated among customer classes on the basis of cost
6 
causation.  That principle is perhaps the most universally accepted tenet of allocating costs
7 
that cannot be directly assigned to a particular customer class.  As such, costs should be
8 
allocated to those classes on the basis of how or why those costs are incurred by the utility.
9 
The results of such studies are normally used in assigning cost and revenue responsibilities
10 
to various customer classes.
11 
Q. 
DO YOU SUPPORT THE PREMISE THAT COST CAUSATION PRINCIPLES
12 
SHOULD GUIDE THE ALLOCATION OF COSTS TO THE CUSTOMER 
13 
CLASSES? 
14 
A.
Yes.  Rates that are based on consistently applied cost causation principles are fair and 
15 
reasonable and further the cause of stability, conservation and economic efficiency.  Other 
16 
factors such as simplicity, gradualism, economic development and ease of administration 
17 
may also be taken into consideration when determining the final allocation of the revenue 
18 
requirement among classes, but the fundamental starting point and guideline should be the 
19 
cost of serving each customer class produced by the ECOSS. 
20 
Q.
PLEASE EXPLAIN THE PURPOSE AND DEVELOPMENT OF A CLASS COST
21 
OF SERVICE STUDY.
22 
5541


--- Page 1345 ---
A.
A class cost of service study allocates and assigns the total cost of providing utility service
1 
to the classes of customers receiving that service.  The development of a class cost of
2 
service study consists of three steps: functionalization, classification, and allocation.
3 
Functionalization refers to the process by which the Company’s investments and expenses
4 
are identified and segregated into different cost categories.  For KEDNY and KEDLI, these
5 
functional categories include supply and storage, transmission, distribution, metering and
6 
billing, collections, sales promotions and procurement.
7 
Once functionalization is complete, the utility’s costs are classified into categories 
8 
of demand-related, energy related and customer-related costs in order to facilitate the 
9 
allocation of costs by applying cost causation principles.  In general, all distribution costs 
10 
are either responsive to increases in natural gas demand or to the number of customers.  
11 
Demand-related costs are those that are needed to serve the winter peak demands of  
12 
distribution customers.  Demand-related costs are fixed and do not vary with the monthly 
13 
and annual commodity consumption of the utility’s customers.  Customer-related costs are 
14 
associated with the number of customers and are costs that are incurred to connect 
15 
customers to the system independent of the customer’s demand and energy requirements.  
16 
Primary examples of customer-related costs are investments in meters, services, and a 
17 
portion of main investment incurred to extend the distribution system to the customer’s 
18 
premises and conform to local and national codes and standards.  In addition, such 
19 
accounting functions as meter reading, bill preparation and revenue accounting are 
20 
generally considered customer-related costs. 
21 
5542


--- Page 1346 ---
Lastly, the functionalized and classified costs are allocated to the various customer 
1 
classes based on each class’ contribution to the respective cost classifications.  In general, 
2 
demand-related costs are allocated based on each class’ contribution to the maximum 
3 
demand placed on the system by the classes or by the customers within the classes. 
4 
Customer related costs are allocated based upon the number of customers in each class, 
5 
weighted to account for the complexity of servicing the needs of the different classes of 
6 
customers.   
7 
Q.
HOW DID THE COMPANIES’ ECOSS CLASSIFY DISTRIBUTION MAINS? 
8 
A.
The RDP explained on pages 17 and 18 of its Direct Testimony that it used a minimum-
9 
system study to classify distribution mains into customer and demand related costs.  Based 
10 
on this study, 47.08% of the distribution system was classified as customer-related and 
11 
52.92% was classified as demand-related.  The customer portion of distribution mains was 
12 
allocated to customer classes based on the number of customers and the demand component 
13 
was allocated based on class contribution to design-day demand. 
14 
Q.
IS THE COMPANIES’ ALLOCATION OF DISTRIBUTION MAIN COSTS ON A 
15 
CUSTOMER AND DEMAND BASIS CONSISTENT WITH THE NATIONAL 
16 
ASSOCIATION OF REGULATORY UTILITY COMMISSIONERS (“NARUC”) 
17 
GAS DISTRIBUTION RATE DESIGN MANUAL DATED JUNE, 1989 (“1989 
18 
NARUC MANUAL”)? 
19 
A.
Yes.  The NARUC Manuals discuss a number of methodologies and approaches to cost 
20 
allocation.  With respect to the allocation of distribution main costs, the 1989 NARUC 
21 
Manual states that “[a] portion of the costs associated with the distribution system may be 
22 
5543


--- Page 1347 ---
included as customer cost.”  (1989 NARUC Manual at 22.)  The 1989 NARUC Manual 
1 
states further that, “[o]ne argument for inclusion of distribution related items in the 
2 
customer cost classification is the zero or minimum size theory.” (Id.)     
3 
Q.
HAS THE COMMISSION RECOGNIZED THE APPROPRIATENESS OF A 
4 
CUSTOMER COMPONENT IN THE COST OF GAS DISTRIBUTION MAINS? 
5 
A.
Yes.  The Commission has accepted the use of a minimum-system methodology to classify 
6 
and allocate distribution costs in past National Grid cases.   
7 
Q.
DO YOU AGREE WITH THE COMPANIES’ CLASSIFICATION AND 
8 
ALLOCATION OF DISTRIBUTION MAINS? 
9 
A.
Yes.  As the RDP pointed out, distribution mains are installed to connect customers to the 
10 
distribution system and to provide capacity to meet the winter peak.  The Companies’ 
11 
ECOSS appropriately utilized a minimum-system study to estimate which portions of 
12 
distribution mains are demand related and customer related, and then allocated costs to the 
13 
various customer classes based on that relationship.  We recommend that the Commission 
14 
adopt the Companies’ minimum-system methodology for classifying and allocating the 
15 
cost of distribution mains. 
16

9

A.
The KEDNY RDP explained its proposal regarding TC/IT customers beginning on page
11

5549

the Company would be able to remote switch over the customers’ equipment to an alternate

fuel in the event it calls an interruption.  Tier 2 customers would be notified of an 
3

4

The Companies did not state in their response how long a Non-firm customer would 
18

Q.
ARE TC/IT CUSTOMERS IMPORTANT IN TERMS OF HELPING KEDNY AND 
3 
KEDLI MANAGE THEIR SYSTEMS DURING PEAK WINTER PERIODS? 
4 
A.
Yes, and the Commission recognized this fact in its TC/IT Order, page 2, as follows: 
5 
“By offering IT and TC service, the Companies can provide non-firm customers with delivery 
6 
service during the vast majority of the year, while also ensuring the reliability of the distribution 
7 
networks when demand for natural gas is highest, generally during cold weather when firm 
8

9 
maintain their distribution networks to serve firm customers when the distribution system 
10 
experiences peak demand. Thus, the distribution networks do not include the additional 
11 
infrastructure that would be required to serve TC and IT customers when the system 
12 
experiences peak demand. This minimizes the cost of the system that must be recovered from 
13 
firm customers.” 
14 
The Commission also stated the following on page 14 of the TC/IT Order: 
15 
“Since the Rate Order, it has become apparent that the downstate region is facing a significant 
16 
and increasing shortage of firm gas transportation capacity.  On November 14, 2018, National 
17 
Grid filed proposed tariff amendments that are intended to provide the Companies flexibility 
18 
in accepting applications for new or additional gas service if they determine there is insufficient 
19 
gas supply and/or capacity to serve the prospective customers in the relevant area of their 
20 
service territories.  While the capacity constraints are more acute on Con Edison’s gas 
21 
distribution network, National Grid’s load is also growing, which underscores the importance 
22 
of continuing interruptible services at reasonable terms.” 
23 
TC/IT customers are an invaluable part of National Grid’s system.  These customers 
24 
are even more important now that National Grid is facing serious system constraints during 
25 
the peak winter season.  Continuing to offer TC/IT service at attractive, cost-based rates 
26 
will be an important part of National Grid’s future system planning and will offer the 
27 
opportunity for the Companies to offer firm service to existing and new customers during 
28 
a time of constrained capacity.

Q.
PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THE MANDATORY SECOND TEST SHOULD BE 
4 
ELIMINATED. 
5 
A.
The addition of a second, unannounced test at the end of January each year commenced in 
6 
2017. The additional test adds costs to customers, increases emissions and creates 
7 
uncertainty. In addition, it is not clear why it is necessary, particularly for customers with 
8 
equipment for automatic-switching controlled by the Companies. The Companies typically 
9 
test their TC/IT customers at the beginning of each winter to ensure that they can respond. 
10 
Once that is established, the tariff imposes numerous obligations on the TC/IT customer to 
11 
maintain adequate alternate fuel supplies and to keep any necessary dual-fuel equipment 
12 
operational. In fact, the Companies have the ability to inspect and test such alternate fuel 
13 
facilities at any time, and the customer has to grant access to the Companies for inspection 
14 
and testing purposes. Finally, as discussed in more detail below, there are significant 
15 
penalties associated with non-compliance, and this alone provides a tremendous incentive 
16 
for maintaining alternate fuel facilities.  
17 
Q.
WHAT IS THE RATIONALE FOR REDUCING THE LEVEL OF THE PENALTY 
18 
UNDER CERTAIN CIRCUMSTANCES? 
19 
A.
The City appreciates the prior revision that changes the unauthorized use penalty from the 
20 
higher to the lesser of (i) two times the sum of the Market Price for natural gas delivered 
21 
to the Company’s city gate on the day of violation plus the transportation rate the Customer 
22 
5562


--- Page 1366 ---
would be subject to if it were a transportation Customer, or (ii) nine times the applicable 
1 
sales rate, using nine times the applicable sales rate is excessive. However, as evidenced 
2 
by the amnesty clause included in the Companies’ tariffs, there may be circumstances 
3 
where the failure to interrupt is not due to a conscious act but, instead, equipment failure. 
4 
For example, if the first “strike” is due to equipment failure, and despite diligent efforts to 
5 
fix the problem, the equipment may not be able to be fixed prior to a second event, 
6 
especially if the second event is in close proximity after the first event. In this case, we 
7 
would request a threshold of within five days of the end of the first event to qualify as 
8 
“close proximity.” The rationale for this threshold is that the inability to fix the equipment 
9 
could be due to long lead times or transportation problems, in particular if there is a 
10 
weekend that falls between the end of the first and the beginning of the second interruption 
11 
event. If that is the case, the imposition of the penalty is not providing any incentive to 
12 
change behavior. Accordingly, and as exemplified in concept by the amnesty clause, 
13 
fairness would dictate that the penalties for the second “strike” should be significantly 
14 
reduced or waived, and the event should not be considered a “strike.” The City 
15 
acknowledges that the waiver of second strike penalty should require submission of 
16 
documentation to show a good faith attempt to fix the equipment.

--- Page 1371 ---
A.
No.  The recommendation to utilize an ECOS study that allocates distribution mains based
1 
on 100% demand should be rejected by the Commission.
2 
Q.
MR. BAUDINO, PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY ALLOCATING DISTRIBUTION MAINS
3 
COSTS BASED ON PEAK DEMAND ONLY IS INAPPROPRIATE.
4 
A.
The two main functions of distribution mains are to deliver gas during the system winter
5 
peak and to connect customers to the system. A properly designed zero-intercept study or
6 
minimum size system study recognizes these two functions by classifying main costs into
7 
demand-related and customer-related costs, which can then be assigned to customer classes
8 
based on their respective contributions to system peak and on the number of customers in
9 
each class.
10 
Peak winter demand is one of the primary drivers of the Companies’ investment in 
11 
gas distribution mains.  The Companies must have sufficient capacity available on their 
12 
systems to satisfy the peak winter heating demand, which is caused mainly by heating 
13 
customers.  If the peak winter demand increases, the Companies may need to invest in 
14 
additional mains to serve the load.  During the non-winter months, substantial excess 
15 
capacity exists on the system.  Use of the Companies’ distribution system during these 
16 
months does not cause additional fixed costs to be incurred by National Grid.  In a similar 
17 
manner to peak winter demand, if the number of customers increases, the Companies may 
18 
need to expand their distribution system investment.  Thus, the number of customers 
19 
connected to the distribution system is another important causative factor in distribution 
20 
main investment.   
21 
Q.
PLEASE CONTINUE. 
22 
A.
The KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Design Panels (“RDP”) described the rationale for the 
23 
5568


--- Page 1372 ---
allocation of distribution mains as follows: 
1 
“Distribution mains are installed to connect customers to the distribution 
2 
system (customer-related) as well as to provide capacity to meet customer 
3 
requirements on the design day (demand-related). Therefore, the cost of 
4 
mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly demand-related.”1 
5 
Similarly, the NARUC Gas Distribution Rate Design Manual  states the following with 
6 
respect to demand or capacity related costs: 
7 
Demand or capacity costs vary with the quantity or size of plant and 
8 
equipment.  They are related to maximum system requirements which the 
9 
system is designed to serve during short intervals and do not directly vary 
10 
with the number of customers or their annual usage.  Included in these costs 
11 
are: the capital costs associated with production, transmission and storage 
12 
plant and their related expenses; the demand cost of gas; and most of the 
13 
capital costs and expenses associated with that part of distribution plant not 
14 
allocated to customer costs, such as the costs associated with distribution 
15 
mains in excess of the minimum size.2 
16 
Q.
IS THE MINIMUM SIZE DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM METHOD AND ZERO 
17 
INTERCEPT METHOD THE SAME THING? 
18 
A.
In concept, yes they are the same.  The minimum size system approach identifies the 
19 
minimum sized distribution main needed to serve customers and then classifies that portion 
20 
of distribution mains as customer-related.  The zero intercept method uses regression 
21 
analysis to identify the cost of a hypothetical “zero sized” main, the cost of which is 
22 
necessary to serve customers connected to the system whether or not they place any demand 
23 
on the system.  While there may be subtle differences between the two methods, both 
24 
recognize that certain distribution main costs should be classified as customer-related and 
25 
allocated based on the number of customers not on peak demand.     
26 
1 KEDNY Rate Design Panel Direct Testimony at page 17, lines 9 through 12. 
2 Gas Distribution Rate Design Manual, NARUC Staff Subcommittee on Gas (June 1989), pp. 23-
24. 
5569


--- Page 1373 ---
Q.
WHAT IS THE RESULT OF FAILING TO RECOGNIZE A CUSTOMER-RELATED
1 
COMPONENT IN THE COST OF DISTRIBUTION MAINS?
2 
A.
The result is a significant misallocation of costs that fails to allocate proper cost
3 
responsibility to the Company’s customer classes.  This point can be illustrated with the
4 
following simple example.  Assume that there is a single industrial customer on KEDNY’s
5 
system with a peak demand of 300 dekatherms (“Dth”).  Further assume that elsewhere on
6 
the system, there is a neighborhood of 750 residential customers with a peak demand of 300
7 
Dth.  In order to connect all of those residential customers to its system, the Company will
8 
have to invest in far more footage of distribution mains for those customers than it would
9 
have to invest in for the one industrial customer.   That extra investment in distribution mains
10 
is due solely to the number of customers on the system, not the peak demands of those
11 
customers.
12 
Q.
HAS THE COMMISSION RECOGNIZED THE APPROPRIATENESS OF A
13 
CUSTOMER COMPONENT IN THE COST OF GAS DISTRIBUTION MAINS?
14 
A.
Yes.  The Commission has accepted the use of a minimum size system concept to classify
15 
and allocate distribution costs in past cases.
16 
Q.
CAN YOU PROVIDE A FEW EXAMPLES OF HOW THE COMMISSION HAS
17 
ALLOCATED DISTRIBUTION MAIN COSTS IN THE PAST?
18 
A.
Yes.  In Case 94-G-0885, a National Fuel Gas Distribution Corporation (“NFG”) proceeding,
19 
the Commission approved both the Administrative Law Judge’s approval of NFG’s use of
20 
the zero intercept method and corresponding rejection of proposals to allocate distribution
21 
5570


--- Page 1374 ---
costs on the basis of demand.3  The Commission noted that: 
1 
The Judge also rejected CPB’s and PULP’s attempt to impeach NFG’s cost 
2 
study. While they criticized the minimum distribution system concept it 
3 
employed, the Judge found that it makes some sense because clearly no 
4 
customer can be served without distribution facilities, and the company’s 
5 
approach effectively emphasized the ‘minimum’ in the minimum distribution 
6 
system.4 
7 
The Commission held that “the true interests of residential customers would not be served by 
8 
over allocating costs to nonresidential customers with competitive alternatives, whose load 
9 
might thus be lost.”5 
10 
Similarly, in Case 93-G-0162, a Niagara Mohawk proceeding, the Commission 
11 
declined to sustain objections to the Company’s cost studies which allocated minimum 
12 
system costs and service line costs on a customer basis.6  The Commission held that the 
13 
“company’s cost estimates are the best presented in the record in these cases.”7 
14

23

11

12 
development strategies as part of rebuttal testimony. 
13

WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO THE PANEL? 
14 
A.
I support a change to the metric. As noted in the NYC Rate Design Panel direct testimony, 
15 
reduction of peak demand usage by firm customers is a paramount concern given the 
16 
Companies’ declared moratoriums on new service. However, I do not have specific metrics 
17 
or targets to suggest at this time, and this effort may be better suited for a collaborative 
18 
involving all parties.

II.
Purpose of Testimony and Recommendations  
1 
Q.
What is the purpose of your testimony?  
2 
A.
The purpose of my testimony is to provide recommendations to improve The 
3 
Brooklyn Union Gas Company’s d/b/a National Grid NY and KeySpan Gas East 
4 
Corporation’s d/b/a National Grid (collectively, “Companies” or “National Grid”) 
5 
proposed leak repair and pipe replacement activities, in order to advance New York 
6 
climate policy to reduce natural gas leaks and methane emissions.   
7 
Q.
Please provide a summary of your testimony and recommendations.   
8 
A.
I recommend that National Grid deploy Advanced Leak Detection (“ALD”) 
9 
technologies to quantify their distribution system leakage, and to use information 
10 
about leak size to prioritize pipeline replacement efforts and to repair the largest 
11 
(i.e., fastest flowing) leaks as quickly as possible. Given that a small number of the 
12 
largest “super emitter” leaks is typically responsible for the majority of total 
13 
emissions, a program aimed at finding and rapidly repairing the largest leaks is a 
14 
relatively easy way to reduce overall system emissions. Because quantifying and 
15 
reducing emissions is a requirement of New York’s recently enacted climate 
16 
legislation, deployment of ALD technologies would provide National Grid a 
17 
straightforward path to compliance. 
18 
I also note that the current incentive structure for reducing the Companies’ 
19 
leak backlog may be counter-productive. ALD technologies have been shown to 
20 
help utilities find more leaks in their system than has been possible with traditional 
21 
technology.  Discovering more leaks would likely add leaks to the backlog. If the 
22 
5582


--- Page 1386 ---
19-G-0309
Direct Testimony of Joseph C. von Fischer 
19-G-0310
4 
incentive structure only rewards the Companies for declining leak backlog counts, 
1 
the Companies are actually dis-incentivized to use a technology that discovers more 
2 
leaks. For these reasons, I suggest that the incentive system be re-examined in light 
3 
of the capabilities of this new technology.

Recent academic findings have demonstrated that observed methane 
1

2

3

4

5

6

7 
found.12 Together, these findings suggest that there are many more leaks than those 
8 
reported in utility inventories. Based on our own published work, and corroborated 
9 
by the PG&E studies, my team and I estimate that, in areas where utilities are using 
10 
traditional leak detection technologies, there are 2.4x as many leaks in the system 
11 
as the utility is aware of.  
12 
And, as I explain in detail below, the motivation for utilities to find more 
13 
leaks is hampered by the regulatory structures for utilities to find and abate leaks.  
14 
Although there exist well-intended incentives for utilities to reduce the number of 
15 
leaks in their backlog,13 an unintended consequence of these policies is that they

Q.
Please explain the role advanced leak detection and data analytics could play 
6 
in addressing these challenges.   
7 
A.
The idea of ALD is that high-sensitivity methane analyzers can be deployed in 
8 
survey vehicles to identify where natural gas is leaking from distribution systems.  
9 
The “advanced” part of this terminology refers in part to the methane sensors using 
10 
a form of laser-absorption spectroscopy14 that can more accurately and precisely 
11 
determine the concentration of methane in the air. In contrast to “traditional 
12 
technology,” the sensors in ALD can quantify much smaller departures from the 
13 
local background concentration and thus find more leaks. Moreover, ALD uses 
14 
advanced data analytics that examine the overall neighborhood patterns in the 
15 
methane concentration to discern when the concentrations are elevated. These 
16 
sophisticated analyses can reveal subtler leak information than traditional 
17 
technologies. Finally, ALD deployments can report not just the presence of a leak, 
18 
but they can also estimate leak size. With leak size information, utilities can 
19

advanced analytics or algorithms that utilize the data acquired from the ALD 
technology to estimate the methane flow rate attributed to a leak indication.

largest leaks fastest. This prioritization means that big leaks are not emitting 
2 
methane for as long, thus reducing a utility’s annual methane emissions. By simply 
3 
re-organizing the timing of repair and replacement to fix the biggest leaks first, 
4 
there is no additional cost.

As other utilities have demonstrated, advanced leak detection technology 
6 
can be deployed in implementing “Super Emitter” programs, which aim to rapidly

detect and repair large grade 3 leaks, leading to significant and rapid GHG

emissions reductions.15 Deploying these methods will also assist the Companies in

IV.   
CSU and EDF Collaboration to Survey Distribution System Leaks
3 
Q.
Please provide a brief overview of EDF and CSU’s collaborative project to 
4 
survey methane leaks from distribution systems, and engagement with gas 
5 
utilities on the use of leak quantification to prioritize pipe replacement and 
6 
leak repair efforts (the “Project”).  
7 
A.
For the last 7 years, I have collaborated with EDF and Google on a unique project 
8 
aimed at gathering data on the location and relative size of methane leaks from 
9 
natural gas distribution systems using three Google Street View (“GSV”) cars that 
10 
are specially equipped with methane sensors.  
11 
The goal of the Project is to document patterns in the location and 
12 
magnitude of natural gas leakage from the distribution systems of different utilities, 
13 
demonstrate the benefits of using leak quantification technology to prioritize 
14 
utilities’ pipe replacement and leak repair activities, and to create the impetus for, 
15 
and facilitate, the integration of this technology into utilities’ regular leak 
16 
operations.   
17 
The GSV vehicles that collected data as part of this initiative used a Picarro 
18 
methane concentration analyzer that has a closed-path design with a sampling 
19 
frequency of one data point every half-second, resulting in samples every 13 feet 
20 
when driving at 20 miles per hour. These vehicles are also equipped with a 
21 
Hemispheres Global Positioning System (“GPS”) Receiver to document patterns in 
22 
5590


--- Page 1394 ---
19-G-0309
Direct Testimony of Joseph C. von Fischer 
19-G-0310
12 
methane concentration in space. Drivers were asked to drive every public street in 
1 
a study area at least twice to ensure accuracy. Re-driving helped confirm the 
2 
persistence of elevated methane readings and characterize their emission rate more 
3 
accurately. 
4 
Data collected in urban systems and during controlled release experiments 
5 
informed our development of a data analysis algorithm to interpret data collected 
6 
through this Project. We conducted a number of “controlled release” studies at CSU 
7 
by releasing methane at known rates and then driving through the resulting plume 
8 
with the GSV car. We analyzed this data for patterns in plume size and shape to 
9 
develop an algorithm that predicts leak size from measured patterns in methane 
10 
concentration. We also validated the leak rate estimates using comparisons with a 
11 
number of more costly and labor-intensive approaches and found that the method 
12 
we used had more than enough precision and accuracy to be used effectively in 
13 
utility leak reduction efforts.

3

5

6

12

gas systems.22 Likewise, across the 6100 natural gas leak indications found in the

13 
A.
Super emitters are the largest leaks on a utility’s system, measuring 10 standard 
14 
cubic feet per hour or greater. A “Super Emitter” Program identifies the highest 
15 
emitting leaks for targeted replacement to satisfy emission reduction 
16 
requirements.47  
17

18

19

Q.
Do the current incentive mechanisms incentivize the Companies to deploy
1 
modern technology such as advanced leak technology that would find and
2 
quantify more leaks?
3 
A.
No. As I noted above, advanced leak detection technology and analytics are
4 
typically able to find many more existing and ongoing leaks than traditional
5 
technologies. At the same time, the current incentive structure rewards the utility
6 
primarily for reporting a lower number of leaks in their backlog at the end of the
7 
year. For these reasons, National Grid is currently disincentivized to use ALD,
8 
which could be expected to find more leaks. At the time of the Companies’ 2016
9 
rate case, ALD was not an established technology. Since that time, ALD has
10 
become a scientifically and commercially established technology, and it has been
11 
adopted by other utilities to find leaks and quantify their emissions.
12 
Q.
Do you have a recommendation to resolve this disconnect?
13 
A.
Yes. The current incentive structure should be revisited, as it ultimately serves to
14 
discourage the Companies from finding more leaks on its system and serves as an
15 
obstacle to achieving New York State climate and methane abatement goals and
16 
policies.
17 
Q.
Please further explain how your recommendation would work in practice.
18 
A.
I recommend that the Companies first complete a methane leak survey of its entire
19 
service territory using advanced leak detection technology. Using the information
20 
gathered from this initial survey, the Companies could then establish a system-wide
21 
baseline leak flow rate. Next, a volumetric leak reduction target could be

III.   
Need for Revisions
18 
Q.
Have there been changes in market conditions over the last decade that have 
19 
affected natural gas utilities?   
20 
A.
Yes. Over the past decade, two major trends have marked the evolution of the 
21 
natural gas business. These two major trends, viewed generally, have had and will 
22 
5620


--- Page 1424 ---
19-G-0309
Direct Testimony of Gregory M. Lander 
19-G-0310
6 
continue to have profound impacts on gas distribution utilities, especially in the 
1 
northeastern United States. The first of these trends is the explosive growth in 
2 
natural gas supply from the Marcellus and Utica shales in the regions of 
3 
northeastern and southwestern Pennsylvania, southeastern Ohio and northern 
4 
West Virginia. The second is the dramatic increase in gas-fired electric 
5 
generation, especially in Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York and New 
6 
England. The second of these trends, driven by plentiful, low-priced natural gas 
7 
has placed strains on the legacy pipeline infrastructure serving the same region. 
8 
The dramatic growth in gas-fired generation has had a particular impact on the 
9 
legacy pipeline infrastructure especially during winter periods when both 
10 
domestic gas fueled heating needs and electric demands have placed simultaneous 
11 
demands on pipelines. In the past, Local Distribution Companies (“LDCs”) like 
12 
the Companies were the primary users of pipelines during the winter. Now, LDCs 
13 
and generators seek to use the same pipelines at the same hours of the day. As a 
14 
result, the flexibility that the LDCs used to have with respect to hourly takes is 
15 
being much more frequently restricted by the pipelines to the LDCs’ specified 
16 
contract rights. At the same time, because the loads of electric generators can be 
17 
as large as (or larger) than many of the LDCs’ take stations for whole swaths of 
18 
their distribution territories, these combined demands are a new and growing 
19 
factor that the industry has to cope with. Thus, LDC capacity planning that 
20 
previously may have viewed its planning criteria as a daily load, now has to 
21 
increasingly plan for peak hours of many more days in the winter than its “design 
22 
5621


--- Page 1425 ---
19-G-0309
Direct Testimony of Gregory M. Lander 
19-G-0310
7 
day.” While in the past LDCs’ on-system peaking resources may have been used, 
1 
or planned to be used, during three to twenty days per winter, now may need to be 
2 
called upon throughout the winter to meet hourly demands that are in excess of 
3 
the LDCs’ hourly contract rights. The significance of this is that even though the 
4 
hours of use of on-system resources may increase, when looked at from an annual 
5 
utilization basis, may not exceed 3% to 6% of 8760 hours per year (i.e., 250 to 
6 
500 hours per year). Given such low load factors and given the cost of 
7 
incremental pipeline capacity, it simply may not make sense to commit to long-
8 
term capacity contracts in light of significant costs, the State’s climate policies, 
9 
and the Commission’s findings on non-pipeline alternatives.1 
10 
Q.
Please explain the consequences of this market evolution.  
11 
A.
In addition to the tightening of pipeline operations which have reduced LDCs’ 
12 
previous flexibility to take gas at a greater hourly rate than their strict contract 
13 
entitlements, producers and marketers have subscribed to large amounts of 
14 
capacity from supply areas both to and past large metropolitan demand centers, 
15 
and, in many cases, all the way from the supply areas to the U.S. Gulf coast to 
16 
supply Liquefied Natural Gas (“LNG”) export facilities. This increase in pipeline 
17 
capacity is a resource, which, if it can flow into (as opposed to past), LDC 
18 
distribution locations can be contracted for by LDCs based upon a price which 
19 
1  Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates, Charges, Rules and 
Regulations of Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corporation for Gas Service, Order 
Adopting Terms of Joint Proposal and Establishing Electric and Gas Rate Plan, Case 
No. 17-G-0460 et al. at page 75 (June 14, 2018) (finding that that non-pipeline 
alternatives should be “explored as a universal practice as an alternative to traditional 
investments.”).  
5622


--- Page 1426 ---
19-G-0309
Direct Testimony of Gregory M. Lander 
19-G-0310
8 
makes it in the supplier’s interest to supply the LDC instead of taking the gas to 
1 
export. Such arrangements would have the effect of reducing the need to build 
2 
additional capacity from supply areas to market, and instead provide and plan for 
3 
the capacity to exist along the “last mile” (i.e., into and from the LDC take 
4 
stations). These combined facts—LDC short duration needs coupled with existing 
5 
capacity moving gas past the LDC demand centers—present an opportunity to 
6 
view capacity planning in a different way than ever before. Thus, a portfolio 
7 
approach, a combination of on-system resources to meet needle hourly peaks plus 
8 
contracted supply otherwise bound for export, have the effect of making LDC 
9 
capacity planning a multi-dimensional exercise. 
10 
Q.
Has National Grid acknowledged the need for refinements to its gas supply 
11 
planning in other jurisdictions?  
12

13 
Public Utilities Commission, National Grid stated:  
14 
In the past, the [Long Range Plan] filings were not controversial and 
15 
tended to raise few complicated issues. But now, the Company needs 
16 
to plan in a way that assures adequate capacity and delivery security 
17 
under supply contracts, the magnitude and implications of which have 
18 
grown substantially. As a result, the current framework and template 
19 
for the Company’s long-range planning is no longer sufficient for an 
20 
appropriate regulatory review.2  
21

23

24 
A.
Yes, the two trends I detailed above have profound impacts on gas distribution 
25 
utilities, both in the northeastern United States and in New York State.

5

6

customers ultimately will be asked to pay. Intervenors historically have not had

A.

5

8

accuracy of projections, and to inform any adjustments needed for future

2 
Q.
Can you describe the appropriate scope and content of a GHG assessment tool 
3 
that would provide the Commission with the information it would need to 
4 
determine consistency with and non-interference with the CLCPA? 
5 
A.
An appropriate GHG assessment methodology would be a holistic analysis of GHG 
6 
emissions within a service territory, taking into consideration all emissions (or at a 
7 
minimum all energy-related emissions) within the geographical footprint of the 
8 
service territory, not solely those emissions that are directly attributable to the 
9 
utility’s own system. Such a holistic methodology would be appropriate primarily 
10 
because of the nature of the GHG emissions limits established in the Act, which 
11 
pertain to economy-wide emissions, including upstream emissions.   
12 
Q.
Is it unreasonable to judge a request by a utility that only owns and operates 
13 
one energy system by such a holistic GHG metric? 
14 
A.
No. It might be unreasonable to judge a utility’s own climate impact by a holistic 
15 
metric, but that is not the nature of this exercise. The purpose of this metric is to 
16 
give the Commission the foundation it needs to find that approving the utility’s 
17 
proposal will not handicap achievement of statewide targets. No methodology 
18 
focused solely on emissions attributable to a specific utility’s system would allow 
19 
the Commission to make such a determination as long-term statewide GHG 
20 
outcomes arise as a result of many factors and actions of multiple actors, all of 
21 
which are interdependent. For example, utility actions and practices affect the 
22 
5646


--- Page 1450 ---
actions and practices of customers, suppliers, and other parties, shaping market 
1 
outcomes that do not arise directly from the utility’s own system. Gas utility supply 
2 
decisions may indirectly affect the level of GHG emissions associated with natural 
3 
gas extraction taking place in various locations; their treatment of natural gas 
4 
customers that are electric generators may affect the rapidity with which the electric 
5 
generation fleet is converted to lower-emitting or non-emitting generation; and their 
6 
practices with respect to line extensions and non-pipeline solutions may affect the 
7 
speed of electrification of building heat. There are also second-order effects; if 
8 
natural gas utilities influence the GHG emissions intensity of the electric generation 
9 
fleet serving their service territory, they will also, indirectly, influence the GHG 
10 
emissions intensity of newly electrified applications, such as transportation and 
11 
electric building heat. Knowing that their rate plans will be evaluated on a holistic 
12 
basis with respect to all these indirect market outcomes aligns the natural gas 
13 
utilities’ business goals with the state’s emissions limits and reduces the effect of 
14 
incentives they might otherwise face to engage in activities that could be expected 
15 
to hinder achievement of the GHG emissions limits. 
16 
Q.
As a practical matter, what steps do gas utilities need to take to enable this 
17 
holistic evaluation? 
18 
A.
Gas utilities need to work with state and local entities to gather the requisite, 
19 
economy-wide information that will make a holistic GHG emissions assessment 
20 
feasible. This will require measuring emissions associated with the Company’s own 
21 
operations, including greenhouse gas emissions resulting from the combustion of 
22 
5647


--- Page 1451 ---
natural gas the Company delivers to customers as well as an accurate assessment 
1 
of methane loss from the Company’s own distribution system. It will require the 
2 
Company to obtain reliable information about the upstream emissions associated 
3 
with the natural gas it delivers, as well as information about greenhouse gas 
4 
emissions in other sectors of the economy. In its fully developed form, this may 
5 
require gathering information from private parties that are not regulated by the 
6 
Commission, such as fuel suppliers, and accounting for methane loss at customer 
7 
premises. Using this economy-wide information, a current status of emissions 
8 
attributable to the Company’s geographical footprint can be established. 
9 
After establishing a current, holistic GHG baseline for its service territory, the 
10 
utility would need to provide projections of GHG emissions for future years based 
11 
on projected economy-wide energy consumption and pertinent emissions factors.  
12 
Projections of energy consumption for each fuel should take into account the 
13 
impacts of energy efficiency, electrification, population growth, and other relevant 
14 
factors. Projections of emission factors for natural gas should take into account the 
15 
estimated impacts from renewable natural gas and biogas and changes in methane 
16 
leakage rate from the natural gas system. Projections of emissions factors for 
17 
electricity should take into account the changing GHG emissions-intensity of the 
18 
generation fleet, as required by the CLCPA. Moreover, since any future projections 
19 
would contain inherent uncertainty and variability, these projections should be 
20 
accompanied by an uncertainty and sensitivity analyses in order to provide the 
21 
Commission with necessary information to evaluate risks.

1

2

3

4

5

13

14

18

In light of the potentially high value of early GHG reductions, the commensurately

Q.
For the years 2014 through 2018, the Companies provide estimated methane 
5

6

11

15 
Detection technology into their business practices system-wide. A comprehensive 
16 
and accurate measurement of methane emissions is crucial to establishing an 
17 
accurate GHG baseline for the Companies and tracking their progress toward 
18 
reducing emissions.
