accurate measurement of methane emissions assist the Companies in efforts to 
2 
meet the goals of the CLCPA?   
3 
A.
As further described in the testimony of Joe von Fisher, such a measurement system 
4 
can provide more accurate and useful tools in the Companies’ leak prioritization 
5 
efforts. Combining advanced leak detection technology with traditional leak 
6 
surveys offers utilities unique insight into their systems that is not possible using 
7 
only traditional leak survey methods. Deploying these methods will also assist the 
8 
Companies in ensuring a more accurate accounting of GHG emissions, consistent 
9 
with the Act.21 Moreover, as stated previously, it is in the best interest of the 
10 
Companies to identify and quantify the largest sources of methane emissions in 
11 
their service territories now to set an accurate GHG baseline because detection of 
12 
such large sources at a comparatively late date could cast doubt on earlier-
13 
demonstrated achievements of GHG reductions and hamper the Companies’ ability 
14 
to have future emissions trajectories deemed to be in compliance with the 
15 
requirements of the Act. 
16 
17 
21  For example, both Companies provide a high level estimate of potential methane 
emissions reductions over the next several years based on each respective company’s 
current facilities assuming LPP retirement pursuant to each company’s proposed 
program.  Gas Infrastructure and Operations Panel, Case 19-G-0309 at page 30; Gas 
Infrastructure and Operations Panel, Case 19-G-0310 at page 29.   
5652


--- Page 1456 ---
VI. 
Prior Efforts to Develop this Holistic Perspective
1 
Q.
Is there any precedent for aligning a utility’s business model with holistic GHG 
2 
outcomes?  
3 
A.
I am not aware of any full deployment of such an approach, but EDF previously 
4 
introduced a similar concept in the Consolidated Edison collaborative that followed 
5 
that utility’s 2016 rate case, where EDF proposed it as the basis of an Earnings 
6 
Adjustment Mechanism (“EAM”). In the collaborative, parties considered various 
7 
ways to use an EAM to align Consolidated Edison’s earnings opportunities with 
8 
favorable GHG outcomes. Most of the discussion in the collaborative concerned a 
9 
metric that would add up specifically identified (“targeted”) emissions-reducing 
10 
activities and reward Consolidated Edison for sufficient levels of such activities. 
11 
EDF encouraged parties to consider a “broad” metric, as an alternative to this 
12 
targeted approach. In the EAM context, the term “broad” provides a useful contrast 
13 
to “targeted,” but other than when referring to the EAM opportunities considered 
14 
in the Consolidated Edison collaborative, the term “holistic” provides a better 
15 
description of the nature of the analysis that I am recommending. 
16 
Q.
Please describe what you meant by a “broad” metric in the EAM context. 
17 
A.
In the context of an EAM, a “broad” GHG metric would assess measured, holistic, 
18 
economy-wide GHG emissions outcomes in the utility service territory and reward 
19 
the utility for the achievement of GHG emissions reductions above and beyond the 
20 
historic trend and/or business-as-usual projections. This would automatically 
21 
recognize GHG reductions of all types, including emissions reductions that result 
22 
5653


--- Page 1457 ---
from improved utilization of utility energy, emissions reductions that result from 
1 
improved price signals, emissions reductions that result from reduced carbon 
2 
intensity of the utility’s energy resources themselves (for example, substituting 
3 
RNG/biogas for conventional natural gas), emissions reductions that result from 
4 
substituting usage of energy provided by a utility for more carbon-intensive 
5 
practices not involving the utility at all (for example, electrification of vehicles, 
6 
substituting natural gas for higher-emitting delivered fuels, or electrifying heating 
7 
applications that would otherwise have been fossil fueled), as well as emissions 
8 
reductions from non-energy sources (for example, capturing fugitive methane 
9 
emissions from waste to produce biogas). 
10 
Q.
Why would a “broad” metric be advantageous for evaluating greenhouse gas 
11 
outcomes in an EAM? 
12 
A.
While an EAM based on a “broad” metric would be more challenging than a 
13 
targeted metric to design as the impact of exogenous factors like weather and the 
14 
state of the economy would have to be isolated – and the proper time horizon might 
15 
be longer than a typical rate case settlement plan – a “broad” metric could overcome 
16 
the various limitations associated with a narrowly-defined targeted GHG reductions 
17 
metric. Compared to the targeted approach, a “broad” metric would be much 
18 
simpler for the utility and its regulator to calculate because it would have fewer 
19 
elements that would have to be calculated solely for purposes of computing the 
20 
metric. The shortcomings of a narrow approach to the EAM are also relevant to my 
21 
reasons for recommending a holistic, emissions-measurement-based assessment in 
22 
5654


--- Page 1458 ---
connection with CLCPA consistency and non-interference. First, the narrow 
1 
approach relies on “deemed” values and does not assess measured GHG emissions 
2 
reductions, which could deviate materially from the values assumed before the fact.  
3 
Additionally, such an approach fails to provide the utility with any incentive for 
4 
ensuring that short-term actions are taken in a manner that is consistent with optimal 
5 
long-term GHG performance. The narrow metric also misses GHG emissions 
6 
reduction opportunities beyond the targeted set of activities, and does not account 
7 
for interactive effects among activities, whether favorable or unfavorable with 
8 
respect to emissions outcomes. It also fails to account for market effects (indirect 
9 
effects that result from the activities that the utility is tracking) as well as any 
10 
activities that are not necessarily known to the utility. For all these reasons, a metric 
11 
based on a set of pre-selected activities, however carefully designed, in effect 
12 
predetermines the utility’s actions, and so fails to provide a significant incentive for 
13 
innovation, including innovation that is needed to achieve the requirements of the 
14 
CLCPA. 
15 
Q.
Did the Collaborative recommend adoption of a “broad” GHG metric as the 
16 
basis of an EAM? 
17 
A.
No, largely for reasons of feasibility. As the Commission observed in the order 
18 
approving the metrics proposed by the Collaborative participants in a Report, “[t]he 
19 
Report…endorses the Broad GHG Reduction metric as a scorecard metric without 
20 
associated financial incentives.  The Broad GHG Reduction metric measures GHG 
21 
reduction in New York City without attributing those reductions to specific 
22 
5655


--- Page 1459 ---
technologies or market activities in the Consolidated Edison service territory based 
1 
on New York City’s annual GHG Emissions Inventory. The Report notes that while 
2 
the parties to the Collaborative agree that the Broad GHG Reduction metric has 
3 
merit, this metric was not selected as an EAM for 2019 due to the complexities of 
4 
developing both a service territory-wide inventory [footnote omitted] and targets to 
5 
meaningfully measure achievement.”22 
6 
Q.
Please describe the complexities of developing a holistic, “broad” metric, 
7 
which made it infeasible to deploy as an EAM in the short term. 
8 
A.
The most immediate barriers were very concrete. Although a comprehensive GHG 
9 
inventory exists for New York City, which is most of Consolidated Edison’s service 
10 
territory, there is no such inventory for Westchester. Additionally, as the 2018 
11 
Report from the Consolidated Edison Collaborative noted, the New York City GHG 
12 
Inventory, which could provide the backbone for such a metric, generally lags too 
13 
far behind to be useful for an EAM on the typical EAM schedule. Other 
14 
complexities would come into play when establishing targets and earnings 
15 
opportunities for a holistic EAM. Compared to a targeted GHG emissions reduction 
16 
EAM, a broad GHG emissions EAM would constitute a far more significant 
17 
departure from conventional performance-based regulation, and would require 
18 
thoughtful consideration of how utility practices can contribute to large-scale 
19 
22  Case 16-E-0060, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates, Charges, 
Rules and Regulations of Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. for 
Electric Service, Order Approving Recommendations of the 2018 Outcome-Based 
Earnings Adjustment Mechanisms Collaborative Report (April 25, 2019) at 4-5. 
5656


--- Page 1460 ---
market outcomes. But in any event, a means to quantify and assess conformity with 
1 
the Act is necessary, and developing those structures sooner (e.g., beginning 
2 
immediately) will improve the Companies’ ability to manage the full range of 
3 
emissions reduction levers available to them and facilitate early emission 
4 
reductions, advancing the goals of the Act.  
5 
Q.
What is the current status of the “broad” metric as it relates to Consolidated 
6 
Edison? 
7 
A.
The 2018 Report of the EAM Collaborative contemplated that it would be reported 
8 
as a Scorecard, and very basic data on GHG emissions from the stationary energy 
9 
and transportation sectors in New York City for the Calendar Year 2017 were 
10 
included in the 2018 EAM report, which was filed in April 2019.23 However, I am 
11 
unaware of any efforts to fill methodological gaps that make it infeasible to include 
12 
the portion of the service territory that is in Westchester or to coordinate with the 
13 
City of New York to expedite the collection and availability of pertinent data to 
14 
address the time lag.   
15 
Q.
Is this holistic approach to greenhouse gas emissions appropriate where, as 
16 
here, the utility under consideration is a gas-only utility, rather than a 
17 
combination utility (as Consolidated Edison is in most of its service territory)? 
18 
23  Case 16-E-0060, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates, Charges, 
Rules and Regulations of Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. for 
Electric Service, Consolidated Edison 2018 Energy Efficiency Earnings Adjustment 
Mechanism Achievement Report (April 1, 2019) at 11. 
5657


--- Page 1461 ---
A.
Yes. First, the holistic approach accurately aligns with the exercise of giving the
1 
Commission the information it needs to determine whether the utility’s proposed
2 
business plans are consistent with and will not interfere with achievement of the
3 
state’s statutory GHG emissions limits. By contrast, any evidentiary showing
4 
limited to the operation of the natural gas system would provide little or no basis
5 
for making any such determination. Moreover, even gas utilities have an
6 
opportunity to contribute – favorably or unfavorably – to GHG emissions outcomes
7 
from sectors other than their own (including vehicular emissions and emissions
8 
from heating buildings that are currently heated using delivered fuels). A holistic
9 
evaluation of service territory emissions properly gives the utility a reason to be
10 
mindful of such opportunities to influence those other sectors when developing
11 
long-term plans, investing in infrastructure, and generally operating its business.
12 
That said, it goes without saying that, compared with a combination utility, a gas-
13 
only utility has fewer levers to pull that affect economy-wide GHG emissions.  That
14 
may be an important consideration when setting targeted levels of economy-wide
15 
GHG emissions reductions for purposes of providing a utility with an incentive in
16 
the form of additional earnings opportunity. However, that consideration is not
17 
particularly relevant where, as here, the question is not whether the utility should
18 
be entitled to additional earnings, but instead concerns consistency (or lack thereof)
19 
with State GHG emissions limits that are themselves not specific to the natural gas
20 
system.
21 
5658


--- Page 1462 ---
Q.
How does your prior thinking about the “broad metric,” and the Consolidated
1 
Edison collaborative experience, inform your recommendations about the
2 
holistic approach to providing evidence for a determination of consistency and
3 
non-interference in the context of the CLCPA?
4 
A.
My prior experience suggests that although the reasons for taking a holistic
5 
approach are compelling, the practical barriers to doing so are substantial. There is
6 
no time to lose in developing detailed, accurate, and timely GHG emissions
7 
inventories for individual service territories, to assess consistency with goals when
8 
the relevant deadlines are upon us and to provide a current baseline and a holistic
9 
way to measure progress in reducing GHG emissions, and for the Companies to
10 
identify and implement practices that facilitate such progress and be recognized for
11 
their achievements in this area by their regulator. These inventories have to be
12 
performed on a recurring basis and cannot be excessively lagging. Although the
13 
utilities themselves will need to provide this information to the Commission to
14 
support Commission approval of their plans, the utilities are not, presently,
15 
especially well situated to create economy-wide emissions inventories. They will
16 
need to work with local and state government entities to create these inventories as
17 
well as with electric utilities in their gas service area. The gas utilities should start
18 
with their systems and get accurate emissions inventories associated with delivery
19 
and consumption of natural gas in their service territory while beginning to work
20 
with local and state government entities and electric utilities on the other
21 
components of the inventory. The CLCPA directs the Department of
22 
5659


--- Page 1463 ---
Environmental Conservation to issue a statewide GHG emissions report within two 
1 
years and each year thereafter.24 The Act also provides guidance on how to develop 
2 
GHG inventories for this report.25 In developing GHG emissions data for their 
3 
geographic footprints, utilities should follow the same guidance to ensure that their 
4 
methodologies are consistent with those being used to develop the statewide 
5 
greenhouse gas emissions inventory and report.  
6 
Q.
Does this conclude your testimony? 
7 
A.
Yes.

of fracked gas infrastructure and hasten the just transition to renewable energy. Since 2011, we
have worked directly with scientists, health professionals, and impacted communities across the

we work with communities to identify and remove barriers to community-owned renewable
energy. We’ve worked with thousands of New Yorkers to prepare and provide public comment
and participate in the regulatory process for over a dozen fracked gas infrastructure projects
across New York.

II.
GAS ISSUES
A. Introduction and Background
Q: What will you address relating to the Company’s business activities? 
A. We have reviewed the Company’s policy overview of its gas business activities, and this
testimony addresses four​ i​ssues relating to these activities.
First, we oppose the Company’s proposals to spend hundreds of millions of ratepayer dollars on 
gas capital investments to replace Leak Prone Pipeline (LPP) instead of retire it and convert 
customers from oil to gas because these proposals conflict with state and city climate goals when 
the unique climate impacts of fracked gas are taken into account.

Second, we oppose the Company’s proposal to invest hundreds of million of ratepayer dollars to 
extend the life of  LNG and CNG facilities.  
Third, we’d like to address that National Grid’s dependence on the Williams NESE Pipeline 
shows a deep disregard for public demand around energy and incorrect calculations of fracked 
gas greenhouse emissions.  
Fourth, taking into account the unique health impacts of shale gas we request funds be used for 
radon testing to insure the safety of the Company’s service.  
Q. What is the overarching context in which the Company’s gas business activities must be
evaluated?
A.Shale gas production in the Appalachia region has increased rapidly since 2012 meaning ​an
increasing amount of the gas supply coming into New York is extracted from the Marcellus
Shale using high volume hydraulic fracking. Nationally, by 2016, 69%  of all wells drilled in this
1
country were fracked and that number has continued to rise. The proposed Williams NESE
Pipeline that much of the Company’s rate case proposal supports would be transporting fracked
gas from Pennsylvania. And in her Direct Testimony  ​Elizabeth D. Arangio confirmed more of
2
the Company’s gas will be fracked gas saying “as supplies from the Marcellus shale region
became abundant and readily accessible, the Companies did not renew expiring long-haul
contracts with Union, TransCanada, and Empire pipelines that delivered more expensive supplies
from Dawn, Canada.” ​Because of the extreme method used to develop gas from the Marcellus
Shale, fracked gas has greater environmental impacts for the climate and on human health  than
3
conventional gas and must be evaluated differently.
B. Gas Proposals Conflict with City & State Greenhouse Gas Reduction Goals
Q.What kind of gas capital expenses is the Company proposing?
A.The company is proposing to replace and expand Leak Prone Pipeline (LPP) and other
pipeline through its Proactive Main Replacement Program, Gas System Reinforcement Program

and Metropolitan Reliability Infrastructure (MRI) Program. In its Future of Heat Panel testimony 
the company says it will replace 225 miles per year for a total of 930 miles over four years. In its 
Future of Heat Panel testimony the Company is also proposing to increase gas demand by 
converting oil customers to fracked gas through its​ Customer Connections Programs adding 
7,000 new customers. The Company claims both these programs will help them meet New York 
State greenhouse gas reduction goals and their own methane reduction goals of 60% by 2035.  
Q.What are New York State greenhouse gas reduction goals?
A:The New York State Energy plan sets a 40% greenhouse gas reduction target for 2030 
and 80% reduction by 2050. The recently passed and signed into law Climate Leadership and 
Community Protection Act (CLCPA) also requires 40 percent emissions reduction by 2030 and 
an increased requirement of 85 percent emissions reductions by 2050.  
Q:What are the city’s goals greenhouse gas emission reduction goals? 
A: Intro 1253 passed by the New York City Council requires buildings over 25,000 square feet 
to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 40% by 2030 and 80% by 2050.  
Q: Can the Company expand gas capacity and meet state and city greenhouse gas 
emissions reduction goals?  
A.No. When the full life cycle of methane leakage is taken into account, gas expansion goes
against city and state goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Methane, the main component of
gas is a powerful greenhouse gas that is 86-106 times more potent a warming agent than C02 for
the first 20 years it’s in the atmosphere. FLIR footage has shown high leakage rates of methane
at the wellhead and all along the transportation route at compressor and metering stations.
Cornell scientist Robert Howarth estimates that when looking at upstream and downstream
emissions from shale gas, leakage rates range between 3.8% and 12% . Even if upstream
4
emissions were not taken into account Howarth estimates the downstream emissions associated
with storing gas and delivering shale gas to market to be 2.5%. With leakage rates like this it is
impossible to meet city and state goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and is more likely
taking us in the wrong direction by increasing emissions.

Q.How are the Company’s assertions about meeting greenhouse gas emission goals
inadequate?
A. When it comes to oil to gas conversions through the Customer Connections Program, the
company primarily bases its claims of reducing greenhouse gas emissions on the fact that when
burned, gas emits less CO2 than oil, but ignores upstream and downstream methane leakage. In
doing so they are presenting an incomplete and misleading representation of greenhouse gas
emissions associated with their projects and their environmental impact. Additional when talking
about reducing greenhouse gas emissions the Company proposes projects to reduce methane
leaks  within their system while at the same time expanding gas capacity and extending the
5
overall life use of pipelines through replacements. Expanding and extending gas capacity will
lead to more fracking and fracking infrastructure needed to transport the gas, thus increasing
overall methane emissions.
Q: Does the Company’s project proposals to limit methane address the issue? 
A: No. While identifying and fixing leaks is important, the technologies proposed to identify 
leaks do not address the upstream emissions especially when paired with pipeline and 
infrastructure enhancements that will overall increase gas use.  
Q:What should the Company do instead of investing in gas capital project to replace 
pipeline and convert customers?  
A:The Company should not invest any new ratepayer funds in expanding gas capacity and 
extending the life of pipelines and should instead invest in gas demand reduction and beneficial 
electrification. The company should look at retiring LPP instead of replacing it and convert 
customers to non-gas alternatives.  
C. LNG & CNG Reliability

Projects,LNG TANK 1 and Tank 2 Upgrade Projects, LNG - Vaporizers 7 & 8 Replacement and 
LNG - Salt Water Pump House.

D: Need for Radon Testing 
Q: What about the Company’s proposal that fracked gas expansion has “environmental 
benefits” is inaccurate?  
A: The Company’s claim their Customer Gas Connections provides “environmental benefits”  
11
and reduces local emission fails to address the unique health threats that come with gas fracked 
from the Marcellus Shale. The Marcellus Shale in northeastern Pennsylvania has higher than 
average levels of uranium and thorium. These elements break down to form radium-226. Signs 
of radon in gas & other fracked gas chemicals in our homes, have been on the ​rise since 200412
when high-volume hydraulic fractured drilling began. Radon is the leading cause of lung cancer 
in non-smokers in the United States .

burdens are greatest earlier in the process so members of the public can provide evidence before 
settlement negotiations begin. We also recommend discovery be available to all members of the 
public not just individuals who have the capacity to intervene as a party. The climate crisis and 
unwanted expansion of fracked gas infrastructure have made New Yorkers more aware of and 
wanting to shape the energy system of New York than ever before.

Q:What did the investigation find? 
A: Nobel’s reporting found that major fossil fuel companies have known for decades that gas has 
high levels of naturally occurring radioactivity and that radioactivity builds up within their 
infrastructure.  Nobel wrote “​In the early 1970s, Exxon learned radioactivity was building up in 
pumps and compressors at most of its gas plants. “Almost all materials of interest and use to the 
petroleum industry contain measurable quantities of radionuclides,” states a never-publicly 
released 1982 report by the American Petroleum Institute, the industry’s principal trade group, 
passed to ​Rolling Stone​ by a former state regulator.​..Despite dire climate warnings, the U.S. 
oil-and-gas industry is in the midst of an epic boom, what a 2018 Department of Energy paper 
calls an “oil-and-gas production renaissance.” Pipelines, power plants, and shipping terminals are 
being developed across the nation at a dizzying pace. But in the excitement of this boom there is 
little mention of the pipes, pumps, and filters in these plants that will become coated with 
radioactivity.”

further denying the radioactivity of the Marcellus Shale saying “the Companies do not accept the 
conclusion asserted in the question that “Marcellus Shale has been proven to have high levels of 
radon and hydraulic fracking uses dozens of carcinogenic chemicals”.

Q: What safety risks exist for Laborers performing work related to natural gas 
20 
transmission and distribution pipeline? 
21 
5701


--- Page 1505 ---
A: Working on natural gas facilities poses many significant risks, both to individual worker 
1 
safety and overall system reliability. Working with natural gas is extremely dangerous and, when 
2 
installing or maintaining gas lines, it is critical to minimize the risk of line ruptures or punctures, 
3 
which can cause accidental ignition or explosion. Even absent ignition, the high pressure in the 
4 
pipes could cause life-threatening damage if there were a rupture. Laborers perform the work of 
5 
digging out a line when it is necessary to access the line for repair, maintenance, or replacement. 
6 
While operators using mechanized equipment dig up the area of within two feet of an existing 
7 
transmission lines, Laborers dig the rest by hand. Given the associated risks, this job requires 
8 
painstaking accuracy. Along with rupture, ignition risks, there are concerns when trenching 
9 
about the potential for “cave ins.” This can happen when Laborers or Welders are in the ditch or 
10 
if Laborers or Welders are walking along the ditch above ground along the edge of the ditch. To 
11 
minimize this risk, Laborers employ safeguards, such as using creating shielding or shoring 
12 
around a trench. There are also risks associated with working in extreme climates, as Laborers 
13 
are frequently required to do. Laborers must constantly be aware of their surroundings, and these 
14 
concerns may be heightened when working in poor weather conditions. Working with and 
15 
directing heavy equipment and machinery presents other safety risks. Laborers are responsible 
16 
for acting as the Operator’s eyes because the Operator can’t see everything going on around him. 
17 
For instance, the Laborer must be alert to unexpected things like a child or dog coming near the 
18 
heavy machinery, and be prepared to signal the Operator to stop immediately. Of course, a 
19 
Laborer must also be alert to the possibility that the Operator could hit a line that had not been 
20 
located correctly. Acting as the Operator’s eyes requires having good communication skills and a 
21 
well-established relationship of trust with the Operator. The reason that the latter is important is 
22 
that each party needs to be able to read the other’s signals. Accidents are more likely to occur if 
23 
5702


--- Page 1506 ---
hand signals are used incorrectly or there is bad communication with the operator, or a Laborer is 
1 
not anticipating properly what the Operator is going to do.  In addition, because most of this 
2 
work happens in the street, there is always the constant danger of workers being injured by the 
3 
surrounding traffic. 
4 
Q: What role does proper training play in ensuring workplace safety and the successful 
5 
completion of assigned tasks? 
6 
A: It plays a very significant role. The need for proper training should be obvious—the work 
7 
these employees are performing is dangerous, and, where done improperly, life-threatening for 
8 
both workers and customers. In recent years, there have been a number of high-profile incidents 
9 
that have highlighted the problems that can occur at gas distribution utilities. Pipeline incidents 
10 
caused by excavation damage can result in fatalities and injuries, as well as significant costs, 
11 
property damages, environmental damages, and unintentional fire or explosions. 
12 
LIUNA is dedicated to making sure its workforce is the most qualified and safest in the industry. 
13 
LIUNA annually invests more than $100 million in training workers in construction and 
14 
environmental skills curriculum. Over the past half-century, LIUNA has developed its own 
15

16 
Through its training program, LIUNA has worked towards offering a standardized course of 
17

18 
In response to new Operator Qualification Regulations, approved under DOT 49 CFR Parts 192 
19 
and 195, LIUNA Training developed Pipeline Safety Worker and Instructor training leading to 
20 
Pipeline Operator Qualification (OQ).

5703

1

3 
Our training goes beyond OQ.  For example, LIUNA offers a 64-hour Pipeline Technology 
4

Q. Why are future approvals for gas expansion unlikely?
1
A. A continuously growing public awareness of the full climate, health and economic
2
costs of burning fossil fuels, including gas, has already risen to such a level that pub-
3
lic authorities, both at the State and City level, have been compelled to enact laws,
4
policies and regulations that require a dramatic reduction in the future use of these
5
fuels. The goal of these laws is to ensure cleaner, healthier air and water, a reduction
6
in climate impacts, and the adoption of more efﬁcient and economical methods for
7
accomplishing those things currently done with fossil fuels such as gas. The result is
8
an unprecedented regulatory and market environment for the Company.
9
In the past, the Company has always been able to assume broad government and
10
public support for increasing its customer base, increasing its capacity to serve, and
11
for making long-term gas capital investments. In the past, the Company has also al-
12
ways been able to assume that the assets they invested in would be used at, or close
13
to, full capacity over all or most of their technical lives. However, our new laws and
14
policies now demand that the Company’s focus shift from seeking perpetual growth
15
to implementing a process of managed decline. The law, policies and public opin-
16
ion now require that the Company focus on reducing the number of customers they
17
serve, reducing the quantity of gas they supply, and crafting a process of managed
18
decapitalization in order to avoid the accumulation of stranded assets as we ﬁnd the
19
useful life of assets ending much earlier than was typical in the past..
20
Q. Why are you so sure that gas sales must fall in the future?
21
A. New York State and New York City have both established aggressive non-optional
22
goals limits on carbon emissions. State law requires an 85% reduction in emissions
23
by 2050 and New York City law requires an 80% reduction. New York City’s limits are
24
deﬁned in Local Law 97-2019 and are expressed using calendar year 2005 as the base
25

Q. Given the current law and policies, why is the Company proposing gas capital invest-
2
ment?
3
A. Because it is all they know to do... The Company has an obligation not only to the
4
public but also to its shareholders. Those shareholders require that the Company be
5
able to show that it has the ability to produce long term proﬁt streams that will beneﬁt
6

7

8
earns an allowed return on equity.
9
Gas utilities are not, in fact, in the “business of selling gas.” At least, that isn’t how
10
they make money. Gas utilities sell gas to their customers at, or near, that commod-
11
ity’s cost. Additionally, even though they spend a great deal to operate and manage
12
their large and complex transmission and distribution systems, those O&M expenses
13
are paid by ratepayers at cost – without a proﬁt. The only way a gas utility makes
14
money in its regulated business is from their allowed return on the equity they in-
15
vest in capital assets. Thus, in order to assure shareholders that there will be future
16
proﬁts, the Company must always be able to demonstrate a plan and ability to ensure
17
that shareholder’s capital is, and will remain, fully invested in capital assets that de-
18
liver a reasonable return on equity. In the past, this has not been a challenge since it
19
has always been possible to obtain approval for additional and ever-growing capital
20
investments. As old assets were retired or depreciated the Company was always able
21
to invest in new gas assets to replace the old. But, times have changed. Continued
22
investment in a large, expensive system whose use is required to decline is simply no
23
longer reasonable.

Given today’s laws, policies, etc., it is clear that continued investment in gas assets

tute an open depreciation study which will include participation from public stake-
9
holders to determine the best cost recovery processes and rates.
10
Q. Accelerated depreciation will increase rates. How can we reduce that impact?
11
A. Given the recent tax law changes, it has become clear that previous rate payers paid
12
too much for deferred Federal Income Taxes. Given that we now know that public
13
policy and law will result in Average Service Lives which are shorter than originally
14
expected, it is clear that previous ratepayers under-paid for asset depreciation. Given
15
that we have both over-payments and under-payments, it would make sense to use
16
the over-payments by previous ratepayers to balance out, as much as possible, the
17
under-payments by those same ratepayers. Thus, the Excess Deferred Federal In-
18
come Tax, which might otherwise be returned to ratepayers as lower rates, should be
19
used instead to reduce the depreciation deﬁciencies which exist now and which will
20
grow in the future.
21
Q. If cost recovery is accelerated, won’t this create windfall proﬁts for the Shareholders?
22
A. No. Accelerated depreciation does not create a proﬁt for shareholders. It simply con-
23
verts the shareholders share of asset values into an equivalent share of capital. If any-
24
thing, one might argue the shareholders would prefer that cost-recovery not be ac-
25
August 30, 2019

5617
5720

Cases 19-G-0309 & 19-G-0310

Direct Testimony
celerated since doing so reduces the amount of equity which is subject to the allowed
1
return on equity. However, failing to accelerate cost-recovery will result in stranded
2
assets. Thus, the shareholders are better off getting their capital returned to them in a
3
form that allows it to be reinvested in assets that are more likely to deliver acceptable
4
returns over time.
5
Q. If the amount of equity invested in gas assets is reduced, how do the shareholders
6

7
A. The Company will either have to ﬁnd ways to invest the equity in non-gas assets or
8
return the equity to its shareholders through dividends or share buy-backs.
9
Q. Other than gas assets, what could the Company invest in?
10
A. As noted before, the company isn’t really in the business of selling gas. They make
11
their money by investing in pipes in the ground. While the gas-pipe business is going
12
away, the pipes-in-the-ground business need not. What needs to change is what is in
13
the pipes. The Company should: Pump heat, not gas.
14
It is clear that district geothermal heating schemes have the potential to serve much
15
of the need once served by gas space and water heating. Such systems are quite com-
16
mon in Europe and the Company has recently operated pilots exploring the technol-
17
ogy. As has been shown, the key capital investment in such systems is that which is
18

19
Like a gas system, a geothermal district heating system is heavily invested in pipes-
20
in-the-ground. It should also be noted that the pipes required for district heating
21
systems will have Average Service Lives which are similar to, if not longer than, the
22
Average Service Lives of the gas pipes that the Company has traditionally invested in
23
but no longer should. Unlike gas pipes, the installation of district heating systems ﬁts

well within existing and anticipated law and policy.
1
Q. This all sounds complicated. Why can’t we wait to deal with these issues later?
2
A. The longer we allow the accumulation of gas asset to continue, the more expensive it
3
will be for ratepayers to support the gas system in the future. The key problem here
4
is that once a new gas capital investment is made, its costs are essentially ﬁxed over
5
the remaining life of the asset. For instance, if the Company invests in a new service
6
connection with a sixty-year life, it will recover one sixtieth of its up-front cost each
7
year, plus the cost of ﬁnancing the remaining un-recovered amount. Then, given that
8
the Company uses volumetric rates to recover its costs of delivery, the ﬁxed costs are
9
spread over the number of units of gas sold each year.
10
Q. Explain why ﬁxed costs are such a problem when sales decline.
11
A. As long as the number of units of gas sold remains unchanged, then the cost-
12
recovered per unit will stay essentially the same each year until costs are fully recov-
13
ered. However, if sales decline, then each year the ﬁxed asset costs will be spread over
14
a smaller number of units of gas than during the year before. That means that after a
15
sales decline, the per-unit cost recovery will increase.
16
For example, if gas consumption were to decline by 80% between now and 2050, then
17
the per-unit cost recovery for an asset installed in 2019 but still in use in 2050 would
18
be 500% greater than it was in 2019.12 This is because, in 2050, the ﬁxed costs would
19
be spread over just 20% of the number of units sold in 2019. If the decline in sales by
20
2050 is only 50%, then the per-unit cost would increase by a still substantial 200%.
21
Q. What is the likely result of the per-unit cost increases that will be driven by reduced
22
gas sales?
23
12Compute the increase by dividing one by one minus the percentage decline. In this case, the formula
would be:
1
(1−.80) = 1
.2 = 5

5722

Bob Wyman
Direct Testimony
A. The result will be a gas “death-spiral.”
1
As gas’ per-unit costs increase, alternatives to gas will become more competitive and
2
those ratepayers who have the capital or credit needed to invest in alternatives to gas,
3
such as heat pumps, will abandon gas and ﬁnd shelter with the cheaper alternatives.
4
However, by abandoning gas, they will drive sales even lower and that will increase
5
the per-unit costs to the point where even more ratepayers decide to abandon gas.
6
The cycle then repeats. As the per-unit costs increase, gas sales will decrease even
7
faster, forcing the per-unit costs increases to accelerate. This is referred to as a “death-
8
spiral.”
9
In time, we will ﬁnd that gas will become known as the “poor-man’s fuel” since the
10
remaining gas users will increasingly be those who can’t afford to abandon it — no
11
matter how much they might wish to. Low and moderate income ratepayers, who
12
have the most limited ﬁnancial resources and the greatest need for more affordable
13
energy, will end up carrying the burden of the stranded assets left behind by those
14
who are ﬁnancially more fortunate.
15

Q.
Please state give a general overview of recent
8

9 
State. 
10 
A.
Recent legislation includes the Climate Leadership and
11 
Community Protection Act, NYISO carbon pricing, NYC Local Law 97, 
12 
and additional efforts to modify NYSERDA or utility-managed incentive 
13 
programs to further buildings energy decarbonization and efficiency. 
14 
Q.
How do you think these initiatives will affect Estates moving
15 
forward? 
16 
A.
My expectation is that these initiatives will require large capital (or
17 
other) expenditures at properties to modify or replace building equipment 
18 
to comply with regulations.  Owners of properties from smaller multi-
19 
family residential to large commercial have substantial sunk costs related 
20 
to natural gas infrastructure and heating plant equipment; which burns 
21 
5742


--- Page 1546 ---
natural gas as a primary fuel.  It is important to consider and calculate the 
1 
full lifecycle costs that Customers will face as decarbonization efforts 
2 
progress.  In addition, customers unable to comply with NYC Local Law 
3 
97 because of the age of the building or other factors may be burdened 
4 
with additional costs such as purchasing renewable energy credits (RECs) 
5 
so as to achieve deductions from the required annual building emissions. 
6 
Q.
Are there any solutions which would continue to use natural gas or
7 
biomethane? 
8 
A.
Yes.  Decarbonizing the natural gas supply is a possible solution to
9 
avoiding the substantial waste associated with the abandonment of any 
10 
portion of the natural gas infrastructure (which infrastructure has been 
11 
increasingly adopted in recent years by Customers) which would be a 
12 
desirable outcome of decarbonization efforts.  Such solutions would 
13 
include the use of renewables such as agricultural or diary industry- 
14 
sourced gaseous fuels like biomethane or hydrogen as discussed below.  
15 
Q.
Do you favor supplementing gas network decarbonization by
16 
heating electrification efforts? 
17 
A.
Heating electrification should be given serious consideration.
18 
Electrification would assist in avoiding expanding the natural gas network 
19 
with its capacity constraints.   One favorable method of managing 
20 
decarbonization by electrification is expanded use of electric domestic hot 
21 
5743


--- Page 1547 ---
water equipment. Specifically, natural gas demand for the sole purpose of 
1 
producing domestic hot water leads to network capacity constraints during 
2 
periods of cold weather. This is caused by the peaking nature of domestic 
3 
hot water demand in the morning coinciding with likely high natural gas 
4 
demand response periods.   
5 
Q.
How would you respond to an argument that carbon-producing
6 
fossil fuels including natural gas are used to generate electricity which 
7 
would produce additional pollution thereby reducing or neutralizing 
8 
decarbonization via conversation of gas-fired hot water equipment to 
9 
electric power?  As a corollary, how would you respond to an argument that 
10 
such electrification may well necessitate the construction of additional 
11 
generation plants and an expansion of the electric gird to accommodate the 
12 
additional usage and demand that would follow electrification?  
13 
A. Taking these arguments one at a time, atmospheric pollution by carbon-
14 
producing combustion is more easily addressed in a baseline electric power 
15 
plant than at individual gas burner tips.  Also, baseload electric generation 
16 
plants in NYS include sources that do not use fossil fuel such as hydro, 
17 
nuclear and utility scale wind and solar. As to the possible necessity for the 
18 
addition of electric utility generation, transmission and distribution plant, I 
19 
note that these would address peak usage and my intent in this testimony is 
20 
that the combination of initiatives and technologies that I am recommending 
21 
5744


--- Page 1548 ---
in this  testimony (when expanded to include electricity - such as electric 
1 
demand response) would reduce peak usage of both gas and electricity such 
2 
that, for this reason, any significant expansion of electric utility plant would 
3 
be unnecessary. 
4 
Q.
Do you see other alternatives to natural gas?
5 
A.
Yes, the conversion of equipment to utilize hydrogen gas, including
6 
blended forms, remains an alternative as I discuss later in my testimony.  
7 
Q.
Is gas demand response an effective means of helping the State and
8 
City to reach its goals? 
9 
A.
Yes, the Company’s pilot gas demand response program should be
10 
significantly expanded to help address the capacity issues and enable the 
11 
State, City and the Company to reach their respective goals for 
12 
maximizing the use of the system and reducing the overall amount of 
13 
fossil fuels consumed. 
14 
Q.
How will these goals be achieved by the use of gas demand
15 
response? 
16 
A.
Gas demand response allows the Company to maximize its gas
17 
network to bring additional commodity gas to its Customers, thereby 
18 
offsetting carbon intensive liquid fossil fuels and reducing carbon 
19 
emissions. A gas demand response program incentivizes Customers to limit 
20 
usage at times of capacity constraints via direct payments to participating 
21 
5745


--- Page 1549 ---
Customers which incentivize them to limit gas use generally and especially 
1 
during such periods. This, in effect, monetizes timely responses during 
2 
system constraint periods.  Customers may utilize electrification and gas-
3 
to-electric switching as a means of achieving demand response goals, which 
4 
not only helps to alleviate capacity limitation issues but also reduces carbon 
5 
emissions.  Peak period gas consumption, most likely driven by domestic 
6 
hot water demand, appears to me to be an appropriate target for 
7 
electrification in the near term.  
8 
Q  
Are there approaches or technologies, in addition to electrification, 
9 
that you believe would be helpful to achieving demand response goals? 
10 
A.
Load shifting is another approach to reducing demand.  An example
11 
of load shifting technology is being implemented by companies such as 
12 
RadiatorLabs, which modify radiator enclosures to store energy and release 
13 
it on demand. It is possible to avoid natural gas consumption during peak 
14 
gas periods with RadiatorLabs’ technology. Pairing this technology with 
15 
advanced electrification technologies can yield significant reductions in gas 
16 
capacity constraints. RadiatorLabs’ technology appears to be a “bridge” 
17 
technology that is able to yield significant reductions in natural gas peak 
18 
load now, while the building sector shifts to low-carbon heating 
19 
technologies. 
20 
5746


--- Page 1550 ---

1

We urge the Parties to consider methods of enhancing or
3 
incentivizing gas demand response via electrification as a means of 
4 
achieving decarbonization goals, reducing overall costs to gas ratepayers, 
5 
maximizing gas network efficiency and utilization, improving local air 
6 
quality, and fostering a market for the development of new methods or 
7 
technologies.  We also urge the Company to expand its existing pilot gas 
8 
demand response program and ultimately make the program permanent.

5747

an overall reduction in fossil-based natural gas consumption.  Alternatively,

Q. Can you provide an explanation of a thermal company?
8 
A. A thermal company is a company that builds, maintains and manages
9 
shared infrastructure (which would include locations in public rights of way 
10 
and on private property) that provides a heating and cooling medium for 
11 
water source heat pumps or similar technologies. A thermal company’s 
12 
distribution facility is most likely comprised of a horizontal water pipe 
13 
network, heat exchangers, pumps and pumping stations, and physical 
14 
connections to customers and heat sources or sinks. The thermal company, 
15 
would provide a platform for sharing thermal energy across various 
16 
customers, and might offer the possibility of establishing a bi-direction 
17 
thermal distribution system similar to the bi-directionality of the electric 
18 
distribution network envisioned by New York States Renewing the Energy 
19 
Vision (REV) plan.  
20 
Q. What other benefits might a thermal company provide?
21 
5748


--- Page 1552 ---
A. A thermal company may also provide a platform for new business 
1 
ventures that provide heat sources or sinks via vertical bore fields 
2 
(geothermal), thermal storage media, or via industrial waste. The New York 
3 
City Department of Environmental Protection (“DEP”) recently established 
4 
an Office of Energy and Resource Recovery, which may facilitate recovery 
5 
of energy resources via thermal energy extraction from the sanitary sewer 
6 
network or production of Renewable Natural Gas from DEP-managed 
7 
wastewater treatment facilities.   If any applicable legal hurdles can be 
8 
surmounted and this can be accomplished by the Company, such a model 
9 
would be complementary to the Company’s goals as expressed in the Future 
10 
of Heat Panel’s direct testimony, the Company’s natural gas business, the 
11 
State of New York’s decarbonization goals and the goals of the Department 
12 
of Public Service. I strongly encourage the Commission to look into 
13 
establishing a regulatory framework for regulated monopolies to establish 
14 
thermal company affiliates. Such a framework, either in conjunction with 
15 
utility affiliates or independently, would provide new private business 
16 
opportunities and hold the possibility of significantly reducing cost risks for 
17 
Customers in light of the State’s decarbonization goals.  
18

Q 
Please discuss the current SC-3 rate and the potential problems 
3 
with its level. 
4 
A.
The Company is proposing an increase in base distribution rates of
5 
over 30% in the tail block for the SC-3 customer class. The overall 
6 
increase in proposed bills to the typical SC-3 customer is pegged at 11%. 
7 
(Exhibit RDP, Schedule 4 Page 8 of 18.). It is important for the Parties in 
8 
this case to realize that this massive increase in base rates is hidden by low 
9 
commodity costs which dampen the overall impact of the rate increase.  
10 
There is no question that the natural gas market has been very favorable to 
11 
the consumer over the past ten years. On the other hand, to expect that 
12 
commodity costs will continue to stay low going forward and yet seek the 
13 
proposed increases in customer bills is inconsistent. It is therefore 
14 
important to call out the real increase here for the SC-3 customer will be in 
15 
the range of 25% on a typical bill. This increase is on top of a greater than 
16 
25% increase in base rates agreed upon in the last rate case. This means 
17 
that base rates will have increased by over 50% in less than four (4) years 
18 
for this rate class, which primarily consists of low- and average-income 
19 
family customers in New York City.  
20 
5751


--- Page 1555 ---
Q. What could happen to the overall bill impact if natural gas prices were 
1 
to return to 10 year or even twenty-year averages? 
2

3 
would then increase by over $1.00 per MMBtu as a result of the purchased 
4 
gas passthrough mechanism which shifts all gas cost risk to the customer. 
5 
Should this return to more historically normal gas prices occur, the overall 
6 
bill impacts of this rate increase would be much larger.

8 
SC-3?

A. The Commission should not be misled by the current environment of
10 
low gas prices in thinking that the rate increase sought by the Company is

likely to be limited to only a 10% increase in rates. The Customers will 
12 
bear ALL the risk associated with potentially higher gas commodity costs 
13 
and, given the uncertainty of deliverability into New York during peak 
14 
periods as well as the uncertainty associated with the price of the 
15 
commodity at the wellhead, any projection of similar gas cost going 
16 
forward is, at best, speculative. The Commission must understand that the 
17 
increase in base rates for this class of customer is exorbitant unless the 
18 
goal of the Commission and other New York State agencies is to raise the 
19 
cost of natural gas delivery in order to shift customer behavior and 
20 
enhance decarbonization goals. If this is an accurate assessment of the 
21 
5752


--- Page 1556 ---
future of heat and/or gas distribution in the state, the Commission must
